qs.q: About how many of the 180 children had the same classification at 12 and 24 months?
o: This is the number of secure infants at 12 months.
qs.x: Correct: Multiply each group by its stability: 108 × 0.82 ≈ 89, 36 × 0.61 ≈ 22, 18 × 0.56 ≈ 10 and 18 × 0.50 = 9, for a total of about 130 children, or 72%. Why the others are wrong: About 90 counts only the stable secure children; 108 is the total number of secure infants; 150 assumes more stability than the table shows. Trap: Averaging the percentages without weighting by group size.

passages.title: Transmission of genetic information from the gene to the protein · passage
text: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are RNAs about 22 nucleotides long that are processed from hairpin precursors and loaded into Argonaute proteins. A loaded miRNA pairs with sites in the 3′ untranslated region (3′ UTR) of target mRNAs. In animals, pairing is usually imperfect; a match between the target and nucleotides 2 to 8 of the miRNA, called the seed, is often enough. Bound Argonaute recruits proteins that block translation and shorten the poly(A) tail, which can lead to mRNA decay. Because a match of only seven nucleotides is required, one miRNA can regulate hundreds of different genes.

miR-122 makes up about 70% of all miRNA in human liver cells but is nearly absent from most other cell types. One of its targets is the mRNA for CAT-1, a membrane transporter for the amino acid arginine, which has seed-matching sites in its 3′ UTR. Researchers used two cell lines: Huh7 liver cancer cells, which make miR-122, and HeLa cervical cancer cells, which do not. In Huh7 cells, they added either a control oligonucleotide or an antisense oligonucleotide that binds and blocks miR-122. In HeLa cells, they added either a control RNA or a synthetic miR-122 mimic. In one HeLa condition, the cells' own CAT-1 gene was silenced and replaced by a CAT-1 gene whose 3′ UTR seed sites had been changed. CAT-1 mRNA was measured by quantitative PCR and CAT-1 protein by western blot, both relative to the matching control.

To make sure the oligonucleotides did not harm the cells, the researchers measured total protein and the level of a housekeeping protein, β-actin, in every sample. Neither changed with any treatment, and the CAT-1 western blot signals were divided by β-actin before comparison.\nT miR-122 has another, unusual role. Hepatitis C virus (HCV) has an RNA genome, and miR-122 binds two sites near its 5′ end, where it protects the viral RNA from degradation. In HCV-infected Huh7 cells, the anti-miR-122 oligonucleotide reduced viral RNA by about 90% within three days.

qs.q: What does the difference between the mRNA and protein changes suggest?
o: Correct: protein changed far more than mRNA.
miR-122 acts on the CAT-1 gene's promoter
qs.x: Correct: Blocking miR-122 raised CAT-1 protein 3.5-fold but mRNA only 1.4-fold, and adding miR-122 cut protein to 0.3 while mRNA fell only to 0.8. Most of the effect is on how much protein is made from each mRNA, with a smaller effect on mRNA stability. Why the others are wrong: Mainly destroying the mRNA would change mRNA and protein about equally; removing miR-122 increased protein, so it normally represses it; miRNAs act on mRNA in the cytoplasm, not on promoters. Trap: Assuming gene silencing always means loss of mRNA.

qs.q: What does the mutant seed-site condition show?
o: HeLa cells cannot take up the mimic
The mimic worked on normal CAT-1.
miR-122 lowers CAT-1 by acting on another gene
The mutant sites would not block that.
CAT-1 protein cannot be measured in HeLa cells
It was measured in every condition.
Repression needs pairing at the seed sites
Correct: changing them removed the effect.
qs.x: Correct: With the mimic present, normal CAT-1 protein fell to 0.3, but CAT-1 with altered seed sites stayed at 0.95. Repression therefore depends on miR-122 pairing directly with those sites in the CAT-1 3′ UTR. Why the others are wrong: An indirect effect through another gene would not be blocked by changing CAT-1's own sites; the same mimic worked in the other HeLa condition; protein was measured throughout. Trap: Overlooking that the only change was in the target's binding sites.

qs.q: Why did the researchers add the mimic to HeLa cells rather than to Huh7 cells?
o: HeLa cells contain no Argonaute protein
The mimic needs Argonaute to work.
Huh7 cells do not express CAT-1
CAT-1 was measured in Huh7 cells.
HeLa cells already make too much miR-122
qs.x: Correct: Huh7 cells already contain large amounts of miR-122, so adding more might change little. In HeLa cells, which lack it, adding the mimic tests whether miR-122 alone is enough to repress CAT-1. The two cell lines provide complementary loss-of-function and gain-of-function tests. Why the others are wrong: The mimic works through Argonaute, which HeLa cells have; Huh7 cells express CAT-1; HeLa cells make almost no miR-122. Trap: Missing why a second cell line was needed.

qs.q: How can one miRNA regulate hundreds of different mRNAs?
o: Each miRNA is many kilobases long
Only a short seed match is needed
Correct: seven nucleotides recur in many 3′ UTRs.
miRNAs are translated into regulatory proteins
qs.x: Correct: Animal miRNAs usually need to match only nucleotides 2 to 8 of the seed. A seven-nucleotide sequence appears by chance in the 3′ UTRs of many genes, so one miRNA can pair with many targets. Why the others are wrong: Mature miRNAs are about 22 nucleotides long; targeting is selective; miRNAs function as RNA. Trap: Assuming that a regulator must match its target perfectly.

qs.q: What does the HCV result suggest about anti-miR-122 as a treatment?
o: It removes a host factor the virus needs
It would have no effect on liver proteins
It would act by blocking a viral enzyme
It would increase HCV RNA by freeing it from repression
qs.x: Correct: HCV depends on miR-122 binding to protect its RNA. Blocking the host miRNA cut viral RNA by about 90%, so the drug works by taking away something the virus needs from the host. Because it also raised CAT-1, it would change the expression of host genes as well. Why the others are wrong: The oligonucleotide targets a host RNA; CAT-1 protein rose; viral RNA fell. Trap: Assuming miRNAs only ever repress their targets.

r: miR-122 mimic, CAT-1 with mutant seed sites

passages.title: Sensing the environment · passage
text: Sound waves enter the ear canal, move the eardrum and the ossicles, and set up a traveling wave along the basilar membrane of the cochlea. The membrane is narrow and stiff at the base, near the oval window, and wide and flexible at the apex. High frequencies produce their largest vibration near the base and low frequencies near the apex, an arrangement called tonotopy. Hair cells on the membrane convert vibration into neural signals. Loud sound can damage these cells, and in mammals they do not regenerate. The ear canal itself acts as a resonating tube that amplifies sound between about 2,000 and 4,000 Hz.

Researchers measured hearing thresholds in three groups of workers at one manufacturing company: office staff with little noise exposure, machine operators with at least 10 years of work in areas averaging 95 dB who seldom wore hearing protection, and machine operators with similar exposure whose earplug use was logged by supervisors at more than 90% of shifts. Workers chose whether to wear earplugs. Each person's hearing threshold at each frequency was measured in a sound booth after at least 16 hours away from work. A higher threshold, in decibels hearing level (dB HL), means worse hearing.

Because hearing tests depend on the listener's responses, the researchers repeated the 4,000 Hz measurement in each ear on a second day. The two measurements differed by no more than 5 dB in 94% of ears, and the average of the two was used. Workers with a history of ear surgery or frequent ear infections were excluded.\nT In a separate test, 20 operators had their hearing measured at the end of an unprotected shift. Their threshold at 4,000 Hz was on average 15 dB higher than their own baseline, but it returned to baseline after 16 hours of quiet. The researchers noted that the average age of the three groups was similar (44 to 46 years).

qs.q: Why is the loss in seldom-protected operators greatest at 4,000 Hz?
o: Low-frequency hair cells are the most fragile
The ear canal boosts sound near this frequency
Correct: those hair cells receive the most energy.
Noise damages the ossicles at 4,000 Hz
The apex of the cochlea receives the most energy
qs.x: Correct: The ear canal's resonance amplifies sound between about 2,000 and 4,000 Hz, so the hair cells tuned to that range receive the strongest stimulation and are damaged first, producing a characteristic notch at 4,000 Hz. Why the others are wrong: Low-frequency thresholds changed little; the apex responds to low frequencies; the passage identifies hair cells as the site of injury. Trap: Assuming noise damages every frequency equally.

qs.q: Where along the basilar membrane is the 4,000 Hz damage most likely located?
o: The apex codes the lowest frequencies.
Correct: higher frequencies map nearer the base.
qs.x: Correct: Because high frequencies vibrate the stiff, narrow base most strongly, the hair cells that respond to 4,000 Hz sit in the basal part of the cochlea. Why the others are wrong: The apex responds to low frequencies; the 4,000 Hz notch shows that damage is localized; the semicircular canals belong to the vestibular system. Trap: Reversing the tonotopic map.

qs.q: What is the most important limitation in concluding that earplugs prevented hearing loss?
o: Thresholds were measured after 16 hours of quiet
Office staff were included as a comparison
Thresholds were measured in a sound booth
Workers chose whether to wear earplugs
Correct: the groups may differ in other ways.
qs.x: Correct: Because workers chose for themselves, those who wore earplugs may differ in other ways, such as noise outside work, attention to health or the specific machines they used. The comparison supports a protective effect but cannot rule out these differences. Why the others are wrong: Testing after 16 hours of quiet removes temporary shifts; a low-exposure comparison group and a sound booth both strengthen the study. Trap: Choosing a design feature that helps the study when asked about a weakness.

qs.q: Why is a temporary threshold shift after a shift an important warning sign?
o: It shows the eardrum has ruptured
Repeated stress can kill hair cells
It means the auditory nerve has been cut
It shows that hearing loss is always temporary
The seldom-protected group had lasting loss.
qs.x: Correct: The 15 dB shift shows that the hair cells were stressed by the noise. They recovered within 16 hours, but repeated stress over years kills hair cells, which mammals cannot replace, producing permanent loss like that seen in the seldom-protected operators. Why the others are wrong: A ruptured eardrum or cut nerve would not recover in 16 hours; the long-term data show lasting loss. Trap: Treating a recoverable change as harmless.

qs.q: Why do even office staff show their highest threshold at 8,000 Hz?
o: Correct: at 44–46 years, some loss is expected.
The ear canal amplifies 8,000 Hz most
Office noise is concentrated at 8,000 Hz
Office staff had little noise exposure.
Thresholds at 8,000 Hz cannot be measured
qs.x: Correct: Presbycusis, the gradual hearing loss of aging, affects the highest frequencies first because the basal hair cells receive the most stimulation over a lifetime. Workers in their mid-forties often show small losses at 8,000 Hz even without noise exposure. Why the others are wrong: Office staff had little noise exposure; the ear canal resonance is at lower frequencies; thresholds at 8,000 Hz were recorded. Trap: Assuming every high-frequency loss is caused by noise.

passages.title: Separation and purification methods · passage
text: Thin-layer chromatography (TLC) is a quick way to follow the progress of a reaction. A small spot of the mixture is placed near the bottom of a glass plate coated with silica gel, a polar stationary phase whose surface is covered with Si–OH groups. The plate is stood in a shallow pool of solvent, the mobile phase, which climbs the plate by capillary action. Compounds that bind the silica strongly, especially through hydrogen bonds, move only a short distance; less polar compounds stay dissolved in the solvent and travel farther. The retardation factor, Rf, is the distance a spot travels divided by the distance the solvent front travels.

A student reduced benzophenone, a ketone, to diphenylmethanol, a secondary alcohol, using sodium borohydride (NaBH₄) in methanol at room temperature. To follow the reaction, the student removed a drop of the mixture at 0, 10 and 30 minutes and spotted it on silica plates next to standards of pure starting material and pure product. In one lane, the 10-minute sample was spotted directly on top of a spot of the product standard, a technique called co-spotting. The plates were run in 4:1 hexane:ethyl acetate, and the solvent front traveled 8.0 cm on every plate. Spots were seen under ultraviolet light, where both compounds absorb because of their aromatic rings.

Before choosing the solvent, the student ran both standards in three hexane:ethyl acetate mixtures. Ethyl acetate is more polar than hexane, so mixtures richer in it compete more effectively with the compounds for the silica surface.

A single plate cannot prove what a compound is. Two different substances can happen to have the same Rf in one solvent, so a match is stronger evidence when it holds in more than one solvent system. For a firm identification, chemists confirm the structure by a spectroscopic method such as nuclear magnetic resonance or infrared spectroscopy.\nT After 30 minutes, the student added dilute acid to destroy the remaining NaBH₄, extracted the product into ethyl acetate and evaporated the solvent, leaving white crystals that gave a single spot at Rf 0.35.

qs.q: What is the Rf of diphenylmethanol on the reaction plates?
o: This divides by the benzophenone distance.
This is the Rf of benzophenone.
This divides the front by the spot distance.
qs.x: Correct: Rf = distance traveled by the spot ÷ distance traveled by the solvent front = 2.8 ÷ 8.0 = 0.35, which matches the value in the solvent table. Why the others are wrong: 0.54 uses the wrong denominator; 0.65 belongs to benzophenone; Rf cannot exceed 1. Trap: Inverting the ratio.

qs.q: Why does diphenylmethanol travel a shorter distance than benzophenone?
o: Its O–H group binds the silica
Correct: stronger binding to the stationary phase.
It has a much larger molar mass
The two masses differ by only 2 g/mol.
It does not absorb ultraviolet light
It is less polar than benzophenone
qs.x: Correct: Diphenylmethanol has an O–H group that can donate a hydrogen bond to the Si–OH groups of the silica. Benzophenone's carbonyl can only accept hydrogen bonds. The alcohol binds the plate more strongly and moves less. Why the others are wrong: Reduction adds just two hydrogens; the alcohol is the more polar compound; both compounds were visible under UV. Trap: Explaining TLC movement by mass rather than by polarity.

qs.q: Which solvent gives the best separation of the two compounds?
o: 9:1, because both spots stay near the origin
Spots near the origin are poorly resolved.
All three separate the compounds equally well
4:1, because the Rf values differ the most
1:1, because both spots travel the farthest
They crowd near the solvent front.
qs.x: Correct: The gap in Rf is 0.26 in 9:1, 0.30 in 4:1 and 0.14 in 1:1. The 4:1 mixture also places both spots in the middle of the plate, where they are easiest to see and measure. Why the others are wrong: In 9:1 the product barely leaves the origin; in 1:1 both compounds run close to the front and close to each other; the separations clearly differ. Trap: Choosing the solvent that makes spots travel farthest.

qs.q: What does the 30-minute plate show?
o: Both compounds are present in equal amounts
The starting material spot is gone.
The benzophenone has been used up
Correct: only the product spot remains.
qs.x: Correct: At 30 minutes, the spot at 5.2 cm (benzophenone) is gone and only the spot at 2.8 cm (diphenylmethanol) remains, so the starting material has been converted. Why the others are wrong: A reaction clearly occurred; the product spot is still there; a single spot means one compound. Trap: Overlooking that a missing spot is as informative as a new one.

qs.q: What does the co-spotted lane add to the analysis?
o: It shows that NaBH₄ has been used up
NaBH₄ is not the spot being tested.
It confirms the new spot is the product
Correct: one round spot means the same Rf.
It measures how much product has formed
TLC spots are not quantitative here.
It shows the product is more polar than the solvent
qs.x: Correct: If the new spot in the reaction mixture were a different compound with a similar Rf, co-spotting it with the standard would usually give an elongated or double spot. A single round spot at 2.8 cm shows that the two run identically, supporting the conclusion that the new spot is diphenylmethanol. Why the others are wrong: Spot intensity on a simple plate gives only a rough sense of amount; NaBH₄ does not appear on the plate; co-spotting compares the sample with a standard, not with the solvent. Trap: Assuming that matching Rf values in separate lanes always proves identity.

r: Reaction, 10 min co-spotted with product standard

passages.title: Principles of bioenergetics and fuel molecule metabolism · passage
text: In most cells, the electron transport chain pumps protons out of the mitochondrial matrix, and the protons flow back through ATP synthase, driving ATP production. The rate of oxygen use is therefore tied to the demand for ATP: when ADP is scarce, ATP synthase slows, the proton gradient builds up, and electron transport slows. Brown adipose tissue (BAT), found in newborns, hibernating animals and small amounts in adults, breaks this link. Its mitochondria contain uncoupling protein 1 (UCP1), which lets protons return to the matrix without passing through ATP synthase. The energy of the gradient is released as heat. Purine nucleotides such as GDP bind UCP1 and close it, while fatty acids released during cold exposure open it.

Researchers housed wild-type mice and mice lacking the UCP1 gene (UCP1 knockout) either at 30 °C, where mice do not need to produce extra heat, or at 4 °C for 7 days, after which BAT had grown and become more active. They isolated BAT mitochondria and measured oxygen use with succinate as the fuel, first without ADP, then with ADP, and in a separate sample without ADP but with GDP. They also measured the membrane potential across the inner membrane, a measure of the proton gradient, without ADP.

The researchers checked that the isolated mitochondria were intact before each measurement by confirming that oxygen use rose when ADP was added and fell again once the added ADP had been converted to ATP. Preparations that did not show this response were discarded.\nT In a separate experiment, mice that had been kept at 30 °C were moved directly to 4 °C. After 6 hours, wild-type mice had a body temperature of 35.5 °C, while UCP1 knockout mice had cooled to 29 °C and were shivering vigorously. Knockout mice that were first moved to 18 °C for a week before the 4 °C test maintained their body temperature, a finding the researchers attributed to slower adaptations such as increased shivering capacity.

qs.q: Why is oxygen use high without ADP in wild-type mitochondria from cold-adapted mice?
o: Correct: the gradient keeps being used up.
Succinate is oxidized without the chain
ATP synthase keeps working without ADP
It needs ADP to make ATP.
qs.x: Correct: Without ADP, ATP synthase is idle, so in ordinary mitochondria the proton gradient builds and slows electron transport. In cold-adapted BAT, protons leak back through abundant UCP1, so the gradient never builds up and oxygen use stays high (210). Why the others are wrong: ATP synthase requires ADP; oxygen is consumed only by the electron transport chain; GDP inhibits UCP1. Trap: Assuming oxygen use always reflects ATP production.

qs.q: What happens when GDP is added to these mitochondria?
o: Oxygen use rises because GDP is a fuel
Closing the leak would raise it.
Oxygen use falls as the leak closes
qs.x: Correct: GDP binds and closes UCP1. Protons can no longer leak back, the gradient builds up, and electron transport slows, cutting oxygen use from 210 to 70. Why the others are wrong: GDP is not oxidized as fuel in this system; ATP synthase still needs ADP; closing the leak would allow the gradient, and the potential, to rise. Trap: Treating every nucleotide as an energy source.

qs.q: Why is the membrane potential lowest in cold-adapted wild-type mitochondria?
o: ADP was present in these samples
The potential was measured without ADP.
qs.x: Correct: Each proton that returns through UCP1 lowers the gradient, so mitochondria with the most UCP1 have the lowest potential (120 mV). The knockout, with no UCP1, keeps the highest potential (175 mV). Why the others are wrong: More pumping alone would raise the potential; the knockout lacks UCP1; ADP was absent. Trap: Linking high oxygen use with a high membrane potential.

qs.q: Why did knockout mice moved directly to 4 °C become cold?
o: They could not make heat in brown fat
They had no mitochondria in brown fat
Their brown fat used too much oxygen
qs.x: Correct: Without UCP1, brown fat cannot run electron transport freely to release heat, so the mice depended on shivering alone and their body temperature fell to 29 °C. Gradual adaptation allowed other mechanisms to compensate. Why the others are wrong: The mice did shiver; knockout BAT oxygen use was low; their mitochondria were present and functional. Trap: Assuming shivering alone can defend body temperature in sudden cold.

qs.q: 2,4-Dinitrophenol carries protons across the inner membrane. Which effect would it most likely have in a person?
o: No effect, because it is not a protein
It acts as a chemical uncoupler.
More oxygen use and a higher temperature
Correct: an uncontrolled leak, like UCP1 everywhere.
Higher ATP production in every cell
Lower oxygen use because the chain stops
qs.x: Correct: Dinitrophenol lets protons cross the inner membrane in every cell, not just in brown fat. Electron transport speeds up, ATP synthesis falls, and the energy is released as heat, which can cause dangerous overheating. It was once sold as a weight-loss drug and caused deaths. Why the others are wrong: ATP production falls because protons bypass ATP synthase; electron transport speeds up rather than stopping; an uncoupler does not need to be a protein. Trap: Thinking faster fuel burning means more ATP.

h: O₂ use, no ADP (nmol/min per mg)

passages.title: Processes of cell division, differentiation, and specialization · passage
text: A cell that has damaged DNA must repair it before replication, or the damage will be copied into both daughter cells. The protein p53 coordinates this response. After damage, p53 escapes its normal rapid destruction and accumulates. It acts as a transcription factor, switching on genes such as CDKN1A, which encodes the protein p21. p21 binds and inhibits cyclin-dependent kinases, so the cell cannot pass from G1 into S phase. If the damage is too severe to repair, p53 also switches on genes that trigger apoptosis, a controlled form of cell death in which the cell shrinks, its DNA is cut into small fragments, and the remains are cleared by neighboring cells.

Researchers compared two human cell lines: line A, which carries two normal copies of TP53, and line B, which carries a mutation in both copies that prevents the protein from binding DNA. Both lines were exposed to 5 gray of ionizing radiation, which creates double-strand breaks. Twenty-four hours later, the fraction of cells in each phase of the cycle was measured by flow cytometry, which sorts cells by DNA content. Apoptotic cells were counted by a stain that detects cut DNA ends.

Protein levels were also measured. Four hours after radiation, line A showed a sixfold rise in p53 protein and a fivefold rise in p21, while line B showed a fivefold rise in p53 protein but no rise in p21. TP53 mRNA levels changed little in either line.

The researchers noted that flow cytometry measures DNA content rather than the phase directly: a cell with the DNA content of G1 could in principle be an arrested cell or one preparing to divide. To check their reading of the data, they repeated the experiment with a chemical that labels cells actively copying DNA, and found that the fraction of labeled cells matched the S-phase fractions in the table.\nT When line B was given a plasmid carrying a normal TP53 gene before radiation, the G1 fraction rose to 81% and apoptosis to 15%, close to the values for line A.

qs.q: Why did line A accumulate in G1 after radiation?
o: The cells entered mitosis and were held there
p53 directly copied the damaged DNA
p21 blocked the kinases that start S phase
Radiation destroyed the cells in S phase
S-phase cells would appear as apoptotic.
qs.x: Correct: Radiation raised p53, which switched on CDKN1A. The p21 protein then inhibited the cyclin-dependent kinases that drive the G1-to-S transition, so cells piled up in G1 (86%) while the S fraction fell to 4%. Why the others are wrong: Selective killing of S-phase cells would not raise the G1 percentage this much and would show in the apoptosis count; p53 regulates transcription rather than replicating DNA; the G2/M fraction decreased. Trap: Assuming any cell cycle arrest happens at mitosis.

qs.q: What does the rise in p53 protein without a rise in TP53 mRNA show?
o: p53 protein is made from p21 mRNA
Each protein has its own gene.
TP53 is transcribed faster after damage
p21 rose only in line A.
p53 is controlled by its destruction rate
Correct: less degradation, not more transcription.
qs.x: Correct: If more protein appears while its mRNA stays constant, the change must come after transcription. Normally p53 is tagged for destruction within minutes; DNA damage blocks this tagging, so the existing protein accumulates. Why the others are wrong: The mRNA did not increase; p21 is made from its own mRNA; p21 did not rise in line B, so the effect is not a general one. Trap: Assuming more protein always means more transcription.

qs.q: Why did p21 fail to rise in line B?
o: Correct: it cannot act as a transcription factor.
Line B lacks the CDKN1A gene
Nothing suggests the gene is missing.
Line B does not make p53 protein
p21 rose normally in line A.
qs.x: Correct: Line B's p53 accumulates after damage but carries a mutation that prevents it from binding DNA. Without binding, it cannot switch on CDKN1A, so no extra p21 is made and the G1 checkpoint does not engage. Why the others are wrong: Line B makes plenty of p53 protein; the plasmid rescue shows the downstream machinery works; p21 rose in line A under the same radiation. Trap: Equating the amount of a transcription factor with its activity.

qs.q: What is the purpose of giving line B a normal TP53 gene?
o: To repair the radiation damage directly
To increase the amount of p53 protein
To show that plasmids cause G1 arrest
Arrest depended on the gene carried.
To show the defect lies in TP53
Correct: restoring it restored the response.
qs.x: Correct: Line B differs from line A in many ways besides TP53. Putting a working copy of the gene back and seeing the G1 arrest (81%) and apoptosis (15%) return shows that the missing function of p53 explains the difference. Why the others are wrong: The problem is the quality of p53, not its quantity; p53 does not repair DNA itself; an empty plasmid would not produce this effect. Trap: Treating a rescue experiment as just another treatment.

qs.q: Why does losing p53 function contribute to cancer?
o: Cells divide more slowly without p53
Correct: the checkpoint and apoptosis are lost.
Cells without p53 cannot replicate DNA
Line B had 25% of cells in S phase.
p53 normally promotes entry into S phase
qs.x: Correct: Without working p53, a cell with broken DNA neither pauses to repair nor dies. Line B kept cycling after radiation (52% G1, 25% S) with only 3% apoptosis. Over many divisions, such cells collect mutations that can drive cancer, which is why TP53 is mutated in about half of human tumors. Why the others are wrong: Line B divided normally; p53 restrains the cycle after damage; DNA replication continued. Trap: Assuming a growth-restraining gene must be needed for growth.

passages.title: Principles of bioenergetics and fuel molecule metabolism · passage
text: Researchers at the University of Greenfield investigated the effect of light intensity on the photosynthetic rate of *Arabidopsis thaliana*. The experiment was conducted in a controlled growth chamber where plants were exposed to four different light intensities: 100, 200, 400, and 800 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹. After a 48‑hour acclimation period, the net CO₂ assimilation rate was measured using a portable infrared gas analyzer. The data were summarized in Table 1 below. The researchers noted a nonlinear increase in photosynthetic rate with light intensity, suggesting the presence of a light saturation point. They also observed that the standard deviation increased at the highest light intensity, indicating greater variability among individual plants. The authors concluded that optimizing light intensity could enhance crop yield, but further studies are needed to determine the optimal intensity for different cultivars.

qs.q: Based on Table 1, which of the following best describes the relationship between light intensity and photosynthetic rate?
o: Photosynthetic rate increases linearly with light intensity.
Rate rises steeply at low intensity, then gains diminish as intensity increases.
Photosynthetic rate decreases at high intensities due to photoinhibition.
Photosynthetic rate is independent of light intensity.
qs.x: Correct: B) The rate rises 2.6 units from 100 to 200, 3.3 from 200 to 400, but only 1.4 from 400 to 800 even though intensity doubles, so gains diminish as the curve approaches saturation. Why the others are wrong: A) Equal increments per light increment are not seen; the slope falls. C) The rate at 800 (10.5) is higher than at 400 (9.1), so there is no decrease. D) The rate changes more than threefold across the range. Trap: Assuming a linear relationship (Option A) ignores the diminishing gains at higher intensities; calling the curve fully flat (a plateau) overlooks that the rate still rose from 9.1 to 10.5.

qs.q: If the researchers wanted to determine whether light intensity has a statistically significant effect on photosynthetic rate, which experimental design element should they include?
o: Randomly assign plants to each light intensity group.
Use only a single plant per intensity to reduce variability.
Measure photosynthetic rate at only the highest light intensity.
Exclude the 200 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹ group to simplify analysis.
qs.x: Random assignment controls for confounding variables and ensures that differences in photosynthetic rate are attributable to light intensity rather than plant-to-plant variation. Trap: Using a single plant per group (Option B) would increase sampling error and reduce statistical power.

qs.q: Calculate the percent increase in average photosynthetic rate from 100 to 200 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹.
qs.x: Correct: A) Percent increase = (5.8 - 3.2) / 3.2 x 100 = 81.25%, about 81.3%. Why the others are wrong: B) 125.0% does not follow from the table values. C) 44.8% divides the 2.6 change by the final value (5.8) instead of the baseline. D) 68.8% does not follow from the table values. Trap: Dividing the change by the final value (2.6 / 5.8 = 44.8%, option C) instead of the baseline understates the increase.

qs.q: Which of the following statements is a common misconception about the data presented?
o: The standard deviation at 800 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹ indicates higher variability among plants.
The increase from 400 to 800 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹ is smaller than from 100 to 200 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹.
The photosynthetic rate at 800 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹ is the highest among all groups.
The data suggest a linear relationship between light intensity and photosynthetic rate.
qs.x: The data clearly show a nonlinear, saturating relationship, not a linear one. Option D is the misconception. Trap: Option B might mislead students into thinking the rate decreases, but it actually increases, just at a slower rate.

qs.q: At 800 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹ the net CO₂ assimilation rate rises only from 9.1 to 10.5 µmol CO₂ m⁻² s⁻¹ even though light doubles. Which factor most likely limits photosynthesis at this point?
o: The rate of photon absorption by chlorophyll, which is still proportional to light intensity
The capacity of the Calvin cycle (Rubisco activity and CO₂ supply) to use the ATP and NADPH being generated
The amount of O₂ available to the light-dependent reactions
The number of water molecules in the thylakoid lumen
qs.x: At saturating light the light-dependent reactions supply ATP and NADPH faster than the Calvin cycle can consume them, so carbon fixation (Rubisco activity, CO₂ supply, RuBP regeneration) becomes limiting and the light-response curve plateaus. Trap: Option A treats light absorption as limiting, but that is true only on the linear, light-limited part of the curve.

passages.title: Sensing the environment · passage
text: Color vision depends on three cone types with peak sensitivities near 420 nm (S), 530 nm (M) and 560 nm (L). Color is coded by comparing their outputs (trichromatic theory), and opponent processing in the retina and thalamus compares red with green and blue with yellow. Red-green color blindness usually results from missing or altered L or M pigments encoded on the X chromosome.
Researchers tested color matching in four participants (Table 1).

qs.q: Why can participant B not distinguish red from green?
o: The M and L comparison is missing
Red light does not reach the retina
Rods cannot detect color at all
Rods are irrelevant to this comparison.
qs.x: Correct: Red-green discrimination depends on comparing signals from the M and L cones; with only one of them, the comparison cannot be made. Why the others are wrong: S cones are present; rods do not mediate color; light reaches the retina. Trap: Assuming a specific cone detects a specific color by itself.

qs.q: Why can participants B and C still tell blue from yellow?
o: Yellow light stimulates only S cones
Yellow stimulates M and L cones more.
Blue and yellow are detected by rods
The S cone output can be compared
They have all three cone types
qs.x: Correct: The blue-yellow channel compares S cone output with the combined output of the remaining longer-wavelength cone, which is intact in both. Why the others are wrong: Each lacks a cone type; rods do not encode color; yellow stimulates longer-wavelength cones. Trap: Expecting the loss of one channel to remove all color vision.

qs.q: How does trichromatic theory explain color perception?
o: A single receptor cannot distinguish color.
The lens separates light into colors
Colors are detected by rods at low light
qs.x: Correct: Any wavelength produces a characteristic pattern of activity across the three cone types, and the brain reads the ratios as color. Why the others are wrong: A single receptor type cannot separate wavelength from intensity; rods are monochromatic; the lens focuses. Trap: Thinking each cone signals one specific color.

qs.q: Why is red-green color blindness more common in men?
o: Lenses do not differ this way.
Correct: men have one X chromosome.
The condition is caused by testosterone
qs.x: Correct: The M and L pigment genes lie on the X chromosome, so a single variant allele affects men, while women usually have a normal copy on the second X. Why the others are wrong: Cone counts, lens filtering and hormones are not the cause. Trap: Looking for a physiological rather than a genetic explanation.

qs.q: What does participant D's result suggest?
o: Light and form are still detected.
S cones alone detect blue and yellow
One cone type gives full color vision
Correct: comparison is impossible with one.
qs.x: Correct: With only one cone type, every wavelength produces a signal that differs only in magnitude, which cannot be separated from a change in brightness. Why the others are wrong: One type is insufficient; vision for form remains; both color channels failed. Trap: Confusing loss of color vision with blindness.

passages.title: Sensing the environment · passage
text: Signal detection theory separates two influences on a yes-or-no judgment. Sensitivity (d′) reflects how well a person can tell signal trials from noise trials. The criterion (c) reflects how willing the person is to say "yes." A criterion of 0 is neutral, a negative value is liberal (more "yes" responses), and a positive value is conservative. Both are calculated from the hit rate (the proportion of signal trials called "yes") and the false-alarm rate (the proportion of noise trials called "yes"). Sensitivity is unaffected by shifts in criterion.

Researchers asked 40 radiology residents to judge whether each of 200 chest X-rays showed a lung nodule. Half of the images contained a nodule confirmed by later CT scanning. In the first session, held at the start of a day shift, residents read one block under neutral instructions. They then read one block after being told that missed nodules lead to delayed cancer diagnoses (liberal instructions) and one block after being told that false alarms lead to unnecessary biopsies (conservative instructions). Block order was counterbalanced. In a second session, the same residents read a neutral block at the end of a 12-hour overnight shift. Mean results are shown in Table 1.

The residents also rated their confidence on each image from 1 (certainly no nodule) to 5 (certainly a nodule). By treating each confidence level as a separate cutoff, the researchers plotted a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve for each block, showing the hit rate against the false-alarm rate at each cutoff. The three start-of-shift curves fell almost on top of one another, while the end-of-shift curve lay closer to the diagonal line that represents guessing. A curve that bends farther toward the upper left corner indicates higher sensitivity at every criterion.\nT The researchers noted that hospitals often track only the number of nodules a reader finds, and that this figure rose after the liberal instructions.

qs.q: What did the change from neutral to liberal instructions mainly alter?
o: The same kinds of images were used.
Correct: c fell while d′ barely changed.
The number of images that contained a nodule
Half the images had nodules in every block.
The residents' ability to see nodules
qs.x: Correct: Under liberal instructions both hits (0.80 to 0.90) and false alarms (0.20 to 0.36) rose, which is the pattern of a lower criterion. Sensitivity was essentially unchanged (1.68 versus 1.64), so the residents became more willing to say "yes" without becoming better at telling the two kinds of images apart. Why the others are wrong: d′ did not improve; the proportion of nodule images was fixed by design; nothing suggests the images changed. Trap: Reading more hits as better detection.

qs.q: What best describes the effect of the overnight shift?
o: The criterion became much more liberal
c moved slightly in the conservative direction.
Sensitivity rose but residents said "yes" less often
Both sensitivity and criterion were unchanged
Sensitivity fell, with little change in criterion
qs.x: Correct: At the end of the shift, hits fell and false alarms rose at the same time. Moving in opposite directions like this is the sign of reduced sensitivity, and d′ dropped from 1.68 to 1.05. The criterion moved only from 0.00 to +0.12. Why the others are wrong: c became slightly more conservative, not liberal; d′ clearly changed; sensitivity went down, not up. Trap: Looking only at the hit rate, which also falls with a conservative shift.

qs.q: The hospital wants residents to miss fewer nodules without making more false alarms. Which approach is most likely to work?
o: Rewarding residents for each nodule they report
Telling residents to report only obvious nodules
Improving image quality or adding rest breaks
Telling residents to report any doubtful shadow
qs.x: Correct: Raising hits while lowering false alarms requires better sensitivity. Clearer images make signal and noise easier to tell apart, and the end-of-shift data show that fatigue lowers d′, so rest should help. Why the others are wrong: Reporting doubtful shadows and paying per nodule both shift the criterion and trade misses for false alarms, as the liberal block shows; reporting only obvious nodules does the reverse. Trap: Assuming that instructions or incentives can improve both kinds of error at once.

qs.q: A resident has a hit rate of 0.95 and a false-alarm rate of 0.60. Compared with the start-of-shift neutral average, this resident most likely has:
o: a more conservative criterion and higher sensitivity
The false-alarm rate is very high.
a more liberal criterion and lower sensitivity
Correct: many false alarms and a smaller gap.
the same criterion and higher sensitivity
a more liberal criterion and higher sensitivity
The hit and false-alarm rates are close together.
qs.x: Correct: Saying "yes" to 60% of normal images shows a liberal criterion. Sensitivity depends on the distance between hits and false alarms on a z-scale; z(0.95) ≈ 1.64 and z(0.60) ≈ 0.25, so d′ ≈ 1.39, below the neutral average of 1.68. Why the others are wrong: Very frequent false alarms rule out a conservative or unchanged criterion; despite the high hit rate, sensitivity is lower than average. Trap: Treating a high hit rate as proof of high sensitivity.

qs.q: Why might counting nodules found be a misleading measure of reader quality?
o: It rises with a liberal criterion alone
Correct: more "yes" responses raise the count.
It cannot rise when instructions change
The count rose under liberal instructions.
It ignores the number of images each resident read
Every resident read the same number.
It depends only on sensitivity, not on criterion
qs.x: Correct: A count of nodules found equals the number of hits, and hits rise whenever a reader says "yes" more often. The liberal block raised this count while d′ stayed flat and false alarms nearly doubled, so the count can improve without any gain in skill. Why the others are wrong: All residents read the same images; hits depend on both sensitivity and criterion; the passage states the count rose after liberal instructions. Trap: Accepting a single outcome measure without checking false alarms.

passages.title: Individual influences on behavior · passage
text: Bipolar disorder involves episodes of mania or hypomania alternating with depression. Lithium reduces the frequency of episodes and lowers suicide risk, but it has a narrow therapeutic index: serum levels must be monitored because toxicity occurs not far above the therapeutic range. Dehydration, NSAIDs and thiazide diuretics raise lithium levels.
In a 1-year randomized trial, 300 patients received lithium, valproate or placebo (Table 1).

qs.q: Why must serum lithium be monitored?
o: Lithium levels do not change over time
They change with hydration and drugs.
Lithium is not absorbed reliably at all
Therapeutic and toxic levels are close
qs.x: Correct: Because levels only modestly above about 1.2 mmol/L can cause toxicity, regular measurement is needed to keep the dose in range. Why the others are wrong: Absorption is reliable; monitoring prevents harm rather than adding efficacy; levels vary. Trap: Thinking monitoring improves the drug's action.

qs.q: Why would a thiazide diuretic raise lithium levels?
o: Thiazides convert lithium into a toxin
Correct: the kidney handles them similarly.
Thiazides block lithium absorption from the gut
qs.x: Correct: Lithium is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule along pathways shared with sodium, so sodium depletion increases lithium retention and raises serum levels. Why the others are wrong: Thiazides act renally and reduce excretion; no conversion occurs. Trap: Reversing the direction of the interaction.

qs.q: Which result shows lithium's benefit most directly?
qs.x: Correct: Halving the proportion of patients with any mood episode relative to placebo is the primary efficacy finding. Why the others are wrong: Serum level and discontinuation rates address dosing and tolerability; the placebo contrast is the key one. Trap: Choosing a safety measure as the efficacy result.

qs.q: Why is a higher discontinuation rate on active drugs expected?
o: Placebo is more toxic than lithium
qs.x: Correct: Pharmacologically active treatments produce adverse effects such as tremor, weight gain and thirst, so more patients stop them than stop an inert pill. Why the others are wrong: Placebo is inert; discontinuation reflects tolerability; allocation was random. Trap: Interpreting discontinuation as treatment failure.

qs.q: Why is randomization important in this trial?
o: It replaces the need for a placebo
A placebo arm was still used.
qs.x: Correct: Patients differ in episode history and severity, which strongly predicts outcome, so random allocation makes the comparison fair. Why the others are wrong: Not all improved; the placebo arm remained; side effects occurred. Trap: Confusing randomization with blinding or with guaranteeing benefit.

passages.title: Making sense of the environment · passage
text: Researchers conducted a study to evaluate the efficacy of a novel cognitive-behavioral intervention (CBI) on reducing anxiety symptoms among adults with generalized anxiety disorder (GAD). Eighty participants were enrolled from two clinics: patients at one clinic formed the CBI group (n=40), and patients at the other formed a wait‑list control group (n=40). Baseline assessments revealed comparable anxiety scores across groups (CBI mean 50.2, SD 5.1; control mean 50.4, SD 5.3). Over a 12‑week intervention period, participants in the CBI group received weekly 60‑minute sessions delivered by trained therapists, while controls received no intervention. Post‑intervention anxiety scores were significantly lower in the CBI group (mean 40.5, SD 4.8) compared to controls (mean 52.0, SD 5.3), yielding a p‑value <0.001. A clinically significant response was defined as a drop of at least 5 points from baseline; 30 of 40 CBI participants and 6 of 40 controls met this criterion. The study also measured secondary outcomes, including depressive symptoms and functional impairment, which showed similar patterns of improvement. The authors noted limitations such as a relatively short follow‑up period and the absence of blinding. Despite these constraints, the findings suggest that CBI may be an effective treatment for GAD, warranting further research with larger samples and longer follow‑up.

qs.q: Which of the following best describes the effect of the CBI on anxiety scores as shown in Table 1?
qs.x: Correct: B) The CBI group's mean fell from 50.2 to 40.5, and at 12 weeks it was well below the control mean (52.0); the between-group p < 0.001 shows this difference is statistically significant. Why the others are wrong: A) scores fell, not rose. C) the CBI mean dropped by about 10 points. D) baseline, post-treatment and p-values are all reported. Trap: Reading the lower post-treatment number as worse anxiety, when on this scale a lower score means fewer symptoms.

qs.q: Which design best matches the study described in the passage?
o: Patients were not selected by outcome.
Patients were not assigned by chance.
Correct: an intervention was given, but each clinic formed one group.
qs.x: Correct: The CBI was delivered by the study, but groups were patients at two different clinics. Similar baseline scores help, yet clinics could differ in other ways, so this is quasi-experimental. Why the others are wrong: No random assignment; selection by clinic, not outcome; and the exposure was assigned by the study rather than observed. Trap: Assuming comparable baseline means prove randomization.

qs.q: Calculate the relative risk (RR) of achieving a clinically significant reduction in anxiety for participants in the CBI group compared to the control group. A clinically significant reduction is defined as a 5-point drop from baseline.
qs.x: Correct: 30 of 40 CBI participants (75%) and 6 of 40 controls (15%) met the criterion, so RR = 0.75/0.15 = 5.0. Why the others are wrong: A) 0.20 inverts the ratio (control over CBI). B) 0.60 is the absolute risk difference (0.75 - 0.15), not a ratio. D) 17.0 is the odds ratio (30/10 divided by 6/34), not the relative risk. Trap: Reporting the absolute risk difference (0.60) or the odds ratio (17.0) instead of the ratio of the two proportions.

qs.q: Which of the following is NOT stated in the passage?
o: The follow‑up period was relatively short.
Secondary outcomes showed improvement patterns similar to the primary outcome.
Participants who dropped out were excluded from the analysis.
qs.x: Correct: The passage never mentions dropouts or exclusions; it reports 40 participants per group and analyzes all of them. Why the others are wrong: A) the authors list a relatively short follow‑up period as a limitation. B) the authors list the absence of blinding as a limitation. C) the passage says secondary outcomes showed similar patterns of improvement. Trap: Assuming dropouts were handled because limitations are listed, when the passage never mentions them.

qs.q: Which conclusion is best supported by the passage and Table 1?
o: The CBI eliminated anxiety symptoms in every treated participant.
More CBI than control participants dropped at least 5 points from baseline.
The effect of the CBI was shown to persist well beyond the 12‑week period.
The control group's mean anxiety score fell substantially over the 12 weeks.
qs.x: Correct: 30 of 40 CBI participants (75%) versus 6 of 40 controls (15%) met the response criterion. Why the others are wrong: A) only 30 of 40 participants responded and the post‑treatment mean (40.5) is still well above zero. C) the follow‑up period was short, so persistence was not tested. D) the control mean went from 50.4 to 52.0, a slight rise, not a fall. Trap: Treating a significant short-term group difference as proof of universal or lasting benefit.

passages.title: Making sense of the environment · passage
text: Researchers investigated the effect of different auditory cues on cognitive performance during a sustained attention task. Twenty-four healthy adults (12 males, 12 females, age 22–35) were randomly assigned to one of four groups: Control (no cue), Condition A (continuous low‑frequency tone), Condition B (intermittent high‑frequency tone), and Condition C (continuous white noise). Each participant completed a 30‑minute vigilance task while their reaction times to target stimuli were recorded. The mean reaction time (RT) and standard deviation (SD) for each group are presented in Table 1. The researchers hypothesized that auditory cues would reduce RT variability, thereby improving sustained attention. Data analysis revealed that Condition A produced the fastest mean RT, followed by Condition C, Condition B, and the Control group. Despite the faster mean RT, Condition B exhibited the largest SD, suggesting increased inconsistency. The authors noted that the low‑frequency tone was associated with the fastest mean RT and the smallest SD, although no statistical test was reported, and they suggested future studies examine neural correlates using EEG.

qs.q: Which condition had the lowest mean reaction time?
o: The control group's mean (350 ms) was higher than Condition A's 320 ms.
Condition B's mean was higher than Condition A's 320 ms, the lowest in the table.
Condition C's mean was higher than Condition A's 320 ms, the lowest in the table.
qs.x: The table shows Condition A had a mean RT of 320 ms, the lowest among all groups. Trap: Choosing the Control group or another condition without comparing all four means; the lowest mean reaction time is Condition A's 320 ms.

qs.q: Which factor was manipulated in this experiment?
o: Age wasn't changed by the researchers; it is a participant characteristic.
Gender mix is a sample characteristic, not something the researchers manipulated.
Task duration was the same for all groups, so it is a controlled variable.
qs.x: The independent variable was the type of auditory cue presented to participants. Trap: Mistaking participant characteristics or task length for the manipulated variable; only the auditory cue type was varied.

qs.q: What is the difference in mean reaction time between Condition A and the Control group?
o: 10 ms is too small; 350 − 320 is 30 ms.
20 ms doesn't match the two means of 350 and 320 ms.
40 ms is too large; the gap between 350 and 320 ms is 30 ms.
qs.x: 350 ms (Control) – 320 ms (Condition A) = 30 ms. Trap: Subtracting the wrong pair of means gives 10, 20 or 40 ms; the control minus Condition A is 350 − 320 = 30 ms.

qs.q: Which of the following is NOT a valid interpretation of the data?
o: Condition A had a lower mean RT than the Control group.
Condition B has the largest SD.
qs.x: Correct: B) Condition B had the largest SD (35 ms, versus 30 ms for Control), so its variability was higher, not lower. Why the others are wrong: A) 320 ms is lower than the Control mean of 350 ms. C) Condition C's SD (28 ms) is below the Control SD (30 ms). D) Condition B's SD of 35 ms is the largest of the four groups. Trap: Reading a larger SD as lower variability; a larger SD means more spread, so the claim that Condition B reduces variability is the misinterpretation.

qs.q: Which statement about Table 1 is supported by the data?
o: Every auditory cue condition had a lower mean RT than the Control group.
Every auditory cue condition had a lower SD than the Control group.
Condition B had the lowest mean RT of the three cue conditions.
Condition C had the largest SD of all four groups.
qs.x: Correct: Control mean RT was 350 ms, and Conditions A, B and C were 320, 340 and 330 ms, all lower. Why the others are wrong: B) Condition B had SD 35, higher than the Control SD of 30. C) Condition B (340 ms) had the highest mean RT of the three cue conditions, not the lowest. D) Condition B (SD 35) had the largest SD; Condition C was 28. Trap: Assuming every cue helped on every measure; Condition B had a higher SD than Control (35 vs 30 ms), so the claim that every condition lowered SD fails.

passages.title: Understanding social structure · passage
text: Max Weber described rationalization as the spread of calculation, efficiency and formal rules into areas of life once governed by tradition or personal judgment. Bureaucracy, with its written rules, specialized roles and hierarchy, is its clearest form. Weber argued that rationalization raises efficiency but can leave people feeling trapped in an impersonal system, and that formal rules sometimes crowd out the goals they were meant to serve, an outcome later called goal displacement. George Ritzer applied these ideas to modern services, arguing that organizations pursue efficiency, calculability, predictability and control, and that these can come at the cost of personal attention.

Researchers studied the introduction of a standardized electronic checklist at 40 primary care clinics in one health system. The checklist prompted the clinician to record a fixed set of items at every visit and would not close until each field was filled. Twenty clinics adopted it in January and the other twenty kept their existing records for that year, with assignment made by the health system according to which clinics had updated computers. The researchers compared the two groups over 12 months using appointment records, chart audits and patient surveys (Table 1).

Patient surveys were sent to a random sample of 50 patients from each clinic, and 61% responded at checklist clinics and 64% at comparison clinics. Burnout was measured with a standard questionnaire given to every clinician at the start and the end of the year; the scores in the table are end-of-year values, and the two groups had started within 0.3 points of each other.\nT In interviews, clinicians at checklist clinics described spending much of the visit facing the screen and said they sometimes deferred a patient's concern to a later visit in order to complete the required fields. Several said the checklist had caught problems they might otherwise have missed. One clinic in the comparison group began using a shortened checklist of its own in month 9.

qs.q: Which feature of the checklist best illustrates Weber's idea of formal rationality?
o: Clinicians work in the same building
Shared space is not a rule system.
Visits vary in length by patient
Variation is the opposite of standardization.
A fixed set of items at every visit
qs.x: Correct: Formal rationality means decisions are governed by explicit, uniform rules rather than by tradition or personal discretion. A checklist that must be completed identically at every visit is exactly this kind of rule. Why the others are wrong: Sharing a building is not a rule; patient choice and variable visit length reflect discretion rather than standardization. Trap: Treating any organized activity as bureaucratic.

qs.q: Which pair of findings best illustrates goal displacement?
o: Correct: the measured task crowds out the purpose.
Shorter visits with more visits per day
Visits were shorter at checklist clinics.
Higher follow-up calls with higher screening
qs.x: Correct: Goal displacement occurs when attention to the formal rule replaces the underlying purpose. Screenings rose to 92%, but the share of patients who felt listened to fell to 58%, and clinicians described deferring patients' concerns to finish the fields. The measured task displaced the care it was meant to support. Why the others are wrong: Efficiency measures and intended results are not displacement; visits were shorter, not longer. Trap: Reading any unwanted side effect as goal displacement.

qs.q: What most limits a causal interpretation of these results?
o: Patient surveys were used as a measure
The study ran for only 12 months
A year is a reasonable period.
qs.x: Correct: Clinics received the checklist based on which had updated computers, so the two groups may differ in funding, staffing or patient population. Differences in outcomes could reflect those features rather than the checklist. Why the others are wrong: Surveys, audits and a 12-month period are all reasonable methods. Trap: Confusing a measurement method with a design flaw.

qs.q: How does the comparison clinic that adopted its own checklist in month 9 affect the study?
o: It makes the two groups more alike
Correct: a true difference may be understated.
It makes the checklist look more effective
It has no bearing on the results
qs.x: Correct: If a comparison clinic starts doing what the intervention group does, the measured difference between the groups shrinks. Any real effect of the checklist would be understated rather than exaggerated. Why the others are wrong: Contamination weakens rather than strengthens an apparent effect; the surveys remain valid; the clinic is part of the comparison group. Trap: Assuming any flaw must exaggerate the finding.

qs.q: Which concept best describes clinicians' sense of being controlled by the system they work in?
o: That describes cohesion through shared beliefs.
That concerns self-image from others' views.
Correct: Weber's image of rationalized constraint.
That describes expectations for people who are ill.
qs.x: Correct: Weber used the image of an iron cage for the way rationalized systems constrain the people inside them, even those who run them. Clinicians facing the screen and deferring patients' concerns describe this experience. Why the others are wrong: The looking-glass self is Cooley's idea about self-concept; mechanical solidarity is Durkheim's term for cohesion in simple societies; the sick role is Parsons's account of expectations for ill people. Trap: Choosing a familiar sociology term without matching it to the situation.

r: Patients reporting the clinician listened carefully (%)
Patients who received a follow-up call about an abnormal result (%)

passages.title: Separation and purification methods · passage
text: Size-exclusion (gel filtration) chromatography separates molecules by size. Small molecules enter the pores of the beads and take a longer path, while large molecules are excluded and pass between beads, so they elute first. Ion-exchange chromatography separates by charge, and affinity chromatography uses a specific binding partner.
A protein mixture was run on a size-exclusion column calibrated with standards (Table 1).

qs.q: Why does thyroglobulin elute first?
o: It binds the beads most tightly
Size exclusion does not rely on binding.
It is the most positively charged
Charge is not the basis here.
It is too large to enter the pores
Correct: it takes the shortest path.
It is the smallest protein present
qs.x: Correct: Molecules larger than the pore size travel only in the space between beads, so they move through in the smallest volume. Why the others are wrong: Binding and charge are not the mechanism; it is the largest. Trap: Assuming big molecules are always retained longer.

qs.q: A protein elutes at 84 mL. What is its approximate mass?
qs.x: Correct: An elution volume of 84 mL falls between aldolase (158 kDa at 72 mL) and ovalbumin (44 kDa at 96 mL), so the mass is roughly 90 kDa. Why the others are wrong: Each corresponds to a different elution range. Trap: Reading the calibration backward.

qs.q: Why must the column be calibrated with standards?
o: Standards block the pores to improve resolution
Elution volume depends on the column
Correct: standards relate volume to mass.
qs.x: Correct: The relation between mass and elution volume depends on bead pore size, column dimensions and flow rate, so known proteins establish the curve. Why the others are wrong: Charge is irrelevant; standards do not block pores; calibration does not change mechanism. Trap: Thinking elution volume is an intrinsic property of the protein.

qs.q: Which technique would best isolate one protein from a complex mixture using a specific antibody?
o: Correct: a specific binding partner captures it.
qs.x: Correct: An immobilized antibody binds its target specifically, allowing other proteins to wash through. Why the others are wrong: The others separate by general physical properties rather than specific recognition. Trap: Choosing a high-resolution but nonspecific method.

qs.q: An elongated protein elutes earlier than a globular protein of the same mass. Why?
o: It binds the beads more weakly
Charge is not the basis here.
It is denser than the globular protein
qs.x: Correct: Size exclusion separates by hydrodynamic volume, and an extended shape sweeps out a larger volume than a compact one of equal mass, so it is excluded from pores sooner. Why the others are wrong: Charge, density and binding are not the separation basis. Trap: Treating molecular mass as the only determinant.

passages.title: Processes of cell division, differentiation, and specialization · passage
text: Researchers investigated the effect of a novel small‑molecule inhibitor, Drug X, on the viability of cultured human cancer cells. Four concentrations of Drug X (0, 10, 50, and 100 µM) were applied to the cells for 48 hours. Cell viability was quantified using an MTT assay, and the results were expressed as a percentage of the untreated control. Each concentration was tested in ten replicate wells (n = 10). The investigators noted a dose‑dependent decrease in viability, with the highest concentration producing the greatest cytotoxic effect. Standard deviations increased slightly with concentration, suggesting greater variability at higher drug doses. The study aimed to determine whether Drug X could be a potential chemotherapeutic agent and to identify a concentration that maximizes efficacy while minimizing toxicity.

qs.q: What is the viability percentage of cells treated with 50 µM Drug X?
qs.x: The table shows that cells exposed to 50 µM of Drug X had a viability of 60%. Trap: Reading the wrong row, such as the 10 µM value (85%) or the 100 µM value (30%), instead of the 50 µM row.

qs.q: Which control group would best account for the solvent used to dissolve Drug X?
qs.x: A vehicle‑only control (e.g., DMSO without Drug X) controls for any effects of the solvent itself. Trap: Choosing untreated cells; they cannot separate solvent effects from drug effects, so a vehicle-only control is needed.

qs.q: Calculate the percent decrease in viability from 10 µM to 100 µM.
qs.x: Percent decrease = (85-30)/85 x 100 = 64.7%. The 55 is a drop of 55 percentage points, not a percent decrease relative to the 10 uM value. Trap: Reporting the 55 percentage-point drop (85-30) as the percent decrease instead of dividing by the starting value of 85.

qs.q: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by the data?
o: Drug X reduces viability at higher concentrations.
qs.x: The table shows viability at 100 µM is 30%, not 50%. The other statements are directly supported by the data. Trap: Assuming viability at 100 µM sits at the halfway point (50%) rather than reading the tabulated value of 30%.

qs.q: Which of the following is a potential clinical implication of these findings?
o: Drug X warrants further study as a chemotherapeutic.
Drug X is safe at high doses.
Drug X has no effect on cell viability.
qs.x: Correct: A) Dose-dependent loss of viability in cultured cancer cells justifies further study, though not clinical use. Why the others are wrong: B) Viability falls to 30% at 100 µM, which is toxicity, not safety. C) Viability falls with dose, so there is an effect. D) Viability decreases, the opposite of increased proliferation. Trap: Treating a cell-culture result as proof of safety or clinical use; the data show only dose-dependent cytotoxicity in vitro.

passages.title: Structure, growth, physiology, and genetics of prokaryotes and viruses · passage
text: Researchers studied the effect of varying concentrations of a novel antimicrobial peptide (AMP) on the growth of Escherichia coli in a controlled in vitro assay. The experiment used a 96‑well plate with eight concentrations (0, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 µg/mL) and three replicates per concentration. After 24 hours of incubation at 37 °C, optical density at 600 nm (OD600) was measured. The data, summarized in Table 1, show a dose‑dependent decrease in bacterial growth, with the lowest OD observed at the highest peptide concentration. Additionally, the researchers performed a time‑kill assay at 32 µg/mL, recording CFU counts at 0, 2, 4, and 6 hours. The results indicated a 3‑log reduction after 4 hours. The study also examined the peptide’s cytotoxicity against mammalian cell lines, reporting an IC50 of 48 µg/mL. These findings describe the peptide’s antibacterial activity and its cytotoxicity at comparable concentrations.

qs.q: Which AMP concentration results in the greatest reduction in OD600 relative to the control (0 µg/mL)?
qs.x: The OD600 at 64 µg/mL (0.08) is the lowest among all concentrations, indicating the greatest reduction compared to the control (1.02). Trap: C (32 µg/mL) shows a substantial reduction but is not the lowest OD.

qs.q: Which experimental design element best supports a dose‑response relationship in this study?
o: A 96‑well plate, eight concentrations, three replicates each
Measuring OD600 after 24 hours of incubation
Performing a time‑kill assay at a single concentration
Assessing cytotoxicity against mammalian cell lines
qs.x: A 96‑well plate with multiple concentrations and replicates provides the necessary data points to establish a dose‑response curve. Trap: B (measuring OD600) is essential but does not alone establish dose‑response.

qs.q: What is the percent reduction in OD600 at 32 µg/mL compared to the control?
qs.x: Percent reduction = [(1.02 – 0.15)/1.02] × 100 ≈ 85.3 %. Trap: Picking B (92.1%), which is roughly the reduction at 64 µg/mL (about 92%), the wrong concentration, instead of the 32 µg/mL value.

qs.q: Which statement is NOT supported by the data presented?
o: Higher AMP concentrations produce greater bacterial growth inhibition.
The peptide exhibits a 3‑log reduction in CFU after 4 hours at 32 µg/mL.
The mammalian IC50 (48 µg/mL) is below the time‑kill dose (32 µg/mL).
The OD600 values decrease in a dose‑dependent manner.
qs.x: Correct: C) 48 µg/mL is higher than 32 µg/mL, so the statement is false. Why the others are wrong: A) OD600 falls from 1.02 to 0.08 as concentration rises; supported. B) The passage reports a 3‑log reduction after 4 hours at 32 µg/mL; supported. D) OD600 decreases at every step in concentration; supported. Trap: Reading the IC50 of 48 µg/mL as lower than the 32 µg/mL used against bacteria; the mammalian IC50 is actually the higher number.

qs.q: Which statement best relates the antibacterial concentration to the mammalian cytotoxicity data?
o: The 32 µg/mL used in the time‑kill assay is below the mammalian IC50 of 48 µg/mL, but only by about 1.5‑fold, so the margin is narrow.
The mammalian IC50 of 48 µg/mL is lower than 32 µg/mL, so more than half of mammalian cells die at 32 µg/mL.
The dose‑dependent OD600 decrease shows the peptide is nontoxic to mammalian cells.
Because the IC50 is 48 µg/mL, the peptide is safe at every concentration tested in the OD600 assay.
qs.x: Correct: 48/32 = 1.5, so the time‑kill concentration is below the IC50 but not by a large factor. Why the others are wrong: B) 48 is higher than 32, not lower. C) OD600 was measured on E. coli and says nothing about mammalian cell toxicity. D) The assay went up to 64 µg/mL, which is above the IC50 of 48 µg/mL. Trap: Concluding that a peptide with a 3-log kill is automatically safe; the IC50 is only 1.5-fold above the concentration used against bacteria.

passages.title: Individual influences on behavior · passage
text: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder involves inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity beginning in childhood and causing impairment in more than one setting. Diagnosis requires symptoms across settings, which is why reports from both parents and teachers are collected. Stimulant medications increase dopamine and norepinephrine signaling in prefrontal circuits.
A clinic evaluated 200 referred children with ratings from two sources (Table 1).

qs.q: Why does the diagnosis require symptoms in more than one setting?
o: Teachers are more accurate than parents
Two settings double the symptom count
Symptoms appear only at school in ADHD
qs.x: Correct: Difficulties confined to one setting often reflect that environment, such as a mismatched classroom or family stress, rather than a pervasive attentional disorder. Why the others are wrong: Counting is not the aim; neither informant is privileged; ADHD symptoms are pervasive. Trap: Treating multi-setting criteria as a way to gather more data.

qs.q: Why might parent and teacher ratings disagree?
o: Both can be accurate about their setting.
qs.x: Correct: A classroom requires sustained seated attention while home allows more movement, so the same child may appear impaired in one setting and not the other. Why the others are wrong: Both can be accurate; parallel forms exist; behavior varies. Trap: Assuming disagreement means error.

qs.q: Which neurotransmitters do stimulant medications mainly affect?
o: These are not the main targets.
These are targets of other drugs.
These are not the main targets.
qs.x: Correct: Stimulants block reuptake and promote release of dopamine and norepinephrine, improving prefrontal signal-to-noise. Why the others are wrong: Each names transmitters not primarily targeted. Trap: Choosing serotonin because it is prominent in other psychiatric drugs.

qs.q: Why is it notable that stimulants improve attention in children without ADHD too?
o: Drug response is not a test
Correct: treatment response is not a test.
It can still be clinically useful.
It shows stimulants do not work
qs.x: Correct: Because stimulants raise attention broadly, improvement on medication cannot be used as diagnostic evidence; diagnosis rests on symptom history and impairment. Why the others are wrong: Broad effects do not make everyone a case; the drugs work; medication can help. Trap: Using treatment response as a diagnostic test.

qs.q: Why do 12% of children rated high at school only still meet criteria?
o: Most such children did not meet criteria.
They were rated high at school.
qs.x: Correct: A parent may minimize or not observe difficulties, so a full evaluation including history and other sources can still establish cross-setting impairment in a minority of cases. Why the others are wrong: Criteria require more than one setting; symptoms were present; school ratings alone usually are not sufficient. Trap: Treating rating-scale patterns as the diagnosis itself.

passages.title: Structure, growth, physiology, and genetics of prokaryotes and viruses · passage
text: Researchers investigated the effect of varying concentrations of a novel antimicrobial peptide (AMP) on the growth of Pseudomonas aeruginosa in vitro. Twenty-four bacterial cultures were inoculated in 96-well plates and exposed to AMP concentrations of 0, 2, 4, 8, 16, and 32 µg/mL for 24 hours. After incubation, optical density at 600 nm (OD600) was measured to assess bacterial growth. The results, summarized in Table 1, show a dose-dependent decrease in OD600, with complete inhibition observed at 32 µg/mL. In addition, the study measured the minimal inhibitory concentration (MIC) by serial dilution and determined the MIC to be 32 µg/mL. The researchers also performed time‑kill assays at each concentration; after 6 hours the reduction in colony‑forming units was 2.5 log at 8 µg/mL and 3.5 log at 32 µg/mL. Statistical analysis (ANOVA) indicated significant differences between concentrations (p < 0.01). The authors concluded that the AMP has potent antibacterial activity and could serve as a lead compound for new antibiotics.

qs.q: Which concentration shows the highest % inhibition?
qs.x: The table indicates that 32 µg/mL achieves 100% inhibition, the highest among the tested concentrations. Trap: The answer may be mistakenly chosen as 8 µg/mL because it shows a large inhibition (60%) but does not reach complete inhibition.

qs.q: Which experimental approach best determines the minimal inhibitory concentration (MIC) of the AMP?
o: A single OD600 reading at one AMP concentration
qs.x: Correct: C) The MIC is the lowest concentration that prevents visible growth, so it requires a series of (typically twofold) dilutions, each scored for growth. Why the others are wrong: A) one reading at a single concentration cannot locate the lowest inhibitory concentration. B) a time‑kill assay measures the rate and extent of killing (log CFU reduction) over time, not the growth-inhibition threshold. D) ANOVA tests differences between group means and does not define a concentration threshold. Trap: Choosing the time‑kill assay because it measures antibacterial activity, although it tracks killing over time rather than the lowest concentration that prevents growth.

qs.q: If the OD600 at 8 µg/mL is 0.40, what is the percent inhibition relative to the control?
qs.x: Percent inhibition = [(1.00 – 0.40)/1.00] × 100 = 60%. Trap: Some students may mistakenly use the OD600 of 0.70 (for 4 µg/mL) or miscalculate the subtraction.

qs.q: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by the data?
o: The AMP completely inhibits growth at 32 µg/mL.
The AMP shows a 2.5‑log reduction at 8 µg/mL after 6 hours.
qs.x: Correct: The table lists the OD600 at 0 µg/mL as 1.00, not 0.85 (0.85 is the value at 2 µg/mL). Why the others are wrong: A) the table shows 100% inhibition and OD600 of 0.00 at 32 µg/mL. B) the passage gives the MIC as 32 µg/mL, the lowest tested concentration with complete inhibition. C) the table and passage both report a 2.5‑log CFU reduction at 8 µg/mL at 6 h. Trap: Confusing the OD600 of the 2 µg/mL well (0.85) with the untreated control value (1.00).

qs.q: Which follow‑up experiment would best test whether the in vitro activity of the AMP is likely to translate into therapeutic benefit?
o: Repeating the same 24‑hour OD600 assay in the same medium and strain.
Measuring OD600 in wells that contain no bacteria.
Testing the AMP in an animal model of Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection.
qs.x: Correct: An animal infection model tests efficacy in a living host, which is the logical step after in vitro activity is shown. Why the others are wrong: A) repeating the same in vitro assay adds replication but no new information on efficacy in a host. B) wells without bacteria only provide a blank reading and say nothing about activity. D) the lowest concentrations had the least inhibition, so they add little about therapeutic potential. Trap: Choosing more in vitro replication because it feels rigorous, though it does not address efficacy in an infection.

passages.title: Social thinking · passage
text: The actor-observer bias is the tendency to attribute one's own behavior to situational factors while attributing the same behavior in others to disposition. It is thought to arise from differences in available information and in what is perceptually salient.
Participants explained both their own and a stranger's lateness, rudeness, and generosity, and each explanation was coded (Table 1).

qs.q: Which rows display the bias most clearly?
qs.x: Correct: The 47-point gap for lateness is the classic actor-observer pattern, whereas generosity shows almost none. Why the others are wrong: The generosity gap is small, and the remaining pairs hold target constant. Trap: Comparing rows that share the same target.

qs.q: Why is the generosity gap small?
qs.x: Correct: For favorable behavior people prefer dispositional self-explanations, which works against the usual actor-observer direction. Why the others are wrong: Situations do affect giving, information was matched, and definitions were standardized. Trap: Expecting the bias to be equally strong for all behaviors.

qs.q: Which added measure would test the information account?
qs.x: Correct: If the bias shrinks when observers report equal knowledge of the context, the information explanation gains support. Why the others are wrong: Duration, behavior count, and age do not index available information. Trap: Measuring effort instead of knowledge.

qs.q: Which bias overlaps with the generosity pattern?
qs.x: Correct: Taking dispositional credit for positive behavior is the self-serving bias. Why the others are wrong: The remaining terms name different phenomena. Trap: Labeling every attribution pattern the fundamental attribution error.

qs.q: What is the main limitation of this design?
qs.x: Correct: Participants explained both targets without assignment, so order and selection effects cannot be excluded. Why the others are wrong: Behavior count, trained coding, and self-report are appropriate here. Trap: Criticizing a feature the design requires.

passages.title: Separation and purification methods · passage
text: Distillation separates liquids by boiling point. Simple distillation works when boiling points differ by more than about 25 °C. Fractional distillation uses a packed column in which repeated vaporization and condensation cycles enrich the vapor in the lower-boiling component.
