An azeotrope is a mixture whose vapor has the same composition as the liquid, so it cannot be separated further by distillation.
Students distilled a 50:50 mixture of ethanol (bp 78 °C) and water (bp 100 °C) and collected fractions (Table 1).

qs.q: Why does fractional distillation give a purer first fraction?
o: Water boils before ethanol in a column
The column heats the mixture more strongly
The column provides surface, not heat.
Correct: each cycle acts like another distillation.
qs.x: Correct: Vapor condenses and revaporizes many times on the packing, and each cycle enriches the vapor in the more volatile component, so the distillate is purer. Why the others are wrong: The column does not add heat or react; ethanol is more volatile. Trap: Thinking the column works by heating.

qs.q: Why can ethanol not be purified beyond about 95.6% this way?
o: It forms an azeotrope with water
Correct: vapor and liquid have the same composition.
Water is more volatile than ethanol
The column is not long enough in any apparatus
qs.x: Correct: At 95.6% ethanol the vapor has the same composition as the liquid, so further distillation gives no enrichment; other methods, such as adding a drying agent, are needed. Why the others are wrong: Ethanol is stable; no column can pass an azeotrope; ethanol is the more volatile component. Trap: Assuming a better column always gives more separation.

qs.q: Why does the head temperature rise during simple distillation?
o: The remaining liquid grows richer in water
Ethanol boils at a higher temperature later
The thermometer drifts upward over time
The heat source is turned up each minute
qs.x: Correct: As ethanol distills off, the pot liquid becomes more water rich, so its boiling point and the vapor temperature both rise. Why the others are wrong: The change is not from the heater or thermometer; pure component boiling points are fixed. Trap: Attributing the temperature rise to the apparatus.

qs.q: Which method would best separate two liquids boiling at 60 °C and 120 °C?
o: That is analytical, not preparative at this scale.
qs.x: Correct: With a 60 °C difference, simple distillation separates the components efficiently without the extra time and equipment of a column. Why the others are wrong: Fractional distillation is more than needed; recrystallization suits solids; TLC is analytical. Trap: Choosing the most powerful method rather than the appropriate one.

qs.q: Why is distillation done under reduced pressure for heat-sensitive compounds?
o: Lower pressure lowers the boiling point
Lower pressure raises the boiling point
qs.x: Correct: Boiling occurs when vapor pressure equals the external pressure, so reducing pressure allows distillation at a lower temperature and avoids decomposition. Why the others are wrong: Pressure reduction lowers boiling points and promotes vaporization; it is not a chemical process. Trap: Reversing the pressure-boiling point relation.

passages.title: Understanding social structure · passage
text: Culture includes material culture, such as objects and technology, and nonmaterial culture, such as values, beliefs, and norms. Cultural lag describes the delay between a material change and the normative adjustment that follows, and subcultures hold distinctive norms within a larger culture.
Researchers surveyed 2,500 adults about a newly common technology and the norms surrounding it (Table 1).

qs.q: Which concept do these results best illustrate?
qs.x: Correct: Widespread adoption with unsettled norms and frequent conflict is the gap between material and nonmaterial culture that cultural lag names. Why the others are wrong: The remaining terms describe evaluative stances and group absorption. Trap: Describing any cultural change as lag without the timing contrast.

qs.q: Which item is material culture?
qs.x: Correct: Material culture consists of physical objects and technology. Why the others are wrong: Norms, interactions, and rules are nonmaterial. Trap: Counting written rules as material because they are recorded.

qs.q: What does the subculture figure add?
qs.x: Correct: A small minority occupies a setting with formal rules, showing normative adjustment proceeding faster in some groups than others. Why the others are wrong: Rejection was not measured, norms are not shared, and ownership was high. Trap: Treating a subculture figure as a measure of resistance.

qs.q: Which figure shows the clearest normative gap?
qs.x: Correct: The contrast between high ownership and low norm clarity measures the gap directly. Why the others are wrong: Conflict is downstream, the subculture figure is narrow, and ownership alone is one side. Trap: Choosing the consequence instead of the gap.

qs.q: Which added measure would show lag closing?
qs.x: Correct: Tracking reported norm clarity across years would show whether nonmaterial culture catches up with the material change. Why the others are wrong: Price, model variety, and cross-national ownership do not measure norms. Trap: Tracking the technology instead of the norms.

r: Share reporting clear norms for its use in meetings
Share reporting conflict over its use at family meals
Share in a professional subculture with written rules

passages.title: Principles of chemical thermodynamics and kinetics · passage
text: Enzymes from organisms that live at different temperatures often catalyze the same reaction with the same active-site residues, yet they differ in speed and in heat tolerance. One explanation is that a protein must be flexible enough to move through the conformational changes of its catalytic cycle but rigid enough to stay folded. A protein from a heat-loving organism may be well suited to high temperatures yet sluggish at room temperature, because the same interactions that hold it together also restrict its motion.

To test this idea, researchers purified adenylate kinase, which catalyzes 2 ADP ⇌ ATP + AMP, from a bacterium that grows best at 37 °C (Enzyme M) and from a related species isolated from a hot spring that grows best at 70 °C (Enzyme T). The two proteins share 74% sequence identity, and every residue that contacts the substrates is conserved. Turnover number (kcat) was measured at several temperatures with saturating substrate (Table 1). Each value is the mean of three runs that differed by less than 5%.

The researchers also measured the melting temperature (Tm), the temperature at which half of the protein is unfolded, using circular dichroism. Enzyme M had a Tm of 47 °C and Enzyme T had a Tm of 82 °C. Inspection of the Enzyme T crystal structure showed that Glu142, a surface residue far from the active site, forms an ion pair with Arg87. A mutant of Enzyme T in which Glu142 was replaced by glutamine (E142Q) had a Tm of 71 °C. At 40 °C, the kcat of E142Q was 5.8 s⁻¹.

Heat tolerance has practical uses. Enzymes from heat-loving organisms are used in laboratory methods that cycle between high temperatures, such as the polymerase chain reaction, and in industrial processes that run hot to keep reactants dissolved and to limit microbial growth. Engineers who want an enzyme that is both stable and fast at moderate temperatures often start by adding or removing surface ion pairs and then testing how the changes affect Tm and kcat separately.\nT In a final experiment, Enzyme M was held at 60 °C for 10 minutes in the presence of substrate. Its activity was then measured after the solution was cooled to 30 °C. The rate was 4% of the rate of an unheated sample. When fresh, unheated Enzyme M was added to the heated solution, the rate returned to the expected value.

qs.q: Which explanation of the kcat values of the two enzymes at 20–30 °C is most consistent with the passage?
o: Enzyme T is too rigid to cycle quickly at low temperature
Correct: the stabilizing interactions that resist unfolding also slow conformational change.
Enzyme T makes the reaction less favorable overall
An enzyme cannot change ΔG of the reaction.
Enzyme T is partly unfolded when the temperature is low
Its Tm is 82 °C, so it is folded at 20–30 °C.
Enzyme T is missing some of the residues that bind substrate
qs.x: Correct: Enzyme T is folded and has the same active site, yet it turns over about eight times more slowly than Enzyme M at 20–30 °C. The passage proposes that the interactions that keep a heat-tolerant protein folded also restrict the motions needed for catalysis, so it is sluggish at low temperature. Why the others are wrong: A Tm of 82 °C means Enzyme T is folded well below that temperature; the substrate-contacting residues are conserved; a catalyst changes the rate, not the free energy change. Trap: Assuming a slow enzyme must be damaged or missing part of its active site.

qs.q: To estimate the activation energy of Enzyme T from Table 1, which plot should the researchers make?
o: kcat against T, which has a slope of Eₐ/R
kcat is not linear in T.
1/kcat against 1/T, which has a slope equal to Eₐ/R
This is not the Arrhenius form.
ln kcat against T in kelvin, which has a slope of −Eₐ/R
ln kcat against 1/T, which has a slope of −Eₐ/R
Correct: the linear form of the Arrhenius equation.
qs.x: Correct: Taking the natural log of k = Ae^(−Eₐ/RT) gives ln k = ln A − (Eₐ/R)(1/T), so a plot of ln k against 1/T (in kelvin) is a straight line with slope −Eₐ/R. Only the points below the Tm should be used. Why the others are wrong: The rate constant rises exponentially, not linearly, with temperature; ln k is linear in 1/T, not in T; a double-reciprocal plot belongs to Michaelis–Menten analysis, not to the Arrhenius equation. Trap: Mixing up the Arrhenius plot with a Lineweaver–Burk plot.

qs.q: What do the results for the E142Q mutant most strongly suggest?
o: The mutation shifts the equilibrium toward ATP and AMP
Enzymes and mutations do not change Keq.
The Glu142–Arg87 ion pair stabilizes the folded enzyme
Correct: Tm fell by 11 °C while kcat stayed the same.
Glu142 is required for the chemical step of catalysis
Glutamine side chains cannot form hydrogen bonds
Glutamine's amide is a good hydrogen bond donor and acceptor.
qs.x: Correct: Replacing the charged Glu with the neutral Gln removes the salt bridge to Arg87. The Tm dropped from 82 °C to 71 °C, but kcat at 40 °C (5.8 s⁻¹) was essentially the same as the wild type (5.9 s⁻¹). The residue therefore contributes to stability, not to catalysis. Why the others are wrong: An unchanged kcat rules out a catalytic role, and Glu142 is far from the active site; glutamine hydrogen bonds well but carries no charge; no enzyme or mutation alters the equilibrium constant. Trap: Assuming any residue whose mutation matters must be in the active site.

qs.q: Which observation shows that the loss of Enzyme M activity at 60 °C is due to the enzyme rather than the substrate?
o: Raising substrate levels after heating restored the rate
This would point to substrate loss, and it was not observed.
Enzyme M activity at 50 °C is lower than at 40 °C
This does not separate enzyme loss from substrate loss.
Fresh enzyme added after heating restored the rate
Correct: the substrate was still usable.
Enzyme M is faster than Enzyme T at 30 °C
This compares enzymes, not substrate stability.
qs.x: Correct: If heat had destroyed the substrate, adding new enzyme would not help. Because fresh enzyme restored the expected rate in the same heated solution, the substrate survived and the original enzyme had been inactivated, consistent with unfolding above its Tm of 47 °C. Why the others are wrong: Comparing the two enzymes at 30 °C says nothing about heat damage; a lower rate at 50 °C is the finding being explained, not evidence for a cause; restoring activity by adding substrate would implicate the substrate. Trap: Choosing a result that restates the observation instead of one that tests the explanation.

qs.q: If kcat were measured at 75 °C, how would E142Q most likely compare with wild-type Enzyme T?
o: Higher, because glutamine is less charged than glutamate
The same, because the active site is unchanged
A folded active site is needed for activity.
Higher, because kcat rises with temperature for both
This holds only while the protein stays folded.
Lower, because most E142Q molecules would be unfolded
Correct: 75 °C is above its Tm of 71 °C.
qs.x: Correct: At 75 °C, more than half of E142Q is unfolded because its Tm is 71 °C, while wild-type Enzyme T, whose Tm is 82 °C, is mostly folded and still speeding up, as its rise from 20 to 35 s⁻¹ between 60 and 70 °C shows. The mutant should therefore be slower. Why the others are wrong: The Arrhenius trend holds only for folded enzyme; an identical active site is useless once the protein unfolds; removing the charge lowered stability rather than raising activity. Trap: Applying the Arrhenius trend past the melting temperature.

passages.title: Social thinking · passage
text: Stereotype threat is the performance decrement that occurs when a person fears confirming a negative stereotype about their group. It is thought to act by consuming working memory with monitoring and anxiety, and it can be reduced by altering how a task is framed.
Students completed a difficult quantitative test under randomly assigned framings, and working memory load was measured concurrently (Table 1).

qs.q: Which result supports the working memory account?
qs.x: Correct: Conditions with higher measured load produced lower scores, consistent with threat occupying capacity needed for the test. Why the others are wrong: Overall score level, condition count, and the direction of the affirmation effect do not support the claim. Trap: Reading any score difference as mechanism evidence.

qs.q: Why does the puzzle framing help?
qs.x: Correct: Removing the claim that the test measures ability removes the stereotype-relevant evaluation. Why the others are wrong: Items and timing were identical, and framing did change the load index. Trap: Attributing the gain to task difficulty.

qs.q: Which finding would most challenge the threat account?
o: Load fell but scores stayed low
qs.x: Correct: If reducing load left performance unchanged, the proposed mediating pathway would be undermined. Why the others are wrong: The remaining results are predictions or assumptions of the account. Trap: Treating a confirmatory result as a challenge.

qs.q: What was randomly assigned here?
qs.x: Correct: Only the framing of the test was assigned by the researchers. Why the others are wrong: Group membership, items, and the load measure were fixed. Trap: Assuming group identity can be randomized.

qs.q: Which practical implication follows?
qs.x: Correct: Presenting assessments as opportunities to solve problems rather than as measures of fixed ability reduced the decrement. Why the others are wrong: Difficulty and timing were not manipulated, and separating groups would raise identity salience. Trap: Recommending a change the study did not test.

passages.title: Structure, growth, physiology, and genetics of prokaryotes and viruses · passage
text: Researchers studied the effect of a novel antibiotic on the growth of *Staphylococcus aureus* in vitro. The experiment involved culturing the bacteria in a nutrient broth and adding the antibiotic at a single concentration (5 µg/mL). Samples were taken just before the antibiotic was added (Day 0) and at 1, 3, 5, and 7 days post-treatment. Bacterial counts were measured by serial dilution and plating, and the antibiotic concentration was confirmed by high-performance liquid chromatography. The goal was to describe the time-dependent bactericidal activity at that concentration; the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) was not determined. The data collected provide insights into both the potency and the kinetics of bacterial killing, which are critical for informing dosing regimens in clinical settings. The researchers plan to use these findings to design subsequent in vivo studies and to evaluate potential resistance mechanisms.

qs.q: Based on the table, which day shows the highest bacterial count?
qs.x: Correct: Day 0 has 1.2×10⁶ CFU/mL, the highest count, and no antibiotic is present yet (0 µg/mL). Why the others are wrong: B) Day 1 is 8.5×10⁵ CFU/mL, lower than Day 0. C) Day 3 is 3.1×10⁵ CFU/mL, lower. D) Day 5 is 1.0×10⁴ CFU/mL, far lower. Trap: Picking a later day by assuming bacteria keep multiplying in broth over time, ignoring that counts fell after the antibiotic was added on Day 0.

qs.q: Which experimental control would best determine whether the observed bacterial killing is due to the antibiotic rather than other variables?
o: A culture with no antibiotic added
A culture with a known ineffective antibiotic
A culture with vancomycin at the same concentration
A culture with the antibiotic but no bacteria
qs.x: A culture with no antibiotic serves as a negative control, showing bacterial growth in the absence of treatment. This allows comparison to antibiotic-treated cultures to attribute effects specifically to the drug. Trap: Option B is tempting because it introduces another antibiotic, but it does not isolate the effect of the novel drug.

qs.q: Calculate the percent reduction in bacterial count from Day 0 to Day 5.
qs.x: Percent reduction = [(1.2×10⁶ – 1.0×10⁴) / 1.2×10⁶] × 100 ≈ 99.2%. The calculation uses the baseline and Day 5 counts. Trap: Using the wrong time point or denominator; for example, the fall to Day 3 is only 74.2%, whereas the fall to Day 5 relative to the Day 0 count is 99.2%.

qs.q: Which of the following statements is best supported by the data in Table 1?
o: The antibiotic is bacteriostatic because bacterial counts never return to baseline.
The MIC is 5 µg/mL since no growth is seen after Day 5.
The antibiotic kills all bacteria within 3 days.
No bacteria were recovered at Day 7, consistent with bactericidal activity at 5 µg/mL.
qs.x: CFU/mL fell from 1.2×10⁶ at Day 0 to 0 at Day 7 at a constant 5 µg/mL, consistent with bactericidal killing. Counts were still 3.1×10⁵ at Day 3, so killing was not complete within 3 days; a single concentration cannot define an MIC; and a progressive fall to zero is not bacteriostatic behavior. Trap: Option B is tempting because the concentration is constant, but an MIC requires testing multiple concentrations, and Day 5 still shows 1.0×10⁴ CFU/mL, so 'no growth after Day 5' is wrong.

qs.q: Table 1 tests only one antibiotic concentration (5 µg/mL). Which additional experiment would be needed to determine the MIC of the antibiotic?
o: Finding the lowest antibiotic concentration that prevents visible growth
Counting bacteria at more time points while keeping the concentration at 5 µg/mL
Measuring bacterial counts at Day 7 only
Adding vancomycin to the cultures treated with 5 µg/mL
qs.x: Correct: The MIC is by definition the lowest concentration that prevents visible growth, so it requires testing several concentrations. Why the others are wrong: B) more time points at one concentration describe kinetics, not the lowest inhibitory concentration. C) a Day 7 count at one concentration cannot compare concentrations. D) adding a second drug confounds the result and does not define the MIC of the novel drug. Trap: Treating the Day 7 count of zero at 5 µg/mL as the MIC, although only one concentration was tested.

passages.title: Social processes that influence human behavior · passage
text: Conformity is a change in behavior to match a group. Asch's line-judgment studies found that many participants gave an obviously wrong answer when confederates did so first. Normative influence is conformity to be accepted; informational influence is conformity because others are believed to be right. Conformity falls sharply when even one other person dissents.
Participants judged which comparison line matched a standard, in groups where confederates gave wrong answers (Table 1).

qs.q: Why does one dissenting confederate reduce conformity so much?
o: Correct: the pressure to agree falls.
qs.x: Correct: A single ally shows that disagreement is possible and removes the sense that one would stand alone, which cuts conforming errors from 34% to 6%. Why the others are wrong: The task, group size and order are unchanged. Trap: Attributing the drop to a change in task difficulty.

qs.q: Why does private responding reduce conformity but not eliminate it?
o: Conformity requires no social context at all
Correct: others may still seem right.
Participants cannot see the lines privately
qs.x: Correct: Writing answers privately removes the fear of disapproval, but some participants still believe the majority must be perceiving something they missed. Why the others are wrong: Vision and recording are unaffected; social context matters. Trap: Treating conformity as entirely about being seen.

qs.q: What distinguishes normative from informational influence?
o: Both involve only private belief change
qs.x: Correct: Normative influence produces public compliance to gain approval, while informational influence produces private acceptance because others are taken as a guide to reality. Why the others are wrong: Each misstates one of the two. Trap: Swapping the definitions.

qs.q: Why did the control condition use participants judging alone?
o: It increases the number of trials
Trial count is not the aim.
It shows the task is easy
qs.x: Correct: With a 1% baseline error rate, the 34% error rate in groups cannot be explained by perceptual difficulty and must reflect social influence. Why the others are wrong: Acuity and trial count are not the point; conformity did occur. Trap: Dismissing a control as unnecessary.

qs.q: Why would conformity differ between cultures?
o: Only one culture has been studied
qs.x: Correct: Replications find higher conformity in cultures that emphasize group cohesion, consistent with normative influence being shaped by social values. Why the others are wrong: Perception is comparable; conformity varies with context; many cultures have been studied. Trap: Looking for a perceptual rather than a normative explanation.

r: Six confederates, one gives the correct answer

passages.title: Principles of chemical thermodynamics and kinetics · passage
text: Le Châtelier's principle states that a system at equilibrium shifts to oppose a change. Adding a reactant shifts the system toward products; removing a product shifts it the same way. Raising temperature shifts an endothermic reaction toward products. Changing pressure shifts gas equilibria toward the side with fewer moles of gas. A catalyst changes neither position nor K.
Students studied the equilibrium N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g), where N₂O₄ is colorless and NO₂ is brown, and ΔH = +57 kJ/mol (Table 1).

qs.q: Why does heating shift the equilibrium toward NO₂?
o: NO₂ is more stable at all temperatures
Heating always favors the gas with fewer moles
qs.x: Correct: Because the forward reaction is endothermic, adding heat is like adding a reactant, so the system shifts toward products. Why the others are wrong: ΔH is positive; mole counts relate to pressure; relative stability varies with temperature. Trap: Mixing up endothermic and exothermic responses.

qs.q: Why does compressing the syringe ultimately lighten the color?
o: Compression removes NO₂ from the tube
qs.x: Correct: Halving the volume first concentrates NO₂, darkening the color, but the system then shifts toward N₂O₄, which has fewer moles of gas, so the color lightens relative to the initial jump. Why the others are wrong: The system is closed; pressure rises; concentration matters. Trap: Reading only the instantaneous change.

qs.q: Why does a catalyst not shift the equilibrium?
o: It changes ΔH of the reaction
It is consumed by the reaction
qs.x: Correct: A catalyst lowers the activation barrier for forward and reverse reactions by the same amount, so equilibrium is reached faster at the same position. Why the others are wrong: Catalysts are not consumed, do not change ΔH, and act in many phases. Trap: Assuming faster means further.

qs.q: How would adding an inert gas at constant volume affect this equilibrium?
o: A shift toward N₂O₄, since total pressure rises
No shift, since partial pressures are unchanged
A shift toward NO₂, since pressure rises
Partial pressures of the reactants do not change.
qs.x: Correct: At constant volume, adding an inert gas raises total pressure but leaves the partial pressures and concentrations of N₂O₄ and NO₂ unchanged, so no shift occurs. Why the others are wrong: Partial pressures determine the shift; the reaction continues. Trap: Using total pressure instead of partial pressures.

qs.q: What happens to the value of K when the temperature is raised?
o: Product formation does not lower K here.
K stays the same at all temperatures
qs.x: Correct: K is temperature dependent; for an endothermic reaction, raising temperature increases K. Why the others are wrong: Concentration changes do not alter K; K varies with temperature and stays finite. Trap: Treating K as a universal constant.

r: Sealed tube placed in hot water
Sealed tube placed in ice water

passages.title: Social thinking · passage
text: Prejudice is an attitude, discrimination is behavior, and stereotypes are beliefs about group attributes. Implicit measures such as reaction-time association tasks are thought to capture automatic associations that may diverge from explicitly reported attitudes.
Researchers measured explicit attitudes, an implicit association score, and two behaviors in 800 adults (Table 1).

qs.q: What pattern do these correlations show?
qs.x: Correct: Explicit attitudes predicted deliberate, controllable responses while implicit scores predicted spontaneous nonverbal behavior, a well-documented double dissociation. Why the others are wrong: Each remaining claim contradicts part of the table. Trap: Ranking the two measures instead of matching them to behavior type.

qs.q: Which outcome is behavioral discrimination?
qs.x: Correct: Seating distance is an observable behavior toward a member of the group. Why the others are wrong: The remaining measures capture attitudes, associations, or beliefs. Trap: Treating a stated intention as behavior.

qs.q: Which criticism of implicit measures do these data not address?
qs.x: Correct: Stability over repeated administrations is a central criticism that a single measurement cannot evaluate. Why the others are wrong: The remaining criticisms are addressed by the table. Trap: Choosing a criticism the data do speak to.

qs.q: Which correlation is strongest overall?
qs.x: Correct: The explicit attitude correlated 0.61 with reported willingness to befriend. Why the others are wrong: Each remaining correlation is smaller. Trap: Assuming the implicit measure must lead because it is less transparent.

qs.q: Which design change would permit causal claims?
qs.x: Correct: Experimentally altering automatic associations and observing behavior change would support a causal interpretation. Why the others are wrong: More outcomes, more participants, and repeated measurement remain correlational. Trap: Treating a bigger correlational study as causal evidence.

r: Seating distance chosen in a waiting room
Hiring recommendation on a rated form
Duration of eye contact during conversation

passages.title: Social processes that influence human behavior · passage
text: Milgram's obedience studies examined compliance with an authority's instructions to deliver increasing shocks to a learner. Obedience was high when the authority was present and legitimate, and fell when the authority was remote, when the victim was close, or when other participants refused. Obedience reflects situational pressures rather than unusual personal cruelty.
Table 1 summarizes obedience rates across variations.

qs.q: Which factor most reduced obedience in these variations?
qs.x: Correct: Seeing peers refuse dropped full obedience to 10%, the lowest rate among these variations. Why the others are wrong: Each reduced obedience less. Trap: Assuming physical proximity to the victim matters most.

qs.q: What do these variations suggest about the cause of obedience?
qs.x: Correct: The same kinds of participants obeyed 65% of the time in one arrangement and 10% in another, which locates the cause in the situation rather than in character. Why the others are wrong: Cruelty and personality cannot explain the variation; the studies were experimental. Trap: Explaining behavior by disposition when the situation varied.

qs.q: Why does the presence of a legitimate authority increase obedience?
o: Participants did not understand the task
qs.x: Correct: Milgram described an agentic state in which people see themselves as carrying out another's will and no longer feel personally responsible. Why the others are wrong: Participants were distressed; no force was used; the task was understood. Trap: Assuming compliance implies enjoyment.

qs.q: Why are these studies difficult to run today?
o: Correct: deception and distress are limited.
Volunteering is not the main obstacle.
The results are no longer of interest
qs.x: Correct: Modern review boards require informed consent, the right to withdraw and protection from severe psychological distress, which the original design did not provide. Why the others are wrong: The topic remains important; equipment and volunteering are not the barriers. Trap: Explaining the change in practice by practical rather than ethical reasons.

qs.q: Why is the nonauthority condition informative?
o: It shows no one obeys instructions
qs.x: Correct: The same instructions from someone without authority produced far less obedience, which shows that perceived legitimacy carries much of the effect. Why the others are wrong: Some still obeyed; authority clearly mattered; distress was not measured. Trap: Reading a reduced rate as no effect.

h: Share continuing to the maximum shock
r: Baseline, authority present, victim in another room
Ordinary person, not an authority, gives orders

passages.title: Social processes that influence human behavior · passage
text: Social facilitation describes improved performance on simple or well-learned tasks when others are present, and impaired performance on complex or novel tasks. Zajonc explained this by arousal, which strengthens dominant responses. Social loafing, in contrast, is reduced individual effort when contributions are pooled and not identifiable.
Participants completed two tasks alone or before an audience (Table 1). Scores are percent correct.

qs.q: Why does an audience help typing but hurt the logic puzzle?
o: Correct: helpful when correct, harmful when not.
qs.x: Correct: Arousal makes the most readily available response more likely; for a well-learned skill that response is usually correct, while for a novel task it is often wrong. Why the others are wrong: Typing improved; puzzles need attention; arousal can impair. Trap: Treating audience effects as uniformly positive or negative.

qs.q: How does social loafing differ from social facilitation?
o: It occurs when effort is hidden.
It occurs only on simple tasks
qs.x: Correct: Social facilitation concerns the effect of being observed on performance, while social loafing concerns reduced effort when individual contributions cannot be identified within a group product. Why the others are wrong: It is not task limited; effort falls; being unobserved is the key. Trap: Confusing the two group effects.

qs.q: Why would a practiced musician perform better in front of a crowd?
o: Audiences have no effect on skilled performers
Correct: arousal aids the dominant response.
Practice is what makes the skill dominant.
qs.x: Correct: For a thoroughly practiced piece, the dominant response is the correct one, so added arousal improves execution. Why the others are wrong: Crowds raise arousal; practice matters; audiences do affect performers. Trap: Assuming expertise removes audience effects.

qs.q: How could the logic puzzle result be reduced in a workplace?
o: Require the task to be done in public first
Early public performance is when impairment occurs.
Add more observers to the room
qs.x: Correct: Practicing until the correct response is dominant means that any arousal from observation enhances rather than disrupts performance. Why the others are wrong: Each adds arousal during the novel phase. Trap: Trying to raise motivation when the problem is excess arousal.

qs.q: Why is it important that the logic puzzle was novel?
qs.x: Correct: Social facilitation theory predicts impairment specifically when the dominant response is not the correct one, which is characteristic of unpracticed tasks. Why the others are wrong: Scoring occurred; arousal remains; the task was harder. Trap: Overlooking why task familiarity is the critical variable.

passages.title: Processes of cell division, differentiation, and specialization · passage
text: Researchers investigated the cytotoxic effects of a novel chemotherapeutic agent on a human breast cancer cell line. Cells were exposed to varying concentrations of the drug (0, 10, 20, 40, and 80 µM) for 48 hours, after which cell viability was assessed using an MTT assay. The results, expressed as a percentage of the untreated control, are summarized in Table 1. The standard deviation for each concentration reflects the variability observed across three independent experiments. The data suggest a dose‑dependent decrease in viability, with the highest concentration (80 µM) reducing viability to 20 % of the control. These findings support further investigation of the drug’s therapeutic potential and warrant additional studies to elucidate its mechanism of action.

qs.q: What is the cell viability at a drug concentration of 20 µM?
qs.x: The table shows that at 20 µM the viability is 70 % of the untreated control. Trap: Option A (45 %) corresponds to the 40 µM concentration, which could mislead readers who overlook the concentration‑viability pairing.

qs.q: Which control would best distinguish an effect of the drug from an effect of the solvent used to dissolve it?
o: A vehicle control containing the solvent used to dissolve the drug.
A positive control using a known cytotoxic agent.
A negative control with no cells.
A time‑zero control measuring viability immediately after drug addition.
qs.x: Correct: A) A vehicle control receives the solvent alone, so any change in viability beyond it is due to the drug. Why the others are wrong: B) A positive control checks that the assay can detect cytotoxicity but does not separate drug from solvent. C) A no-cell blank corrects background absorbance. D) A time-zero control sets the starting viability, not the solvent effect. Trap: Choosing a positive control because it validates the assay, even though only a vehicle-only control isolates the solvent effect.

qs.q: What is the percent decrease in viability from the control to the 80 µM concentration?
qs.x: The control is 100 %. At 80 µM viability is 20 %, so the decrease is 100 % – 20 % = 80 %. Trap: Option B (50 %) might be chosen by students who mistakenly calculate the difference between 70 % (20 µM) and 20 % (80 µM) instead of comparing to the control.

qs.q: Which statement about the data is FALSE?
o: The viability decreases as drug concentration increases.
The standard deviation increases with higher drug concentrations.
The 10 µM concentration shows a lower viability than the 20 µM concentration.
The 0 µM concentration serves as the control and is set to 100 % viability.
qs.x: Viability falls with dose (100, 85, 70, 45, 20 %) and the SD rises monotonically (2, 3, 4, 5, 6), so A, B and D are true. C is false because 10 µM (85 %) has higher, not lower, viability than 20 µM (70 %). Trap: Option B looks suspicious because of the word 'increases', but the SD does increase at every step (2 to 6).

qs.q: Assuming viability falls linearly between the 20 µM and 40 µM points, at about what concentration would viability be 50% of control?
qs.x: Correct: C) Between 20 and 40 µM viability falls from 70% to 45%, or 1.25 percentage points per µM; dropping from 70% to 50% needs 16 µM, so about 36 µM. Why the others are wrong: A) 25 µM would give about 64%. B) 30 µM would give about 58%. D) 40 µM gives 45%, which is below 50%. Trap: Picking 40 µM because 45% is the closest tabulated value, without interpolating between the 20 and 40 µM points.

passages.title: Understanding social structure · passage
text: Social capital refers to resources available through social relationships. Bonding capital links similar people and supplies support, while bridging capital links different groups and supplies access. Communities with higher social capital often show better collective outcomes.
Investigators followed 90 neighborhoods for five years, measuring capital indicators and outcomes (Table 1).

qs.q: Which capital type best predicts employment gains here?
qs.x: Correct: Employment rose most in neighborhoods with high bridging capital, consistent with access to outside opportunity. Why the others are wrong: Bonding alone produced little gain, and the two types differ in effect. Trap: Assuming close community ties drive economic opportunity.

qs.q: What does bonding capital typically supply?
qs.x: Correct: Bonding capital provides solidarity and support among similar people. Why the others are wrong: The remaining options describe bridging, authority, and economic capital. Trap: Treating all social ties as interchangeable resources.

qs.q: Which limitation most affects causal claims?
qs.x: Correct: Neighborhoods were classified rather than assigned, so prior differences could drive both capital levels and employment change. Why the others are wrong: The remaining features are strengths. Trap: Treating a cohort design as experimental.

qs.q: Which type lost employment?
qs.x: Correct: Neighborhoods low on both measures were the only group to decline. Why the others are wrong: Each remaining type gained. Trap: Misreading the sign of the smallest gain.

qs.q: Which added measure would clarify the pathway?
qs.x: Correct: If bridging capital works by supplying access to opportunity, measuring referrals tests that pathway directly. Why the others are wrong: Population size, tenure, and prices do not measure access. Trap: Adding outcomes rather than the proposed mechanism.

passages.title: Social inequality · passage
text: Environmental justice concerns the unequal distribution of environmental hazards and benefits across social groups. Studies examine siting of polluting facilities, exposure levels, and whether disparities arise from siting decisions or from subsequent movement of residents.
Researchers examined 300 census tracts near industrial facilities (Table 1).

qs.q: What do these columns together show?
qs.x: Correct: Particulate exposure rises steadily with the share of low-income residents, which is the disparity environmental justice research describes. Why the others are wrong: The distribution is graded, the income direction is implausible, and most facilities are recent. Trap: Treating a graded disparity as random variation.

qs.q: Which question does the siting column help answer?
qs.x: Correct: Knowing when facilities were built addresses whether hazards were placed in already low-income areas or whether residents moved in afterward. Why the others are wrong: Harm, income accuracy, and comparability are different questions. Trap: Reading a timing variable as an exposure measure.

qs.q: Which design would best resolve the siting debate?
o: Finer exposure data do not help.
qs.x: Correct: Following neighborhood composition from before each facility was built distinguishes discriminatory siting from subsequent residential change. Why the others are wrong: More tracts, finer exposure data, and current surveys leave the timing unresolved. Trap: Improving exposure measurement when the question concerns sequence.

qs.q: Which quartile has the highest low-income share?
qs.x: Correct: The most exposed tracts have the largest share of low-income residents. Why the others are wrong: Each remaining quartile is lower. Trap: Reading the exposure column.

qs.q: Which added measure would link exposure to health?
qs.x: Correct: Health outcome data are needed to connect the documented exposure disparity to consequences for residents. Why the others are wrong: Facility counts, area, and rent do not measure health. Trap: Adding exposure detail instead of outcomes.

h: Mean annual particulate exposure, micrograms per cubic metre
Share of residents in the lowest income quartile

passages.title: Demographic characteristics and processes · passage
text: The demographic transition describes movement from high birth and death rates to low ones. Stage one has both high, stage two has falling deaths with births still high and rapid growth, stage three has falling births, and stage four has both low.
Researchers compiled vital statistics for four countries (Table 1).

qs.q: Which country is in stage two?
qs.x: Correct: Stage two is marked by mortality decline while fertility remains high, producing the fastest growth. Why the others are wrong: The remaining countries show both rates high, falling births, or both low. Trap: Assigning stage by growth rate alone.

qs.q: Which country shows the smallest natural increase?
qs.x: Correct: Natural increase is births minus deaths, which is only one per thousand in Country Z. Why the others are wrong: Each remaining country has a larger gap. Trap: Using the growth rate column, which also includes migration.

qs.q: Why can the growth rate differ from natural increase?
qs.x: Correct: Population growth combines natural increase with net migration, so the two columns need not match. Why the others are wrong: No counting or reporting problems were described, and the rates are current. Trap: Treating growth rate and natural increase as the same quantity.

qs.q: What characterizes stage four?
qs.x: Correct: In stage four birth and death rates are both low and population growth is minimal. Why the others are wrong: The remaining descriptions name earlier stages. Trap: Assuming stage four means population decline.

qs.q: Which additional measure would most improve stage assignment?
qs.x: Correct: The total fertility rate adjusts for age structure and so classifies fertility behavior more reliably than the crude birth rate. Why the others are wrong: Size, area, and income are not fertility measures. Trap: Using population size as a demographic stage indicator.

passages.title: Unique nature of water and its solutions · passage
text: Researchers studied the effect of varying environmental parameters on the growth rate of a marine bacterium, *Pseudoalteromonas marina*. The experiment was conducted in triplicate using a controlled incubator. In the control group, the temperature was maintained at 22 °C, the pH at 7.8, the nutrient concentration at 0.5 g L⁻¹, and the incubation time was 48 h. In the experimental group, the temperature was increased to 28 °C, the pH was lowered to 6.5, the nutrient concentration was doubled to 1.0 g L⁻¹, and the incubation time was extended to 72 h. At the end of incubation, bacterial density was measured using optical density at 600 nm. The control group exhibited an optical density of 0.45, whereas the experimental group reached 1.20. The researchers concluded that the combined changes in temperature, pH, nutrient concentration, and time together increased bacterial growth.

qs.q: Based on the data presented, which environmental parameter showed the greatest percent change relative to its control value?
qs.x: Correct: C) Nutrient concentration doubled from 0.5 to 1.0 g/L, a 100% increase. Why the others are wrong: A) Temperature rose 6 °C from 22 °C, about 27%. B) pH fell 1.3 from 7.8, about 17%. D) Incubation time rose 24 h from 48 h, 50%. Trap: Comparing raw differences across different units (24 h versus 6 °C versus 1.3 pH units) makes incubation time look largest; percent change relative to control puts them on one scale.

qs.q: Which modification to the experimental design would most directly test whether temperature alone is responsible for the observed increase in bacterial growth?
o: Include a second experimental group with temperature 28 °C but pH 7.8, nutrient concentration 0.5 g L⁻¹, and time 48 h.
Add a third group with temperature 22 °C, pH 6.5, nutrient concentration 1.0 g L⁻¹, and time 72 h.
This changes temperature, pH, nutrients and time all at once, so no single cause can be identified.
Run the experiment with temperature 28 °C, pH 6.5, nutrient concentration 1.0 g L⁻¹, but time 48 h.
This changes temperature and also pH and nutrients, so temperature's effect can't be separated out.
Repeat the original experiment but measure growth at 24 h intervals.
Measuring more often adds detail but doesn't separate temperature from the other variables.
qs.x: Group A isolates temperature as the variable by keeping all other parameters at control levels, allowing assessment of temperature’s independent effect. Trap: Option C is tempting because it keeps temperature high, but it still changes time, confounding the effect.

qs.q: Calculate the percent increase in optical density from the control to the experimental group.
o: 200% would mean OD tripled to 1.35, not 1.20.
267% comes from dividing 1.20 by 0.45 without subtracting the baseline first.
qs.x: Percent increase = (1.20 − 0.45)/0.45 × 100 = 166.7 % ≈ 167 %. Trap: Students sometimes subtract the control from the experimental and then divide by the experimental value, yielding an incorrect 63 %.

qs.q: What is the approximate change in hydrogen ion concentration between the control (pH 7.8) and experimental (pH 6.5) conditions?
qs.x: Correct: B) [H⁺] = 10⁻ᵖᴴ, so the ratio is 10^(7.8 - 6.5) = 10¹.3, about 20-fold higher at pH 6.5. Why the others are wrong: A) This treats the 1.3-unit pH difference as a fold change. C) 13 comes from multiplying 10 by 1.3 rather than raising 10 to the 1.3 power. D) 1.2 is the ratio 7.8/6.5 of the pH numbers, which ignores the logarithmic scale. Trap: Treating pH as a linear scale, so a 1.3-unit change is read as a 1.3-fold (or 1.2-fold) change in hydrogen ion concentration.

qs.q: Which conclusion is supported by the data and design described?
o: Density was higher in the experimental (OD 1.20) than control (0.45).
Raising the temperature to 28 °C alone increased bacterial growth.
The four changed parameters were shown to act synergistically.
Lowering the pH to 6.5 reduced bacterial growth.
qs.x: Correct: A) The measured optical densities were 1.20 (experimental) and 0.45 (control). Why the others are wrong: B) All four parameters changed together, so temperature alone cannot be credited. C) Synergy would need single-factor and combined groups to compare; none were run. D) The experimental group, which had the lower pH, grew more, and pH was not varied alone. Trap: Attributing the growth increase to one parameter or to synergy, even though all four parameters changed at once and no single-factor groups were run.

passages.title: Unique nature of water and its solutions · passage
text: Researchers investigated the antibacterial activity of a novel amphipathic peptide, designated AP‑42, against *Escherichia coli* cultured under controlled laboratory conditions. The study employed a factorial design with two independent variables: peptide concentration (0, 5, 10, 20, 40 µg/mL) and medium pH (5.5, 7.0, 8.5). For each treatment combination, bacterial growth was monitored by measuring optical density at 600 nm (OD600) over a 24‑hour period, and the maximum specific growth rate (μmax) was calculated from the exponential phase. The results, summarized in Table 1, indicate a dose‑dependent inhibition of growth at neutral and alkaline pH, whereas acidic pH attenuates the peptide’s efficacy. The authors concluded that AP‑42 exhibits potent antibacterial activity, particularly at pH 7.0 and 8.5, and suggested its potential as a therapeutic agent for infections in body sites with neutral to slightly alkaline pH. The data also raise questions about the peptide’s mechanism of action and its stability across pH ranges.

qs.q: Which peptide concentration at pH 7.0 produced the lowest μmax?
o: 5 µg/mL gave a higher μmax than 40 µg/mL; growth falls as concentration rises.
10 µg/mL still allowed more growth than the highest concentration.
20 µg/mL gave a higher μmax than 40 µg/mL.
qs.x: At pH 7.0 the μmax values decrease with increasing peptide concentration. The lowest μmax (0.15 h⁻¹) occurs at the highest concentration tested, 40 µg/mL. Trap: Option C (20 µg/mL) is tempting because it also shows a marked reduction, but it is not the lowest.

qs.q: Which of the following best describes the experimental design used in this study?
o: No participants were randomized to treatment and control arms in a clinical sense; two factors were varied in combination.
A cohort study follows a group over time without manipulating variables.
A case-control study compares groups chosen by outcome, which isn't what was done here.
qs.x: The investigators varied two independent variables (peptide concentration and pH) simultaneously and measured the outcome for each combination, which is the hallmark of a factorial design. Trap: Option A is plausible because the study involved controlled conditions, but it is not a randomized trial.

qs.q: If the μmax at 10 µg/mL and pH 7.0 is 0.45 h⁻¹, what is the percent reduction in μmax compared to the control (0 µg/mL) at the same pH, given the control μmax is 1.20 h⁻¹?
o: 25% would leave a μmax of 0.90 h⁻¹, not 0.45.
37.5% is the fraction remaining (0.45 ÷ 1.20), not the reduction.
qs.x: Reduction = (1.20 – 0.45)/1.20 = 0.75/1.20 = 0.625 = 62.5%. Trap: Option C (50%) is a common mis‑calculation if the difference is divided by the treated value instead of the control.

qs.q: Which statement is most likely incorrect regarding the peptide’s activity?
o: Activity is enhanced at higher pH
This is consistent with the data: the peptide works better at higher pH.
Activity is reduced at acidic pH
This is consistent with the data: acidic pH reduces activity.
This is consistent with the data: more peptide means more inhibition.
qs.x: The data show a clear dose‑dependent inhibition; activity is not independent of concentration. Trap: Option A may seem plausible because the peptide performs best at neutral/alkaline pH, but the statement is true, not false.

qs.q: Which additional experiment would best help elucidate the mechanism of action of AP‑42?
o: Determine the peptide’s secondary structure by circular dichroism
Circular dichroism shows the peptide's shape, not what it does to bacteria.
Measure the peptide’s half‑life in serum
Serum half-life is a pharmacokinetic question, not a mechanism question.
Assess the peptide’s effect on bacterial membrane potential
Evaluate the peptide’s toxicity in mammalian cell lines
Toxicity to mammalian cells is about safety, not how the peptide kills bacteria.
qs.x: Measuring changes in membrane potential directly probes whether the peptide disrupts bacterial membranes, a common antibacterial mechanism for amphipathic peptides. Trap: Option A is useful for structural characterization but does not reveal functional mechanism.

passages.title: Social inequality · passage
text: Social reproduction describes how advantage is transmitted across generations through schooling, networks, and credentials. Tracking, differential parental involvement, and unequal school resources are proposed channels, and interventions that change one channel may leave others intact.
Investigators followed 3,000 students from entry to graduation across schools with different practices (Table 1).

qs.q: Which practice combination worked best?
qs.x: Correct: Opening access and adding support produced both the highest advanced-course participation and the highest graduation rate. Why the others are wrong: Each remaining practice produced lower figures on both measures. Trap: Treating access alone as sufficient.

qs.q: What does the last row add?
qs.x: Correct: Open enrollment without added staffing produced smaller gains, showing that changing a rule without resources limits the effect. Why the others are wrong: Open enrollment still beat tracking, and staffing clearly mattered. Trap: Reading a weaker result as a failed policy.

qs.q: Which limitation most affects these conclusions?
qs.x: Correct: Because schools selected their own practices, school characteristics may explain the differences rather than the practices themselves. Why the others are wrong: The remaining features are appropriate. Trap: Reading a multi-school comparison as a randomized trial.

qs.q: Which channel does tracking represent?
qs.x: Correct: Tracking is a school practice that sorts students into different curricula, which is an institutional channel. Why the others are wrong: Involvement, networks, and credentials were not measured here. Trap: Naming a channel the study did not examine.

qs.q: Which added measure would test durability?
qs.x: Correct: Following students after graduation shows whether the gains persist into later education or work. Why the others are wrong: Grades, course counts, and teacher ratings are measured during school. Trap: Confusing more detail with longer follow-up.

h: Share of low-income students in advanced courses

passages.title: Demographic characteristics and processes · passage
text: Migration is described by push factors that drive people from an origin and pull factors that attract them to a destination. Internal migration occurs within a country, while immigration and emigration cross borders, and chain migration follows established networks.
A survey of 1,800 recent movers recorded stated reasons and destination choice (Table 1).

qs.q: Which reason is a push factor?
qs.x: Correct: Losing employment at the origin pushes people to leave. Why the others are wrong: Wages, reunification, and ties operate at the destination. Trap: Classifying any economic reason as a push factor.

qs.q: Which row best illustrates chain migration?
qs.x: Correct: Almost all movers citing reunification went to places where family already lived, which is the network-following pattern chain migration describes. Why the others are wrong: Each remaining row shows a lower share with existing ties. Trap: Choosing the most commonly cited reason instead of the most network-dependent one.

qs.q: Which limitation most affects these conclusions?
qs.x: Correct: Asking for the single most important reason hides the way push and pull factors typically operate together. Why the others are wrong: Sample size, self-report, and category count are appropriate here. Trap: Treating a forced single answer as a complete account of motive.

qs.q: What is emigration?
qs.x: Correct: Emigration is departure from one's country of origin. Why the others are wrong: The remaining options describe entry, internal movement, and return. Trap: Reversing immigration and emigration.

qs.q: Which added measure would test the network account?
qs.x: Correct: If prior contact with people at the destination predicts the move, the network pathway gains support. Why the others are wrong: Distance, age, and recency do not index network ties. Trap: Using geographic proximity as a proxy for social ties.

h: Share moving to a place with existing family ties

passages.title: Social interactions · passage
text: Impression management is the regulation of information about the self to shape how others perceive us. Goffman distinguished front-stage behavior, performed for an audience, from back-stage behavior, where the performance is relaxed.
Participants completed a self-description task believing it would be seen by a potential employer, a close friend, or no one, and the content was coded (Table 1).

qs.q: Which comparison shows front-stage behavior?
qs.x: Correct: Self-promotion rose sharply when an evaluating audience was expected, which is the front-stage performance Goffman described. Why the others are wrong: The friend comparison shows a small shift, and the remaining pairs hold audience type constant or vary two factors. Trap: Reading any audience effect as front-stage performance.

qs.q: What does the anonymity row show?
qs.x: Correct: Removing identifiability cut self-promotion nearly in half, indicating the behavior depends on being evaluated as an identified person. Why the others are wrong: Each remaining claim conflicts with the table. Trap: Treating an audience label as the active variable rather than accountability.

qs.q: Which added measure would test Goffman's back-stage claim?
qs.x: Correct: Back-stage behavior is defined by the absence of an audience, so unobtrusive observation when participants believe no one is watching tests the claim. Why the others are wrong: Extra audiences, longer tasks, and typing speed do not create a back-stage condition. Trap: Adding another audience when the claim concerns having none.

qs.q: Which row shows the most modesty?
qs.x: Correct: Modest statements were most common when writing for a close friend. Why the others are wrong: Each remaining row is lower. Trap: Assuming the no-audience row must be the most modest.

qs.q: Which term names managing a spoiled identity?
o: That assigns a role to another.
qs.x: Correct: Stigma management refers to controlling information about a devalued attribute. Why the others are wrong: The remaining terms describe performance, role demands, and casting others. Trap: Using front-stage behavior as a synonym for all impression management.

passages.title: Demographic characteristics and processes · passage
text: Fertility is measured by the crude birth rate and by the total fertility rate, the average number of children per woman. Replacement-level fertility is about 2.1 in low-mortality settings, and fertility typically falls as female education and labor force participation rise.
Researchers compared regions on fertility and related measures (Table 1).

qs.q: Which region is nearest replacement level?
qs.x: Correct: A total fertility rate of 2.2 is closest to the replacement figure of about 2.1. Why the others are wrong: Each remaining region is further from replacement. Trap: Choosing the lowest rate rather than the one nearest replacement.

qs.q: What pattern do the three columns show?
qs.x: Correct: Total fertility declines monotonically as female schooling and paid work both increase. Why the others are wrong: Each remaining claim contradicts the table. Trap: Assigning the pattern to one correlate when both move together.

qs.q: Why can this comparison not separate the two correlates?
qs.x: Correct: Because schooling and paid work rise together across these regions, their separate contributions cannot be estimated. Why the others are wrong: Sample size, measurement, and replacement level are not the obstacle. Trap: Blaming sample size for a collinearity problem.

qs.q: What does the total fertility rate measure?
qs.x: Correct: The total fertility rate is the average number of children a woman would have at current age-specific rates. Why the others are wrong: The remaining options define other measures. Trap: Confusing the total fertility rate with the crude birth rate.

qs.q: What would below-replacement fertility imply long term?
qs.x: Correct: Sustained fertility below replacement shrinks successive cohorts unless net migration compensates. Why the others are wrong: Decline is delayed by age structure, the child share falls, and the structure does change. Trap: Expecting immediate decline when momentum is present.

h: Share of women in paid work

passages.title: Principles of chemical thermodynamics and kinetics · passage
text: Hess's law states that the enthalpy change of a reaction is the sum of the enthalpy changes of any set of steps that lead from the same reactants to the same products, because enthalpy is a state function. Standard enthalpies of formation allow ΔH°rxn = Σ ΔH°f(products) − Σ ΔH°f(reactants).
Students used a calorimeter and published values (Table 1). All values are in kJ/mol.

qs.q: What is the calculated ΔH° for complete combustion of one mole of glucose?
qs.x: Correct: Products give 6(−393.5) + 6(−285.8) = −4,076 kJ; subtracting the reactant's −1,273 kJ gives −2,803 kJ, close to the measured −2,800 kJ. Why the others are wrong: Each omits a term or reverses the sign. Trap: Forgetting the coefficients of 6.

qs.q: Why is ΔH°f of O₂ zero?
o: Its formation is thermally neutral by coincidence
It is a definition, not a coincidence.
It is an element in its standard state
Oxygen does not participate in reactions
Enthalpy is measured relative to a reference.
qs.x: Correct: Standard enthalpies of formation are defined as zero for elements in their most stable form at standard conditions, which provides the reference point. Why the others are wrong: Enthalpy is relative; O₂ reacts; the value is definitional. Trap: Treating the zero as a physical measurement.

qs.q: Why is enthalpy called a state function?
o: It changes with the path taken
That describes work and heat separately.
It can be measured only in a calorimeter
Correct: the path does not matter.
It applies only to combustion reactions
qs.x: Correct: Because ΔH depends only on the states, any convenient sequence of steps gives the same total, which is the basis of Hess's law. Why the others are wrong: Path dependence applies to heat and work individually; ΔH can be calculated; it is general. Trap: Confusing enthalpy with heat along a specific path.

qs.q: Why does the measured value differ slightly from the calculated one?
o: Hess's law fails for large molecules
Enthalpy is not conserved in combustion
qs.x: Correct: A 3-kJ difference out of 2,800 kJ is within experimental uncertainty from incomplete combustion, heat escaping the calorimeter and sample impurities. Why the others are wrong: Hess's law holds; energy is conserved; the tabulated values are measurements. Trap: Treating a small discrepancy as a failure of theory.

qs.q: Why can glucose combustion be calculated by Hess's law even though cells oxidize glucose in many steps?
o: The overall change is path independent
Cells release a different total energy
The total enthalpy change is the same.
It also gives CO₂ and water.
Enzymes change the enthalpy of reaction
qs.x: Correct: Cellular respiration starts and ends with the same species, so the total enthalpy change matches combustion even though the energy is captured in ATP rather than released as heat. Why the others are wrong: The total is the same; catalysts do not change ΔH; the products match. Trap: Confusing how energy is released with how much is released.

passages.title: Attitude and behavior change · passage
text: Cognitive dissonance theory proposes that acting against one's own attitude produces an unpleasant state of tension. People can reduce the tension by changing the attitude so that it fits the behavior. A competing view, self-perception theory, holds that people simply infer their attitudes from their behavior, as an outside observer would, without any tension being involved. One way to separate the two accounts is to give people a different explanation for any tension they feel. If tension drives attitude change, people who can blame their tension on something else should have less need to change their attitude.

Researchers recruited 150 undergraduates who opposed a proposed $400 increase in the student activity fee. Each wrote a persuasive essay in favor of the increase. In the high-choice conditions, the experimenter said that writing the essay was voluntary, although all participants agreed. In the low-choice condition, participants were told the essay was required. Before writing, high-choice participants swallowed an inert capsule described as a memory supplement. One group was told it had no side effects. A second group was told it often makes people feel tense, and a third group was told it often makes people feel relaxed. A control group wrote no essay. Afterward, participants rated their own tension and their attitude toward the fee increase (Table 1).

Self-perception theory makes a different prediction for the capsule conditions. If people simply read their attitudes from their behavior, a story about the capsule should not matter, because the behavior, a freely written essay, was identical across the three high-choice groups. Dissonance theory predicts that the capsule story should matter a great deal, because it changes how people explain the tension they feel. The researchers chose the fee increase because a pilot survey showed that 88% of students opposed it, so writing in favor would be inconsistent with the views of most participants.\nT Participants were assigned to conditions at random, and the person who scored the attitude scales did not know each participant's condition.

qs.q: Why did the high-choice, no-side-effects group shift its attitude more than the low-choice group?
o: Choosing the act freely creates more dissonance
Correct: choice removes the outside excuse.
High-choice participants were paid for agreeing
Required essays are more persuasive to the writer
The required essay produced little change.
Low-choice participants did not write an essay
qs.x: Correct: When the essay is required, the instruction itself explains the behavior, so there is little tension to resolve. When people believe they chose to argue against their own view, the inconsistency is theirs to explain, tension rises (6.2 versus 3.1), and attitudes move toward the essay (7.9 versus 3.6). Why the others are wrong: The required essay produced almost no change; no reward was offered; both groups wrote essays. Trap: Assuming that saying something always changes attitudes, regardless of choice.

qs.q: Which interpretation best fits the group told the capsule causes tension?
o: They chose not to write the essay after hearing the warning
The capsule reduced their tension, so dissonance disappeared
The warning made the essay feel required
Choice was still described as voluntary.
They blamed their tension on the capsule
Correct: misattribution removed the need to change.
qs.x: Correct: This group felt as tense as the other high-choice groups (6.0) but changed its attitude very little (4.0). Having a ready external cause for the tension meant the essay no longer seemed responsible for it, so there was no pressure to change the attitude. Why the others are wrong: Tension was still high, so the capsule did not remove it; every participant wrote an essay; the choice instructions were the same as in the other high-choice groups. Trap: Equating a lack of attitude change with a lack of arousal.

qs.q: Why did the group told the capsule would relax them show the largest attitude change?
o: The capsule raised their liking for the experimenter
The relaxing suggestion made them agree more readily
Agreement was the same in all groups.
They felt less tension than the other high-choice groups
They blamed even more of their tension on the essay
Correct: more tension attributed to the act.
qs.x: Correct: These participants expected to feel calm, yet they felt tense (6.4). The only remaining explanation was the essay, so they attributed even more of the tension to their own counter-attitudinal act and shifted their attitude the most (9.6). Why the others are wrong: All high-choice participants agreed to write; liking was not measured; their tension was the highest of any group. Trap: Expecting a relaxant to reduce attitude change because it should reduce arousal.

qs.q: Which result would most weaken the claim that tension drives the attitude change in this study?
o: Low-choice participants report only a little tension
High-choice participants report the most tension
Attitudes shift equally in every high-choice group
The control group reports the lowest tension
That is expected under both theories.
qs.x: Correct: Self-perception theory predicts that attitudes follow behavior whatever people believe about their arousal. If the misattribution groups had changed just as much as the no-side-effects group, tension would not be doing the work. The actual drop to 4.0 in the tension-capsule group is what favors dissonance theory. Why the others are wrong: Low tension in the control and low-choice groups and high tension in the high-choice groups are all consistent with, or support, the dissonance account. Trap: Choosing a result that agrees with the claim when the question asks what would weaken it.

qs.q: A patient who chose a painful and costly rehabilitation program later rates it as more helpful than a patient assigned to the same program. Which process does this most directly illustrate?
o: Correct: a costly, chosen effort is valued more.
That concerns compliance after a small request.
That concerns explaining other people's behavior.
That concerns credit for success and failure.
qs.x: Correct: Effort justification is a form of dissonance reduction. Freely choosing something painful and expensive conflicts with the thought that it might not be worth it, so people resolve the tension by valuing it more. The assigned patient has an outside explanation and less need to justify the effort. Why the others are wrong: Self-serving bias concerns taking credit for success and blaming failure on circumstances; the foot-in-the-door effect involves agreeing to a large request after a small one; the fundamental attribution error concerns judging others. Trap: Choosing a familiar social-psychology term that sounds related but describes a different process.

h: Attitude toward fee increase (1 = strongly oppose, 15 = strongly favor)
r: Low choice, no side effects mentioned
High choice, no side effects mentioned
High choice, capsule said to cause tension
High choice, capsule said to relax

passages.title: Nervous and endocrine systems and how they coordinate organ systems · passage
text: Researchers studied the effect of a novel neuroprotective agent on neuronal survival after ischemic injury in a rodent model. Eighty rats were randomly assigned to one of four groups: a control group receiving vehicle, a low‑dose group (10 mg/kg), a medium‑dose group (30 mg/kg), and a high‑dose group (50 mg/kg). After 24 hours of induced ischemia, neuronal survival was quantified by counting surviving neurons in the hippocampal CA1 region. Results were expressed as mean ± standard deviation (SD) and compared using one‑way ANOVA with post‑hoc Tukey tests. The study found a dose‑dependent increase in neuronal survival, with the high‑dose group showing a statistically significant improvement (p < 0.01) over the control. The authors concluded that the neuroprotective agent could be a promising therapeutic candidate for ischemic stroke. The data table below summarizes the key findings for each treatment group.

qs.q: Which treatment group exhibited the highest mean neuronal survival after ischemic injury?
qs.x: The high‑dose group (50 mg/kg) reported the greatest mean neuronal survival (68.3 ± 5.9 neurons/section), surpassing all other groups. Trap: Choosing the control or a lower dose; the highest mean neuronal survival is the high-dose group's 68.3 neurons/section.

qs.q: Which feature of the experimental design described in the passage most directly reduces the chance that pre‑existing differences between rats explain the differences in neuronal survival?
o: Random assignment of rats to treatment groups
Counting surviving neurons in the hippocampal CA1 region
Analyzing the data with one‑way ANOVA and post‑hoc Tukey tests
qs.x: Correct: Random assignment spreads pre-existing differences among rats evenly across groups by chance, so they are unlikely to account for group differences. Why the others are wrong: B) Counting neurons in CA1 defines the outcome measure and does nothing about group composition. C) ANOVA with Tukey tests is a statistical analysis applied after the data are collected and does not alter who is in which group. D) Several doses allow a dose-response to be seen but do not balance rat characteristics across groups. Trap: Selecting the dose-response feature because the passage stresses a dose-dependent effect, although it does not address baseline differences between animals.

qs.q: Calculate the absolute difference in mean neuronal survival between the high‑dose and control groups.
qs.x: Difference = 68.3 - 45.2 = 23.1 neurons/section. Trap: Option B (28.1) is not obtained by any correct operation; adding SDs (5.3 + 5.9 = 11.2) or subtracting the wrong rows also gives wrong values.

qs.q: Which statement is a common misinterpretation of the study’s findings?
o: The low‑dose group’s difference from control did not reach p < 0.05 (p = 0.08).
The high-dose group's improvement over control was statistically significant (p < 0.01).
Mean neuronal survival rose with increasing dose.
The study proves the agent will work in humans.
qs.x: Correct: A rodent study cannot prove efficacy in humans; the statement that it does is the misinterpretation. Why the others are wrong: A) the low-dose p-value in Table 1 is 0.08, above 0.05, so this is accurate. B) the table reports p < 0.01 for the high dose, so this is accurate. C) mean survival rose from 45.2 to 52.1, 58.7 and 68.3 neurons/section with dose, so this is accurate. Trap: Treating a significant result in rats as proof of efficacy in humans.

qs.q: How do these findings contribute to the broader understanding of neuroprotection after ischemic injury?
o: They demonstrate that any drug can protect neurons.
They support dose‑dependent neuroprotection by targeted agents.
They prove that ischemic injury is reversible.
They show that vehicle controls are unnecessary.
qs.x: The study provides evidence that increasing doses of a specific agent enhance neuronal survival, aligning with the concept that targeted neuroprotective strategies can mitigate ischemic damage. Trap: Option A overstates the generalizability of the results.

passages.title: How light and sound interact with matter · passage
text: Researchers investigated the effect of varying concentrations of the inhibitor X on the activity of enzyme Y. The enzyme activity was quantified by measuring the absorbance at 340 nm, which correlates with product formation. Five concentrations of inhibitor X (0, 5, 10, 20, and 40 µM) were tested in triplicate. The results are summarized in Table 1 below. The data show a clear dose‑dependent decrease in absorbance, suggesting inhibition of enzyme Y. The researchers noted that at concentrations above 20 µM, the absorbance values plateaued, indicating possible saturation of the inhibitory effect. The study aims to determine the IC50 value of inhibitor X and to evaluate whether the inhibition follows a competitive or non‑competitive mechanism.

qs.q: Based on Table 1, which concentration of inhibitor X results in the greatest reduction in enzyme activity compared to the control?
o: 5 µM reduced activity less than the higher concentrations did.
20 µM reduced activity by 44%, just short of 40 µM's 45.6%.
qs.x: Absorbance at 40 uM (0.68) is the lowest, a reduction of (1.25-0.68)/1.25 = 45.6% versus 44.0% at 20 uM. The effect is nearly plateaued but 40 uM is still marginally greatest. Trap: Choosing 20 uM because inhibition plateaus there; the 40 uM value is still slightly lower.

qs.q: Which control would best show that inhibitor X itself does not change the 340 nm reading independent of the enzyme?
o: Inhibitor X at each concentration in assay buffer with no enzyme
Enzyme and substrate with no inhibitor (0 µM)
Enzyme without substrate at 40 µM inhibitor
qs.x: Correct: Inhibitor X in buffer with no enzyme reveals any absorbance or reaction contributed by X alone. Why the others are wrong: B) this is the 0 µM control already in the table and contains no inhibitor. C) a buffer‑only blank contains no inhibitor, so it cannot reveal an effect of X. D) without substrate no product forms, so this does not isolate the inhibitor's effect on the reading. Trap: Option C tempts readers to treat a buffer blank as a control for the inhibitor.

qs.q: Calculate the percent inhibition of enzyme Y at 10 µM inhibitor X relative to the control.
o: 30% comes from treating the 0.30 drop as a percentage without dividing by 1.25.
50% would need absorbance to fall to about 0.63.
qs.x: Percent inhibition = (1.25 - 0.95)/1.25 x 100 = 0.30/1.25 x 100 = 24%. Trap: Reporting 30% (the raw absorbance difference x100) without dividing by the control value of 1.25.

qs.q: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by Table 1?
o: Absorbance fell as inhibitor concentration rose from 0 to 20 µM.
Absorbance at 40 µM was only 0.02 lower than at 20 µM.
Enzyme activity was completely abolished at 40 µM.
Absorbance at 10 µM was lower than at 5 µM.
qs.x: Correct: Absorbance at 40 µM was still 0.68, versus 1.25 for the control, so substantial activity remained. Why the others are wrong: A) values were 1.25, 1.10, 0.95 and 0.70. B) 0.70 minus 0.68 is 0.02. D) 0.95 is lower than 1.10. Trap: Option C tempts readers to equate a plateau with zero activity.

qs.q: Which broader pharmacological concept does this study exemplify?
o: The study measured enzyme activity, not how strongly a drug binds a receptor.
Absorption is about how a drug enters the body, which wasn't measured.
Clearance is about how a drug is removed, which wasn't measured.
qs.x: The study demonstrates a classic dose–response curve, where increasing inhibitor concentration leads to progressively greater inhibition of enzyme activity. Trap: Students may confuse binding affinity (A) with the observed dose–response relationship.

passages.title: Unique nature of water and its solutions · passage
text: Researchers investigated the impact of a novel probiotic strain, L. fermentum X, on the gut microbiome composition and fecal pH levels in a controlled mouse model. Twenty-four male C57BL/6 mice were randomly assigned to three groups: Control (no probiotic), Placebo (vehicle only), and Treatment (daily oral gavage of 1×10⁹ CFU L. fermentum X). Over a 4‑week period, fecal samples were collected weekly and analyzed for pH and microbial diversity via 16S rRNA sequencing. The probiotic group exhibited a statistically significant reduction in fecal pH (6.5 versus 7.2 in the Control group), alongside an increase in beneficial Bacteroidetes relative abundance. No adverse effects were observed. The study suggests that L. fermentum X may modulate gut acidity and microbial balance, potentially influencing host metabolic pathways.

qs.q: Which statement best describes the change in mean fecal pH observed in the Treatment group compared to the Control group?
o: The mean fecal pH increased by 0.7 units.
pH fell from 7.2 to 6.5, so it didn't increase.
The mean fecal pH decreased by 0.7 units.
The mean fecal pH decreased by 0.5 units.
The mean fecal pH remained unchanged.
The mean changed by 0.7 units, so it wasn't unchanged.
qs.x: Mean pH fell from 7.2 to 6.5, a 0.7‑unit decrease. Trap: Option A misleads by stating an increase rather than a decrease.

qs.q: Which comparison best isolates the effect of L. fermentum X itself from the effect of the gavage vehicle?
o: Control at week 1 versus Control at week 4
qs.x: Correct: Treatment and Placebo mice both received gavage, so they differ only in the probiotic (6.5 versus 7.1, a 0.6 difference). Why the others are wrong: A) Control mice received no gavage, so this comparison mixes probiotic and vehicle effects. C) this comparison shows only the vehicle effect (0.1 unit). D) this compares the same untreated group over time and says nothing about the probiotic. Trap: Comparing Treatment with the untreated Control, which confounds the probiotic with the vehicle and gavage procedure.

qs.q: What is the percent reduction in mean fecal pH from Control to Treatment?
o: 12.5% would be a drop of 0.9 units.
15.8% is too large for a 0.7 drop from 7.2.
20% would be a drop of about 1.4 units.
