qs.x: Percent reduction = (7.2 − 6.5)/7.2 × 100 ≈ 9.7 %. Trap: Using the wrong baseline for percent change; the 0.7 pH drop must be divided by the Control mean (7.2), not the Treatment mean.

qs.q: Which conclusion is NOT supported by the data presented?
o: L. fermentum X lowers fecal pH in mice.
The data support this: treated mice had lower fecal pH.
The probiotic group had a higher mean pH than the Control group.
The vehicle alone had a minor effect on pH.
The data support this: the vehicle had only a small effect.
No adverse effects were observed in the Treatment group.
The passage supports this: no adverse effects were seen.
qs.x: The Treatment group’s mean pH (6.5) is lower than the Control group’s (7.2), so option B is false. All other statements are supported by the data. Trap: Option A is tempting because it states the correct effect, but the question asks for the unsupported conclusion.

qs.q: Which broader physiological concept is most directly linked to the observed decrease in fecal pH?
o: Insulin resistance isn't directly tied to gut pH.
Renal acid-base balance concerns blood pH, not the gut lumen.
Brain neurotransmission doesn't explain a drop in fecal pH.
qs.x: Lower fecal pH often reflects increased SCFA production by gut microbes, which acidify the lumen. SCFAs are linked to metabolic health, making option B the most relevant link. Trap: Option A might attract students due to the metabolic focus, but insulin resistance is not directly measured here.

passages.title: Attitude and behavior change · passage
text: The elaboration likelihood model distinguishes central-route processing, in which argument quality drives persuasion under high motivation and ability, from peripheral-route processing, in which cues such as source attractiveness or message length drive persuasion under low motivation or ability.

Adults read a message supporting a new campus policy. Personal relevance was manipulated by saying the policy would start next year or in ten years. Argument quality and source expertise were varied independently (Table 1).

qs.q: Which pattern indicates central-route processing?
o: Source expertise mattered under low relevance
Argument quality mattered under high relevance
Expert sources produced change under high relevance
Attitude change was positive in every cell
qs.x: Correct: Under high relevance, strong arguments produced far more change than weak ones regardless of source, which is the signature of effortful argument scrutiny. Why the others are wrong: The expertise effect under low relevance is peripheral, overall direction says nothing about route, and the expert cells differ mainly by quality. Trap: Reading any large effect as central processing.

qs.q: Which cell pair isolates the peripheral cue?
o: High relevance expert versus low relevance expert
Low relevance strong versus high relevance weak
qs.x: Correct: Holding relevance low and argument quality constant while varying source expertise isolates the effect of a peripheral cue. Why the others are wrong: The remaining comparisons vary quality, relevance, or both. Trap: Comparing cells that differ on more than one factor.

qs.q: Why is peripheral persuasion typically less durable?
o: It depends on source memory alone
qs.x: Correct: Attitudes formed without elaboration lack supporting argument structure, so they are less resistant to counterargument and decay faster. Why the others are wrong: Immediate magnitude, repetition, and source recall do not define durability. Trap: Equating a large initial shift with a lasting one.

qs.q: Which added condition would best test ability rather than motivation?
o: Tell participants the policy starts sooner
Offer a reward for reading carefully
qs.x: Correct: A distraction limits the cognitive capacity available for elaboration while leaving motivation intact, which separates ability from motivation. Why the others are wrong: Timing and rewards manipulate motivation, and length functions as a cue. Trap: Treating all manipulations of elaboration as equivalent.

qs.q: What does the low-relevance, non-expert cell show?
qs.x: Correct: Without motivation or a credible cue, neither message produced meaningful change. Why the others are wrong: The quality gap was negligible, change was positive, and no expert cue was present. Trap: Reading a trivial difference as an effect.

passages.title: Responding to the world · passage
text: In classical conditioning, a neutral stimulus paired with an unconditioned stimulus (US) comes to elicit a conditioned response. Taste aversion learning is unusual: a single pairing works, and the delay between tasting and illness can be hours. This selectivity (preparedness) reflects the adaptive value of associating flavors, rather than sights or sounds, with sickness.
Rats drank flavored water and then received one of several treatments. Later, consumption of the flavored water was measured (Table 1).

qs.q: Why does nausea produce aversion to flavor but shock does not?
o: They avoided the light paired with shock.
Nausea is more painful than shock
Pain intensity is not the explanation.
Shock is not an unconditioned stimulus
It is a strong US for other associations.
qs.x: Correct: Animals readily link tastes with internal illness and external cues with external pain, a selectivity that reflects evolved predispositions. Why the others are wrong: Shock conditions other cues well; rats detect shock; intensity is not the factor. Trap: Ranking stimuli by strength instead of by biological fit.

qs.q: Why is the 6-hour delay result notable for conditioning theory?
o: Most conditioning needs a short delay
Delay has no effect on any learning
qs.x: Correct: In typical classical conditioning, intervals longer than seconds to minutes produce weak learning, yet taste aversion forms across hours, which fits the slow onset of real food poisoning. Why the others are wrong: Delays weaken most conditioning; learning occurred; the delay did matter. Trap: Generalizing one exception to all conditioning.

qs.q: In this experiment, what is the unconditioned stimulus?
o: It is part of the apparatus.
Correct: it causes nausea without learning.
qs.x: Correct: Lithium chloride produces nausea naturally, so it is the US; the flavor becomes the conditioned stimulus. Why the others are wrong: The flavor is the CS, avoidance is the CR, and the bottle is context. Trap: Mislabeling the CS as the US.

qs.q: A patient receiving chemotherapy develops nausea at the sight of the clinic. Which process explains this?
qs.x: Correct: The clinic becomes a conditioned stimulus through pairing with the nausea-inducing drug, producing anticipatory nausea before treatment. Why the others are wrong: No reinforcement of a voluntary response occurs; direct experience explains it; habituation reduces responses. Trap: Choosing operant conditioning for any learned clinical response.

qs.q: Why does the light-shock result support the preparedness idea?
o: Correct: matching cue types learn best.
Shock produces no learning at all
qs.x: Correct: Rats learned to avoid the light paired with shock while ignoring the flavor, which shows that cue-outcome pairings follow biologically sensible lines. Why the others are wrong: The light was conditioned; shock produced learning; preference is irrelevant. Trap: Concluding a stimulus cannot be conditioned at all.

passages.title: Attitude and behavior change · passage
text: The foot-in-the-door technique obtains compliance with a large request by first securing agreement to a small one, which shifts self-perception toward being a helpful person. The door-in-the-face technique works in reverse, using reciprocal concession after an extreme request is refused.

Canvassers approached 600 households about placing a large yard sign supporting road safety. Some were first asked to sign a petition, others to accept an extreme request, and others were asked directly (Table 1).

qs.q: Which result best supports a self-perception account?
o: Removal times were shortest in the direct group
qs.x: Correct: Longer retention after the small request suggests participants came to see themselves as supporters rather than merely yielding to pressure in the moment. Why the others are wrong: The extreme-request effect reflects concession, and the direct group is a baseline with few placements. Trap: Treating compliance rates alone as evidence about mechanism.

qs.q: What does the last row suggest?
o: That row used no extreme request.
qs.x: Correct: Compliance fell sharply when a different canvasser made the second request, indicating the effect depends partly on continuity of the interaction. Why the others are wrong: The petition still outperformed baseline, no concession was involved, and retention remained long. Trap: Concluding a technique failed when it merely weakened.

qs.q: Which design flaw most threatens these conclusions?
qs.x: Correct: Without random assignment, pre-existing differences between households could produce the compliance differences independently of technique. Why the others are wrong: Recording, single-site sampling, and constant message content are not internal-validity threats here. Trap: Confusing limited generalization with confounding.

qs.q: Which request sequence defines door-in-the-face?
o: Extreme request, then a smaller one
Small request, then a larger one
qs.x: Correct: Door-in-the-face begins with an extreme request that is expected to be refused, so the smaller follow-up appears as a concession. Why the others are wrong: Each remaining sequence describes the other technique or a control. Trap: Reversing the two sequences.

qs.q: Which measure would best distinguish the two mechanisms?
o: Number of signs on nearby lawns
Total time spent with the canvasser
qs.x: Correct: Self-perception predicts a shift in self-image, whereas reciprocal concession does not, so measuring self-image separates the accounts. Why the others are wrong: Duration, neighborhood signs, and income do not distinguish the mechanisms. Trap: Choosing a measure that both accounts predict equally.

h: Share agreeing to the large sign
Mean days before the sign was removed
r: Extreme request first, then the sign

passages.title: Responding to the world · passage
text: In operant conditioning, reinforcement schedules affect response rate and persistence. Continuous reinforcement rewards every response. Fixed-ratio schedules reward after a set number of responses and produce bursts with brief post-reinforcement pauses; variable-ratio schedules reward after an unpredictable number and produce high steady rates that resist extinction. Fixed-interval schedules produce scalloped patterns.
Pigeons were trained on different schedules, then reinforcement was discontinued (Table 1).

qs.q: Why is the variable-ratio group most resistant to extinction?
o: It received the most total reinforcements
It was trained for the longest time
Correct: the animal cannot tell when reward stopped.
qs.x: Correct: Because reinforcement already came after unpredictable numbers of responses, a long run without reward resembles normal training, so responding continues far longer. Why the others are wrong: Reinforcement rate, effort and training were matched. Trap: Attributing persistence to the amount of reward.

qs.q: Why does the fixed-interval schedule give a lower response rate?
o: Pigeons cannot track time at all
Only one response after the interval is needed.
qs.x: Correct: Only the first response after the interval elapses is reinforced, so rapid early responding gains nothing and animals pause then accelerate near the end. Why the others are wrong: Reinforcement occurs; pigeons track intervals; fewer responses are required. Trap: Confusing interval and ratio requirements.

qs.q: Which schedule describes a slot machine?
o: Payouts would come on a clock.
Correct: payouts come after unpredictable numbers of plays.
qs.x: Correct: Slot machines pay after an unpredictable number of plays, which produces high steady play and strong persistence. Why the others are wrong: Each would make payouts predictable in count or time. Trap: Confusing variable ratio with variable interval.

qs.q: A parent sometimes gives in to a child's tantrums. Why does this make tantrums persistent?
qs.x: Correct: Occasional success creates a variable-ratio pattern, which is the most resistant to extinction, so the behavior continues through many unrewarded episodes. Why the others are wrong: Reinforcement is intermittent, not continuous; giving in rewards; extinction is possible. Trap: Thinking inconsistent reward weakens a behavior.

qs.q: Why does continuous reinforcement extinguish fastest?
o: Correct: every response used to pay.
It produces the highest response rate
It involves no learning at all
qs.x: Correct: When every response has been rewarded, the first few unrewarded responses are a clear signal that conditions have changed, so responding stops quickly. Why the others are wrong: Its rate was the lowest; learning occurred; it uses the most rewards. Trap: Assuming more reward always means stronger behavior.

passages.title: Responding to the world · passage
text: Observational learning occurs when behavior is acquired by watching a model, without direct reinforcement of the observer. Bandura's work identified four necessary processes: attention, retention, reproduction and motivation. Vicarious reinforcement, in which the model is seen to be rewarded, raises the chance that the observer performs the behavior.
Children watched a video of an adult acting aggressively toward a toy, with different endings, then played alone (Table 1). Aggressive acts were counted over 10 minutes.

qs.q: Why do children who saw the model rewarded act most aggressively?
o: They could not remember the video
They were themselves rewarded with candy
Aggression is unlearned in all children
qs.x: Correct: Seeing the model rewarded increases the observer's expectation that the behavior pays, which raises performance even though the child was never reinforced. Why the others are wrong: Children got no reward; memory was required; the control group differed. Trap: Confusing vicarious with direct reinforcement.

qs.q: Why do children who saw the model scolded still act somewhat aggressively?
o: Their rate matched the control group
They did not watch the video
qs.x: Correct: Observers acquire the behavior regardless of the model's outcome; consequences mainly affect whether they choose to perform it, so a small amount of imitation remains. Why the others are wrong: They watched; scolding discourages; their rate exceeded control. Trap: Equating no performance with no learning.

qs.q: Which process is required for a child to copy a complex action?
o: Observational learning does not require it.
Behavior is not inherited this way.
qs.x: Correct: Bandura identified attention, retention, reproduction and motivation; without retaining a representation, the behavior cannot be reproduced later. Why the others are wrong: Direct reinforcement is not required; classical conditioning and inheritance are different processes. Trap: Assuming all learning requires reinforcement of the learner.

qs.q: Why does this design include a group with no video?
o: It tests whether children can see
It proves that videos cause aggression
Causal claims need the comparison itself.
It increases the number of conditions only
It shows the baseline rate of aggression
qs.x: Correct: Without a no-video baseline of 1.9 acts, there would be no way to judge how much each video ending raised aggression. Why the others are wrong: Vision is not tested; the group serves a purpose; the claim rests on the comparison. Trap: Dismissing a control as a formality.

qs.q: Why might these findings not generalize to everyday media exposure?
o: A brief lab session differs from daily life
Children in the study were not real participants
Observational learning does not occur outside labs
qs.x: Correct: Short exposure, an unfamiliar setting, a specific toy and immediate opportunity to imitate differ from the varied and socially regulated conditions of daily media use. Why the others are wrong: Participants and measurements were real; observational learning is general. Trap: Rejecting the mechanism rather than questioning generalization.

passages.title: Social interactions · passage
text: Nonverbal communication includes facial expression, gaze, posture, gesture, and paralanguage. Some facial expressions of basic emotion show high cross-cultural recognition, while gestures and display rules vary widely by culture.
Participants from four regions identified photographed expressions and culture-specific gestures (Table 1).

qs.q: Which stimulus type shows the strongest cultural specificity?
qs.x: Correct: Gesture recognition fell by 57 points across regions, far more than any other stimulus, which marks it as culturally learned. Why the others are wrong: Each remaining type shows a modest decline. Trap: Assuming all nonverbal channels are equally universal.

qs.q: What does the facial expression row support?
qs.x: Correct: High but not perfect cross-regional accuracy supports a universal core modified by cultural factors. Why the others are wrong: The remaining claims overstate or contradict the row. Trap: Reading high accuracy as evidence of complete universality.

qs.q: Which concept explains why expressions are suppressed in some settings?
o: Correct: cultural norms for showing emotion.
qs.x: Correct: Display rules are culturally learned norms governing when and how strongly emotions may be shown. Why the others are wrong: The remaining terms name a theory, vocal features, and spatial behavior. Trap: Explaining suppression by the absence of the emotion.

qs.q: What is paralanguage?
qs.x: Correct: Paralanguage covers nonverbal vocal features such as tone, pitch, and rate. Why the others are wrong: The remaining options name verbal content, gesture, and posture. Trap: Including word choice in paralanguage.

qs.q: Which design feature strengthens these comparisons?
qs.x: Correct: Presenting the same photographs and clips to every region ensures that differences reflect the viewers rather than the stimuli. Why the others are wrong: Region count, outcome choice, and age range do not control stimulus differences. Trap: Mistaking sample breadth for stimulus control.

passages.title: Social interactions · passage
text: Attraction is shaped by proximity, which increases mere exposure and the chance of interaction, and by similarity, reciprocity, and physical attractiveness. The mere exposure effect describes increased liking for repeatedly encountered stimuli.
Residents of a new apartment building were surveyed about friendships after one year, with assignment to units made by lottery (Table 1).

qs.q: Why does the lottery strengthen this study?
o: The survey came after a year
qs.x: Correct: Random allocation of units means residents did not choose neighbors they already liked, so proximity can be treated as an assigned variable. Why the others are wrong: Survey timing, group count, and self-report do not address selection. Trap: Treating a long follow-up as a substitute for assignment.

qs.q: Which mechanism do the encounter data support?
qs.x: Correct: Friendship rates rose with reported encounters, which is the pathway the mere exposure account predicts. Why the others are wrong: None of the remaining factors were measured in this study. Trap: Invoking a mechanism the design did not assess.

qs.q: Which finding would most complicate the proximity account?
qs.x: Correct: If friendship rates were unrelated to encounter frequency, proximity could not be acting through exposure and interaction. Why the others are wrong: Each remaining result is consistent with the account. Trap: Treating a predicted result as a complication.

qs.q: Which comparison isolates floor separation?
qs.x: Correct: Comparing residents four doors apart on one floor with residents on different floors sharing a stairwell holds walking distance roughly constant while varying floor. Why the others are wrong: The remaining comparisons vary two factors or hold floor constant. Trap: Comparing the extreme rows.

qs.q: What is the mere exposure effect?
qs.x: Correct: Repeated encounters with a neutral stimulus tend to increase liking for it. Why the others are wrong: The remaining options name other determinants of attraction. Trap: Merging exposure with similarity.

h: Share naming the other as a friend

passages.title: Social inequality · passage
text: Health insurance affects access through coverage breadth, cost sharing, and network adequacy. Underinsurance describes having coverage that still leaves high out-of-pocket costs, and coverage alone does not guarantee timely care.
A survey of 5,000 adults recorded coverage type and care experiences (Table 1).

qs.q: Which group best illustrates underinsurance?
qs.x: Correct: Adults with high-deductible plans had coverage but still faced substantial out-of-pocket burden and frequent cost-related delay, which is the definition of underinsurance. Why the others are wrong: The uninsured are not insured at all, and the remaining groups show lower cost burden. Trap: Equating any access problem with underinsurance.

qs.q: Which barrier does the narrow network row highlight?
qs.x: Correct: With low cost burden but elevated delay, the limiting factor is the availability of participating providers. Why the others are wrong: Cost burden was low, coverage was present, and literacy was not measured. Trap: Attributing every access problem to cost.

qs.q: Which inference is unwarranted?
qs.x: Correct: People select or are sorted into coverage types by income, employment, and health, so a causal claim is not supported. Why the others are wrong: Each remaining statement is descriptive. Trap: Treating coverage categories as an assigned treatment.

qs.q: Which group least often had a usual source of care?
qs.x: Correct: Uninsured adults least often reported a usual source of care. Why the others are wrong: Each remaining group was higher. Trap: Reading the delay column.

qs.q: Which policy would the table most support?
qs.x: Correct: Because covered adults with high deductibles still delayed care, reducing cost sharing addresses the gap the table documents. Why the others are wrong: Coverage counts alone miss underinsurance, narrower networks worsen access, and data publication does not change costs. Trap: Measuring success by coverage rates alone.

h: Share delaying care due to cost
Mean out-of-pocket spending as a share of income
Share with a usual source of care

passages.title: Structure, function, and reactivity of biologically relevant molecules · passage
text: Glucose in solution cyclizes when the C5 hydroxyl attacks the C1 aldehyde, forming a six-membered pyranose ring with a new stereocenter at C1 (the anomeric carbon). β-D-glucopyranose has the C1 OH equatorial; α-D-glucopyranose has it axial. The two anomers interconvert through the open-chain form, a process called anomerization, and reducing sugars have a free anomeric carbon that can be oxidized.
Students dissolved pure α-D-glucose in water and followed the optical rotation over time (Table 1).

qs.q: Why does the rotation change over time?
o: The ring opens permanently to the straight chain
The open form is a minor intermediate.
Correct: the mixture reaches a fixed ratio.
qs.x: Correct: α-D-glucose opens to the aldehyde and recloses as either anomer until the equilibrium mixture of about 36% α and 64% β is reached, which has a rotation of +52.7°. Why the others are wrong: Glucose does not decompose; water is not an oxidant; the open chain is less than 1% at equilibrium. Trap: Thinking the sugar changes identity.

qs.q: Why is the β anomer favored at equilibrium?
o: It is a different sugar entirely
It cannot convert back to the α form
qs.x: Correct: In the chair conformation, an equatorial substituent at C1 avoids steric interactions, so the β anomer is slightly lower in energy and more abundant. Why the others are wrong: Both have the same groups; they are the same sugar; interconversion is reversible. Trap: Explaining the ratio by composition rather than conformation.

qs.q: Which carbon of glucose is the anomeric carbon in the pyranose ring?
o: Correct: it becomes a hemiacetal carbon.
C5 contributes the ring oxygen's carbon.
C6 stays outside the ring as CH₂OH.
C3, in the middle of the chain
qs.x: Correct: The aldehyde carbon C1 becomes the hemiacetal (anomeric) carbon when C5's hydroxyl attacks it. Why the others are wrong: C5's OH supplies the ring oxygen; C6 remains exocyclic; C3 is unchanged. Trap: Confusing the attacking hydroxyl's carbon with the anomeric carbon.

qs.q: Why is glucose a reducing sugar but sucrose is not?
o: Sucrose contains no carbonyl or anomeric carbons at all
qs.x: Correct: A reducing sugar needs a free anomeric carbon that can open to an aldehyde. In sucrose, glucose and fructose are joined through both anomeric carbons, so neither ring can open. Why the others are wrong: Its anomeric carbons exist but are blocked; glucose has a hemiacetal; size is irrelevant. Trap: Assuming all disaccharides are nonreducing.

qs.q: Why does the rotation stop changing after about 4 hours?
o: Correct: the ratio no longer changes.
qs.x: Correct: Once the forward and reverse anomerization rates are equal, the composition and therefore the observed rotation are constant. Why the others are wrong: Glucose remains in solution; the instrument reads a value; no crystallization occurs. Trap: Reading a constant value as the end of the reaction rather than equilibrium.

passages.title: Structure, function, and reactivity of biologically relevant molecules · passage
text: Esters hydrolyze to a carboxylic acid and an alcohol. Base-catalyzed hydrolysis (saponification) is effectively irreversible because the carboxylate product is deprotonated. Acid-catalyzed hydrolysis is reversible. Aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) is an ester that hydrolyzes to salicylic acid and acetic acid, which is why old aspirin tablets smell of vinegar.
Students measured the rate of aspirin hydrolysis at 37 °C in buffers of different pH (Table 1).

qs.q: Why does hydrolysis speed up at high pH?
o: Protons catalyze faster at high pH
Proton concentration is low at high pH.
Correct: a stronger nucleophile is present.
The ester becomes nonpolar at high pH
Polarity is not the key factor.
qs.x: Correct: Hydroxide is a far better nucleophile than water, so it attacks the ester carbonyl directly and the rate rises steeply with pH. Why the others are wrong: Protons are scarce at high pH; polarity is not the issue; the ionized form is more soluble. Trap: Assuming acid catalysis dominates at every pH.

qs.q: Why does lowering the temperature slow hydrolysis so much?
o: Fewer collisions exceed the activation energy
Correct: rate constants fall with temperature.
The pH changes to 2 at low temperature
Aspirin becomes a different compound when cold
qs.x: Correct: The Arrhenius relation means the fraction of collisions with enough energy falls sharply as temperature drops, so the rate constant falls from 0.085 to 0.011 h⁻¹. Why the others are wrong: Water is liquid; pH is buffered; aspirin is unchanged. Trap: Looking for a phase or chemical change rather than kinetics.

qs.q: How many hours are needed for 75% of aspirin to hydrolyze at pH 7.4 and 37 °C?
o: This is half of one half-life.
qs.x: Correct: After one half-life 50% remains, and after two half-lives 25% remains, so 75% has hydrolyzed in about 16.4 hours. Why the others are wrong: Each uses the wrong number of half-lives. Trap: Confusing the fraction remaining with the fraction reacted.

qs.q: What are the products of aspirin hydrolysis?
o: The acyl group is acetyl, not ethyl.
qs.x: Correct: Cleaving the ester bond gives the phenol-containing salicylic acid and acetic acid, whose smell gives old tablets a vinegar odor. Why the others are wrong: No ethanol or sugar is formed; hydrolysis changes the molecule. Trap: Confusing the alcohol and acid portions of the ester.

qs.q: Why should aspirin tablets be stored in a cool, dry place?
o: Light converts aspirin into salicylic acid
Hydrolysis, not light, is the issue here.
Cold air removes the acetyl group
Water and heat both speed hydrolysis
qs.x: Correct: Hydrolysis requires water and accelerates with temperature, so keeping tablets dry and cool preserves the active ester. Why the others are wrong: The mechanism is hydrolysis; cold slows it; dryness slows it. Trap: Reversing the role of moisture.

passages.title: Translational motion, forces, work, energy, and equilibrium in living systems · passage
text: A centrifuge spins samples in a circle of radius r at angular speed ω. Particles experience a centripetal acceleration a = ω²r directed toward the axis. Relative centrifugal force (RCF, or "g-force") is this acceleration divided by g. Sedimentation rate rises with RCF, so larger accelerations separate smaller particles.
A laboratory rotor has a radius of 0.10 m at the tube bottom. Samples were spun at different speeds and the time for a marker protein to pellet was recorded (Table 1). Note 1 rpm = 2π/60 rad/s.

qs.q: Why does RCF rise fourfold when speed doubles?
o: RCF depends on the radius squared
Then doubling would only double it.
qs.x: Correct: a = ω²r, so doubling the angular speed multiplies the acceleration by four, as seen from 1,006 to 4,023 × g. Why the others are wrong: Radius is fixed; the dependence is quadratic; acceleration does not depend on mass. Trap: Assuming a linear relation.

qs.q: What is the centripetal acceleration at 6,000 rpm?
o: This drops a factor of ten.
qs.x: Correct: a = ω²r = (628)² × 0.10 ≈ 394,000 × 0.10 ≈ 39,400 m/s², which is about 4,000 × g. Why the others are wrong: Each omits the square or a factor. Trap: Forgetting to square the angular speed.

qs.q: In which direction does the net force on a sedimenting particle point?
o: Correct: centripetal force keeps it on its circular path.
Gravity is small compared with the centrifugal effect.
Away from the axis, pushing the particle out
There is no outward real force.
qs.x: Correct: Circular motion requires a net inward (centripetal) force; particles pellet outward because the liquid cannot supply enough inward force for the denser particles. Why the others are wrong: The "centrifugal force" is not a real force in an inertial frame; the net force is inward. Trap: Treating the outward sensation as a force.

qs.q: Why does pelleting time fall as RCF rises?
o: Higher speeds lower the liquid's viscosity to zero
The tube becomes shorter at high speed
Particles become denser at high speed
qs.x: Correct: Sedimentation velocity is proportional to the applied acceleration, so a 16-fold higher RCF pellets the protein in about one-sixteenth of the time. Why the others are wrong: Viscosity, geometry and density do not change. Trap: Looking for a change in the particles rather than in the field.

qs.q: Two proteins have the same mass but different shapes. Which will sediment faster?
o: Both sediment at exactly the same rate
The more compact one, with less drag
Correct: shape affects the friction coefficient.
The more elongated one, since it is longer
qs.x: Correct: Sedimentation depends on mass, buoyancy and the frictional drag coefficient, which is smaller for compact shapes, so the compact protein moves faster. Why the others are wrong: Elongated shapes have higher drag; shape matters; salt is not required. Trap: Considering mass alone.

passages.title: How light and sound interact with matter · passage
text: In the Kowalski laboratory, researchers measured dehydrogenase activity in a liver homogenate by following production of NADH, which absorbs light at 340 nm with a molar extinction coefficient of 6,220 M⁻¹cm⁻¹, whereas NAD⁺ does not absorb appreciably at this wavelength. The homogenate was diluted 50-fold in assay buffer before use, and 1 mL reactions in a 1 cm cuvette contained saturating substrate and NAD⁺ at 25 °C. Absorbance at 340 nm was recorded every minute. A blank containing all components except substrate was run in parallel to correct for non-enzymatic changes. The initial linear region of the progress curve was used to calculate velocity. The researchers wished to report the activity of the undiluted homogenate and to compare it with a published value from a different laboratory. The spectrophotometer was zeroed against buffer, and all readings fell within the instrument's linear range. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: What is the change in A340 of the sample between 0 and 2 minutes, according to Table 1?
o: 0.124 is the change per minute, not over 2 minutes.
0.299 is the 2-minute reading itself; you still need to subtract the 0.05 starting value.
qs.x: A(2 min) − A(0 min) = 0.299 − 0.05 = 0.249. Trap: Subtracting the 0 min reading from the 3 min reading (0.423 - 0.05 = 0.373) instead of the 2 min reading.

qs.q: Why is a blank lacking substrate included?
o: To ensure the enzyme is saturated
A blank without substrate can't show whether the enzyme is saturated.
To increase the extinction coefficient of NADH
The extinction coefficient is a fixed property of NADH; a blank can't change it.
To detect absorbance changes that occur without the enzyme-catalyzed reaction
A blank doesn't convert anything; it measures background change.
qs.x: The blank accounts for background drift (e.g., contaminating reductants, instrument drift) independent of the reaction under study. Trap: Believing the blank saturates the enzyme or raises the signal, when its purpose is to reveal non-enzymatic absorbance change.

qs.q: Using Beer–Lambert, what is the initial rate of NADH formation in the cuvette (µM/min), and what activity does the undiluted homogenate have (µM/min)?
o: 20 µM/min in the cuvette; 20 µM/min in the undiluted homogenate
This forgets to multiply by the 50-fold dilution for the homogenate.
0.02 µM/min in the cuvette; 1 µM/min in the undiluted homogenate
0.02 µM/min misplaces the decimal; ΔA per min ÷ 6220 M⁻¹cm⁻¹ gives about 20 µM/min.
1000 µM/min in the cuvette; 50000 µM/min in the undiluted homogenate
1000 µM/min in the cuvette multiplies by 50 one time too many.
20 µM/min in the cuvette; 1000 µM/min in the undiluted homogenate
qs.x: Rate = (ΔA/min)/(ε·l) = 0.1244/6220 = 20 µM/min in the cuvette. Multiply by the 50-fold dilution to get 1000 µM/min for the undiluted homogenate. Trap: Forgetting the 50-fold dilution and reporting the cuvette rate of 20 µM/min as the activity of the undiluted homogenate.

qs.q: Which statement about this assay is INCORRECT?
o: NADH absorbs at 340 nm while NAD⁺ does not
This is true: only NADH absorbs at 340 nm.
Substrate must be saturating for the rate to approximate Vₘₐₓ
This is true: saturating substrate makes the rate approach Vₘₐₓ.
Both NAD⁺ and NADH absorb strongly at 340 nm, so the signal reflects total coenzyme
The initial linear portion of the curve gives the most reliable velocity
This is true: the early linear part reflects the initial velocity.
qs.x: Only the reduced coenzyme absorbs at 340 nm; that selective absorbance makes the assay possible. Trap: Believing NAD⁺ also absorbs strongly at 340 nm so the signal tracks total coenzyme; only NADH absorbs there, which makes the assay work.

qs.q: Which type of assay couples an enzyme of interest to NADH oxidation so that its activity can be monitored at 340 nm?
o: A radioactive assay using ³²P-labeled ATP
A radioactive ATP assay tracks phosphate transfer, not NADH at 340 nm.
A gel assay using SDS-PAGE mobility
SDS-PAGE separates proteins by size; it doesn't measure activity over time.
Coupling PK's pyruvate to LDH and NADH use
An immunoassay using antibodies against the enzyme
An immunoassay measures how much enzyme is present, not its activity.
qs.x: Pyruvate kinase produces pyruvate; LDH then oxidizes NADH to NAD⁺, causing a decrease in A340 proportional to pyruvate kinase activity. Trap: Choosing a radioactive, gel or antibody assay, none of which links enzyme activity to NADH absorbance at 340 nm.

passages.title: Translational motion, forces, work, energy, and equilibrium in living systems · passage
text: Tendons store elastic energy. For small stretches a tendon behaves like a spring, with force F = kx and stored energy U = ½kx². In running, the Achilles tendon stretches during landing and recoils during push-off, returning much of the stored energy and lowering the metabolic cost of running.
Researchers measured force and elongation in cadaver Achilles tendons (Table 1), then estimated energy return during a running stride.

qs.q: How much energy is stored in tendon 1 at peak load?
o: This drops a factor of ten.
This omits the factor of ½.
This multiplies force by elongation in millimeters.
qs.x: Correct: U = ½kx² = ½ × 180,000 N/m × (0.010 m)² = 9.0 J. Why the others are wrong: Each omits the ½ or mishandles units. Trap: Using millimeters instead of meters.

qs.q: Why does tendon elasticity lower the cost of running?
o: It removes the need for muscle contraction
It prevents the foot from touching the ground
Stored energy is returned at push-off
It converts heat into mechanical work
Heat is not recovered this way.
qs.x: Correct: Energy stored while the tendon stretches during landing is released during recoil, so muscles supply less of the work needed for each stride. Why the others are wrong: The foot lands; heat is not converted back; muscles still contract. Trap: Treating elastic storage as a replacement for muscle work.

qs.q: Which tendon is stiffest, and what does that mean?
o: Tendon 1, which has the largest peak force
Tendon 2, which stretches least per newton
qs.x: Correct: Stiffness is force per unit elongation; tendon 2 has the highest k, so it elongates least for a given force. Why the others are wrong: More stretch means less stiff; peak force alone is not stiffness. Trap: Equating strength with stiffness.

qs.q: What is the unit of the spring constant k?
o: That is force expressed differently but not the standard form here.
This is a rate of force change.
qs.x: Correct: k has units of N/m, since F = kx. Why the others are wrong: N·m is energy or torque; N/s is a rate. Trap: Confusing the units of stiffness and energy.

qs.q: Why does the energy returned by a real tendon fall short of ½kx²?
o: The tendon gains mass during loading
Correct: tendons are not perfectly elastic.
qs.x: Correct: Real tendons show hysteresis: the unloading curve lies below the loading curve, and the difference appears as heat, so about 90–93% of stored energy is returned. Why the others are wrong: Energy is conserved; mass is constant; forces were measured. Trap: Assuming biological springs are ideal.

passages.title: Transmission of heritable information and processes that increase genetic diversity · passage
text: Hemophilia A is caused by loss-of-function variants in F8, a gene on the X chromosome that encodes clotting factor VIII. Men with one variant allele and no normal copy have factor VIII activity below about 40% of normal and bleed excessively; activity below 1% causes spontaneous joint bleeding. About 45% of severe cases are caused by a single recurrent inversion in intron 22 of F8, which can be detected with a long-range PCR test.

Women with one variant allele are carriers. In each of their cells one X chromosome is randomly silenced early in development, so a carrier's liver cells form a mosaic in which some cells make factor VIII and others do not. Most carriers have about half the normal activity and no symptoms, but some have low enough activity to bleed after surgery or childbirth.

A clinic studied one family. Man I-1 had severe hemophilia A caused by the intron 22 inversion. His daughter II-2 married an unaffected man, II-3. They have two sons (III-1 and III-2) and three daughters (III-3, III-4 and III-5). III-5 had heavy bleeding after a tooth extraction. The clinic measured factor VIII activity and ran the inversion test on each family member (Table 1).

Knowing a woman's carrier status matters for planning. A carrier who is pregnant may choose prenatal testing, and her delivery can be managed to lower the risk of bleeding in an affected newborn, for example by avoiding instruments that can injure the baby's head. Carriers with low factor VIII levels can be treated with desmopressin or factor concentrate before surgery. For these reasons the clinic offered testing to every woman in the family, including those with no symptoms, and explained the results to each one in a separate genetic counseling visit.\nT In a survey of 300 women from other families whose carrier status was known from DNA testing, factor VIII activity ranged from 22% to 116% in carriers and from 55% to 180% in non-carriers.

qs.q: Why is II-2 certain to be a carrier even before testing?
o: Hemophilia A is inherited as a dominant trait
She received her father's only X chromosome
Correct: fathers pass their X to every daughter.
Her mother must also have been a carrier
The mother's status does not matter here.
Her factor VIII level is near half of normal
She was certain to be a carrier before any test.
qs.x: Correct: A man has one X chromosome, and every daughter receives it, so I-1's daughter must carry his F8 inversion. Her test result (one copy, 47% activity) confirms this. Why the others are wrong: The disorder is X-linked recessive, not dominant; her mother's genotype is irrelevant because the variant came from her father; the question asks why she was certain before testing. Trap: Basing an obligate-carrier conclusion on a lab value instead of on the pattern of inheritance.

qs.q: What is the most likely reason that III-5 has bleeding symptoms?
o: Her normal X was silenced in most liver cells
Her normal F8 allele interferes with the variant protein
She inherited the inversion from both parents
Her father II-3 has no inversion.
She has Turner syndrome and so has only one X chromosome
She shows one copy plus a normal allele.
qs.x: Correct: III-5 carries one inversion and one normal allele. Random X inactivation usually leaves about half of the cells making factor VIII, but by chance the normal X was silenced in most of her liver cells, so her activity is only 14%. Why the others are wrong: Her father lacks the inversion, so she cannot be homozygous; a normal allele does not interfere with anything; the test detected one variant copy, and nothing suggests a missing X. Trap: Assuming a symptomatic female must have two variant alleles.

qs.q: If II-2 and II-3 have another child, what is the probability that the child is a son with hemophilia A?
o: Correct: 1/2 chance of a son × 1/2 chance he inherits the variant X.
This is the chance for a son, not for any child.
Only half of her sons are affected.
qs.x: Correct: The child is a son with probability 1/2, and a son inherits his mother's variant X with probability 1/2, so the chance of an affected son is 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4. Why the others are wrong: 1/8 adds a factor that does not exist; 1/2 is the risk for a son already known to be male; not every son is affected, as III-2 shows. Trap: Answering for sons when the question asks about any child.

qs.q: Based on the survey, why is factor VIII activity alone an unreliable way to tell whether a woman is a carrier?
o: Activity cannot be measured in women
It was measured in every woman in Table 1.
Factor VIII activity is normal in every carrier
Carrier and non-carrier activity ranges overlap
Correct: values from 55% to 116% fit either group.
Carriers have higher activity than non-carriers
Carrier activity is lower on average.
qs.x: Correct: Carriers ranged from 22% to 116% and non-carriers from 55% to 180%, so a woman with activity between 55% and 116% could belong to either group. III-3 (61%, no inversion) and III-4 (52%, one copy) illustrate how close the values can be. A DNA test is needed for a firm answer. Why the others are wrong: Many carriers have reduced activity; carriers average lower, not higher; the table shows the test works in women. Trap: Treating a lab value with overlapping ranges as diagnostic.

qs.q: If III-1 received gene therapy that restored normal factor VIII production in his liver, what would be true of his future daughters?
o: Half of them would be carriers
Every daughter gets his single X.
Liver therapy does not change germ cells.
They would all have hemophilia A
They also receive a normal X from their mother.
Correct: his sperm still carry the inversion.
qs.x: Correct: The therapy changes his liver cells, not his germ cells. His sperm still carry the X with the inversion, and every daughter receives that X, so all of his daughters would be carriers. Why the others are wrong: Somatic gene therapy is not inherited; daughters always receive their father's X, so the fraction is all, not half; they would also receive an X from their mother, which is normal unless she is a carrier. Trap: Assuming a somatic cure is passed to children.

passages.title: Assemblies of molecules, cells, and groups of cells · passage
text: Differential centrifugation separates cell components by size and density. A tissue homogenate is spun at increasing speeds; each pellet is collected before the supernatant is spun again faster. Marker enzymes identify which organelles are in each fraction.
Rat liver was homogenized in isotonic sucrose and spun in four steps. Activities of four marker enzymes were measured in each pellet, expressed as percent of the total activity recovered (Table 1).

qs.q: Which fraction is richest in mitochondria?
o: Correct: succinate dehydrogenase is a mitochondrial marker.
This contains microsomes from the ER.
qs.x: Correct: Succinate dehydrogenase (complex II) is in the inner mitochondrial membrane, and 84% of its activity is in P2. Why the others are wrong: P1 holds nuclei (DNA polymerase); P3 holds ER fragments (glucose-6-phosphatase); the supernatant holds soluble cytosolic enzymes such as lactate dehydrogenase. Trap: Assuming the biggest pellet holds the most important organelle.

qs.q: Why did the researchers use isotonic sucrose?
o: To supply energy to the mitochondria
Sucrose is not used by mitochondria.
To keep organelles from swelling or bursting
Correct: isotonic solution prevents osmotic damage.
To make all organelles the same density so they pellet together
Density differences are needed for separation.
The enzymes must stay active to be measured.
qs.x: Correct: Isotonic sucrose matches organelle osmolarity, so membranes stay intact and enzymes stay where they belong. Why the others are wrong: Mitochondria cannot use sucrose; equal density would prevent separation; denatured enzymes could not be assayed. Trap: Thinking sucrose is added as a nutrient.

qs.q: Which fraction would contain the most ribosome-studded membrane fragments?
o: Nuclei and unbroken cells pellet here.
Correct: rough ER forms microsomes that pellet at high speed.
qs.x: Correct: Homogenization breaks the ER into small vesicles called microsomes, which pellet only at about 100,000 g and carry glucose-6-phosphatase. Why the others are wrong: Lower speeds pellet larger organelles; microsomes are removed before the final supernatant. Trap: Confusing free ribosomes with rough ER fragments.

qs.q: Some succinate dehydrogenase appears in P1. What is the best explanation?
o: The enzyme is secreted from cells
The 1,000 g spin breaks open the mitochondria in the sample
Breaking them would release enzymes to lighter fractions.
Some mitochondria pellet with whole cells
qs.x: Correct: Differential centrifugation gives enriched, not pure, fractions; unbroken cells and clumped organelles carry some mitochondria into P1. Why the others are wrong: Nuclei lack this enzyme; it is not secreted; broken mitochondria would move to lighter fractions. Trap: Expecting perfect separation.

qs.q: Which enzyme's distribution shows that most cells were broken open?
o: Correct: a cytosolic enzyme was released.
DNA polymerase, found mostly in the P1 pellet
This shows where nuclei went, not cell breakage.
qs.x: Correct: Lactate dehydrogenase is a soluble cytosolic enzyme; 91% in the supernatant shows that most cells released their cytosol. Unbroken cells would carry it into P1. Why the others are wrong: These markers show organelle locations, not cell lysis. Trap: Choosing a marker that tracks organelles rather than cytosol.

passages.title: Structure, function, and reactivity of biologically relevant molecules · passage
text: Triacylglycerols are esters of glycerol and three fatty acids. Saponification with sodium hydroxide cleaves them to glycerol and three fatty acid salts (soaps), which are amphipathic: a nonpolar tail and an ionized carboxylate head. Above a critical concentration, soap molecules form micelles with tails inward, which solubilize grease.
Students saponified 100 g of a fat and analyzed the products (Table 1). The average molar mass of the fat was 860 g/mol.

qs.q: Why are three moles of NaOH needed per mole of fat?
o: NaOH acts as a catalyst only
Soap molecules each need three sodium ions
Each of three ester bonds is cleaved
qs.x: Correct: A triacylglycerol has three ester linkages, and base-mediated hydrolysis consumes one hydroxide per ester, giving a 1:3 ratio that matches 0.110 and 0.330 mol. Why the others are wrong: Glycerol is a product; NaOH is a reactant; each soap carries one sodium. Trap: Treating the base as a catalyst.

qs.q: Why does soap remove grease from skin?
o: Micelles trap oil in nonpolar cores
Soap chemically digests fats into glucose
Grease dissolves in water once warmed
qs.x: Correct: Soap tails dissolve in the grease while the charged heads face water, so oil is suspended as micelles and rinses away. Why the others are wrong: Soap does not digest fats; water stays polar; grease alone is insoluble. Trap: Assuming the cleaning action is chemical breakdown.

qs.q: What percentage yield of glycerol was obtained from 100 g of fat?
o: This uses the mass of glycerol directly.
Correct: 0.110 mol obtained of 0.116 mol possible.
Yield cannot exceed the theoretical amount.
qs.x: Correct: 100 g ÷ 860 g/mol = 0.116 mol of fat, which could give 0.116 mol of glycerol; 0.110 ÷ 0.116 ≈ 95%. Why the others are wrong: Mass percentage is not yield; the soap value is a different species. Trap: Comparing masses instead of moles.

qs.q: Why is a soap molecule described as amphipathic?
o: It has polar and nonpolar regions
Correct: an ionic head and a hydrocarbon tail.
It can act as an acid or a base
It dissolves in neither water nor oil
qs.x: Correct: The long hydrocarbon chain is nonpolar and the carboxylate head is charged, so the molecule interacts with both water and oil. Why the others are wrong: Amphoteric describes acid-base behavior; soap interacts with both phases; one head group is present. Trap: Confusing amphipathic with amphoteric.

qs.q: Why do soaps form scum in hard water?
o: Hard water has too few ions
Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ form insoluble salts
Hard water protonates all soap heads
Hard water is not strongly acidic.
qs.x: Correct: Divalent cations bind two carboxylate heads each, forming insoluble calcium and magnesium salts that precipitate as scum, which is why detergents with sulfonate heads are preferred. Why the others are wrong: Hard water is not acidic; soap is not volatile; hard water is ion rich. Trap: Thinking hardness acts through pH.

passages.title: Assemblies of molecules, cells, and groups of cells · passage
text: Microtubules are hollow polymers of α/β-tubulin dimers. A dimer binds GTP on its β subunit before it adds to the growing plus end, and the GTP is hydrolyzed to GDP shortly after incorporation. As long as the newest dimers still hold GTP, the end forms a stable cap and growth continues. If hydrolysis catches up with the tip and the cap is lost, the GDP-bound lattice peels apart and the microtubule shrinks rapidly. This switch from growth to shrinkage is called a catastrophe, and the alternation between the two states is called dynamic instability.

Researchers attached short, stable microtubule seeds to a glass surface and added purified tubulin with GTP or with GMPCPP, a GTP analog that is hydrolyzed about 10,000 times more slowly. They recorded individual microtubules by microscopy for 20 minutes and measured growth and shrinkage rates and the number of catastrophes per minute of growth. Some trials included paclitaxel (taxol) or nocodazole, two drugs used to study microtubules (Table 1).

The researchers also examined the ends of shrinking microtubules by electron microscopy. In the GTP and nocodazole samples, the protofilaments at shrinking ends curled outward like the peeled skin of a banana, which is the shape expected when GDP-tubulin is released from the lattice. In the taxol samples, the few shrinking ends seen had short, straight protofilaments. Because taxol binds the inside surface of the microtubule wall, they proposed that it holds the protofilaments together even after hydrolysis has occurred.\nT To link these effects to cell division, the researchers treated cultured human cells with each drug for 12 hours and counted the fraction of cells in mitosis (the mitotic index). Cells in mitosis were identified by condensed chromosomes. Untreated cells had a mitotic index of 4%; taxol-treated cells, 38%; and nocodazole-treated cells, 41%. In both drug groups, most mitotic cells had chromosomes that were condensed but not aligned at the metaphase plate.

qs.q: Why were no catastrophes observed with GMPCPP?
o: GMPCPP speeds hydrolysis at the tip
It is hydrolyzed far more slowly.
The cap is never lost without hydrolysis
Correct: the whole lattice stays GTP-like.
GMPCPP forms covalent bonds between dimers
GMPCPP blocks dimers from adding to the plus end
qs.x: Correct: A catastrophe begins when hydrolysis reaches the tip and removes the GTP cap. Because GMPCPP is hydrolyzed about 10,000 times more slowly, the end keeps a stable cap throughout the experiment. Why the others are wrong: Growth with GMPCPP (1.1 µm/min) was close to that with GTP, so addition was not blocked; tubulin dimers associate noncovalently; GMPCPP slows hydrolysis rather than speeding it. Trap: Explaining the result by a change in growth when the data show growth was normal.

qs.q: Which explanation best accounts for the effect of raising tubulin from 10 µM to 20 µM?
o: More tubulin speeds GTP hydrolysis in the lattice
More tubulin removes the need for bound GTP
Faster addition keeps a longer GTP cap at the tip
More tubulin slows shrinkage after a catastrophe
qs.x: Correct: Doubling tubulin roughly doubled the growth rate. When dimers add faster than their GTP is hydrolyzed, more GTP-tubulin accumulates at the tip, so the cap is harder to lose and catastrophes fall from 0.30 to 0.12 per minute. Why the others are wrong: Faster hydrolysis would raise, not lower, catastrophe frequency; the shrinkage rate did not change; GTP binding is still required. Trap: Overlooking the unchanged shrinkage rate in the table.

qs.q: Taxol and nocodazole have opposite effects in vitro. Why do both raise the mitotic index?
o: Spindles need microtubules that grow and shrink
Both drugs stop DNA replication in S phase
That would lower the mitotic index.
Both drugs speed cells into mitosis
The cells are stuck, not speeded up.
Both drugs cause the spindle to fall apart completely
qs.x: Correct: To capture and align chromosomes, spindle microtubules must keep growing and shrinking. Taxol nearly freezes them (shrinkage 4 µm/min, 0.02 catastrophes per minute) and nocodazole keeps them short (growth 0.4 µm/min), so in both cases chromosomes fail to align and cells pile up in mitosis. Why the others are wrong: Taxol does the opposite of depolymerizing; blocking S phase would keep cells out of mitosis; the unaligned chromosomes show arrest, not faster entry. Trap: Assuming that two drugs with the same outcome must work the same way.

qs.q: Which cell-cycle control is most likely holding the drug-treated cells in mitosis?
o: The DNA damage checkpoint at G2/M
Those cells would not enter mitosis.
Correct: it waits for every kinetochore to attach.
qs.x: Correct: Condensed chromosomes that have not aligned at the metaphase plate show that cells entered mitosis and stopped before anaphase. The spindle assembly checkpoint prevents anaphase until every kinetochore is properly attached to spindle microtubules. Why the others are wrong: The G1 restriction point and the G2/M DNA damage checkpoint act before mitosis begins; cytokinesis comes after anaphase. Trap: Picking a checkpoint by name without matching it to the stage the cells are in.

qs.q: A new compound, Z, is proposed to act like taxol. Which in vitro result would best support this?
o: Growth speeds up when tubulin is doubled
The mitotic index of cultured cells rises
Shrinkage slows and catastrophes become rare
Correct: this matches the taxol row.
Growth slows and catastrophes become frequent
qs.x: Correct: In Table 1, taxol's signature is a sharp drop in shrinkage rate (25 to 4 µm/min) and in catastrophe frequency (0.30 to 0.02 per minute). Seeing the same pattern with compound Z would support a taxol-like stabilizing action. Why the others are wrong: Slower growth with more catastrophes is the nocodazole pattern; a higher mitotic index cannot tell the two mechanisms apart; faster growth at higher tubulin is normal behavior. Trap: Choosing a result that is consistent with the claim but also with the opposite claim.

passages.title: Nervous and endocrine systems and how they coordinate organ systems · passage
text: Parathyroid hormone (PTH) raises blood Ca²⁺ by stimulating bone resorption, increasing renal Ca²⁺ reabsorption, reducing renal phosphate reabsorption, and stimulating the kidney to make calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D), which increases intestinal Ca²⁺ absorption. Low Ca²⁺ is detected by the calcium-sensing receptor on parathyroid cells.
An endocrine service reviewed four patients with abnormal Ca²⁺ (Table 1). Reference ranges: Ca²⁺ 8.5–10.2 mg/dL, PTH 15–65 pg/mL, phosphate 2.5–4.5 mg/dL.

qs.q: Why is phosphate low in Patient A?
o: PTH stimulates phosphate absorption in the gut
Calcitriol raises gut phosphate absorption, not lower it.
High Ca²⁺ blocks phosphate release from bone
qs.x: Correct: PTH inhibits proximal tubule phosphate reabsorption, so excess PTH causes phosphate loss in urine. Why the others are wrong: Gut absorption would raise phosphate; adenomas do not store phosphate; bone resorption releases phosphate. Trap: Expecting Ca²⁺ and phosphate to move in the same direction.

qs.q: What explains high PTH with low Ca²⁺ in Patient B?
o: This raises Ca²⁺ and lowers PTH.
A parathyroid adenoma secretes excess PTH
An adenoma would cause high Ca²⁺.
qs.x: Correct: In kidney disease, phosphate builds up and calcitriol falls, so Ca²⁺ drops and the parathyroids respond by secreting more PTH. Why the others are wrong: Adenomas cause hypercalcemia; removal lowers PTH; PTHrP suppresses PTH. Trap: Calling any high PTH an adenoma.

qs.q: Why is PTH low in Patient C?
o: The lung tumor has spread to and destroyed the parathyroids
There is no evidence of destruction.
qs.x: Correct: PTH-related peptide acts on PTH receptors and raises Ca²⁺; the parathyroid calcium-sensing receptors detect the high Ca²⁺ and stop PTH secretion. Why the others are wrong: Glands are not destroyed; standard assays do not detect PTHrP as PTH; kidney failure raises PTH. Trap: Expecting PTH to rise whenever Ca²⁺ is high.

qs.q: What is the most likely cause of Patient D's findings?
qs.x: Correct: Low PTH with low Ca²⁺ and high phosphate after neck surgery suggests the parathyroid glands were removed or damaged. Why the others are wrong: Vitamin D excess raises Ca²⁺; secondary hyperparathyroidism raises PTH; PTHrP raises Ca²⁺. Trap: Missing the clue in the notes column.

qs.q: Which treatment would best correct Patient D's Ca²⁺ in the long term?
o: Correct: bypasses the missing PTH step.
A drug that blocks the calcium-sensing receptor
Few parathyroid cells are left to respond.
Removal of the remaining parathyroid tissue
qs.x: Correct: Without PTH, the kidney makes little calcitriol, so oral Ca²⁺ is poorly absorbed. Giving active vitamin D with Ca²⁺ restores intestinal uptake. Why the others are wrong: Calcium alone is poorly absorbed; receptor drugs need functional glands; removing tissue worsens the problem. Trap: Overlooking PTH's role in activating vitamin D.

passages.title: Transmission of heritable information and processes that increase genetic diversity · passage
text: In Drosophila melanogaster, the recessive alleles b (black body), pr (purple eyes) and vg (vestigial wings) lie on chromosome 2. A student crossed females heterozygous at all three loci (b pr vg / b⁺ pr⁺ vg⁺, all wild-type alleles on one homolog) with males homozygous recessive at all three (b pr vg / b pr vg). Male Drosophila do not undergo crossing over, but this does not affect a testcross because the male contributes only recessive alleles.

The 2,000 progeny were classified by phenotype (Table 1). Map distances were calculated as the percentage of recombinant offspring between each pair of genes, counting double crossovers in both intervals.

qs.q: Which two classes are the double-crossover progeny?
o: Correct: they are the two least frequent classes.
These arise from a single crossover between b and pr.
Wild type and black, purple, vestigial
These are the most frequent parental classes.
These arise from a single crossover between pr and vg.
qs.x: Correct: Double crossovers require two independent exchange events and are therefore the rarest classes (16 + 16). Why the others are wrong: The most common classes are parental; the remaining pairs are single-crossover products. Trap: Picking the rarest single class rather than the rarest reciprocal pair.

qs.q: Comparing the parental and double-crossover classes, which gene is in the middle?
o: vg, because vestigial is the most common phenotype
Phenotype frequency does not identify the middle gene.
b, because black appears in the most classes
Frequency of a trait does not identify gene order.
The order cannot be found without a reciprocal cross
A three-point testcross alone gives the order.
pr, the only allele that switches
Correct: double crossovers swap the middle gene relative to the outer two.
qs.x: Correct: Parental b pr vg becomes double-crossover b pr⁺ vg: only pr changes, so pr lies between b and vg. Why the others are wrong: Gene order comes from comparing parental and double-crossover classes, not from how common a phenotype is, and no reciprocal cross is needed. Trap: Assuming genes are in the order they are named.

qs.q: What is the map distance between b and pr?
o: This counts the pr–vg recombinants instead.
This is the full b–vg distance.
qs.x: Correct: Recombinants between b and pr are the single crossovers in that interval (120) plus the double crossovers (32): 152 / 2,000 = 7.6%. Why the others are wrong: 6.0 leaves out double crossovers; 23.0 is the pr–vg interval; 30.6 is the b–vg total. Trap: Forgetting that each double crossover is also a crossover in each interval.

qs.q: The expected frequency of double crossovers, if the two intervals were independent, is 0.076 × 0.23 ≈ 0.0175. What does the observed frequency of 0.016 suggest?
o: Strong positive interference that prevents all double crossovers
Double crossovers did occur at near the expected rate.
The genes are on different chromosomes and assort independently
Recombination frequencies well under 50% show linkage.
Correct: coefficient of coincidence ≈ 0.91, so interference ≈ 0.09.
Crossing over happened in males as well as females
Males contribute only recessive alleles here.
qs.x: Correct: Coincidence = observed / expected = 0.016 / 0.0175 ≈ 0.91, and interference = 1 − 0.91 ≈ 0.09, a small effect. Why the others are wrong: Complete interference would give zero double crossovers; frequencies below 50% mean linkage; and male crossing over is irrelevant in this testcross. Trap: Reading any shortfall of double crossovers as complete interference.

qs.q: Why was a testcross to a triple-recessive male used rather than a cross between two heterozygotes?
o: It makes crossing over happen more often in the heterozygous female
The tester does not change the female's recombination rate.
Offspring phenotypes reveal the female's alleles
Correct: the tester adds only recessive alleles.
It ensures all offspring are female and easier to score
It removes the need to count large numbers of offspring
Large counts are still needed for accurate frequencies.
qs.x: Correct: Because the male contributes b pr vg, every recessive phenotype reflects the female's gamete, so recombinant gametes can be counted directly. Why the others are wrong: The tester does not alter recombination, sample size still matters, and both sexes are produced. Trap: Thinking the tester parent influences recombination.

passages.title: Nervous and endocrine systems and how they coordinate organ systems · passage
text: During fasting, falling glucose lowers insulin and raises glucagon. Glucagon acts on the liver through a Gs-coupled receptor, raising cAMP. In the first day, glycogenolysis supplies most glucose; after that, gluconeogenesis from lactate, glycerol and amino acids becomes the main source. With prolonged fasting, the liver also makes ketone bodies from fatty acids, and the brain gradually uses them as fuel.
Healthy volunteers fasted for 5 days under medical supervision. Blood samples were collected each morning (Table 1).

qs.q: Why does glucose stay near 65 mg/dL rather than continuing to fall?
o: Muscle releases free glucose from its glycogen
Glycogen stores increase as the fast goes on
Glycogen is depleted in about a day.
Insulin secretion rises to protect the brain
Gluconeogenesis and ketone use spare glucose
Correct: production rises and demand falls.
qs.x: Correct: The liver makes glucose from lactate, glycerol and amino acids, while rising ketones let the brain use less glucose, so glucose levels off. Why the others are wrong: Glycogen falls; insulin drops; muscle cannot release free glucose. Trap: Assuming glycogen is the main source throughout a fast.

qs.q: Why do ketone bodies rise steeply by day 3?
o: The brain releases ketone bodies into the blood
qs.x: Correct: Low insulin and high glucagon activate lipolysis; fatty acids reach the liver, where β-oxidation produces acetyl-CoA that is converted into ketone bodies. Why the others are wrong: The brain uses but does not make ketones; ketones come from fat; insulin is low. Trap: Thinking the brain makes its own ketones.

qs.q: Which second messenger mediates glucagon's effects in the liver?
o: This is used by nitric oxide signaling.
Correct: glucagon receptors couple to Gs.
qs.x: Correct: Glucagon activates Gs, adenylyl cyclase and cAMP, which activates PKA. Why the others are wrong: cGMP is used by NO; IP₃ is a Gq messenger; IRS belongs to the insulin pathway. Trap: Mixing up the second messengers of different receptors.

qs.q: Why is the brain's use of ketone bodies important for survival during prolonged fasting?
o: It allows the brain to use fatty acids directly
Fatty acids do not cross into the brain well.
It spares protein used for gluconeogenesis
Correct: less muscle is broken down.
qs.x: Correct: Less glucose demand means less gluconeogenesis from amino acids, which preserves muscle protein during a long fast. Why the others are wrong: Fatty acids are not a main brain fuel; insulin remains low; glycogen is not refilled. Trap: Forgetting the protein cost of gluconeogenesis.

qs.q: Which change would be expected in urinary nitrogen between day 1 and day 5?
o: It falls as protein breakdown slows
It rises steadily throughout the fast
It does not change during fasting
qs.x: Correct: Early in a fast, amino acids supply gluconeogenesis and urinary nitrogen is high; as ketones replace glucose in the brain, protein breakdown and nitrogen loss fall. Why the others are wrong: Nitrogen loss falls later; it does not reach zero; it does change. Trap: Assuming catabolism increases steadily the longer one fasts.

passages.title: Transmission of heritable information and processes that increase genetic diversity · passage
text: Sickle cell disease is caused by homozygosity for the HbS allele of the β-globin gene (HBB). Heterozygotes (HbAS) are largely healthy and are partly protected against severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria. Researchers screened 1,000 randomly selected newborns at a regional hospital in a malaria-endemic area using hemoglobin electrophoresis.

They found 640 HbAA, 330 HbAS and 30 HbSS newborns. The team compared these counts with the counts expected under Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium. They also screened 1,000 adults aged 20–40 years from the same region and found 590 HbAA, 404 HbAS and 6 HbSS individuals.

qs.q: What is the frequency of the HbS allele among the newborns?
o: This is the frequency of HbSS genotypes.
This is the frequency of newborns carrying any HbS allele.
qs.x: Correct: Each heterozygote carries one HbS allele and each HbSS newborn carries two: 330 + 60 = 390 alleles out of 2,000, so q = 0.195. Why the others are wrong: 0.165 omits homozygotes; 0.36 is a carrier-or-affected proportion; 0.03 is a genotype frequency. Trap: Confusing genotype frequency with allele frequency.

qs.q: Using q = 0.195, how many HbAS newborns would be expected under Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium?
o: This is q² × 1,000, the expected HbSS count.
This is pq × 1,000, missing the factor of 2.
This is p² × 1,000, the expected HbAA count.
qs.x: Correct: 2pq = 2 × 0.805 × 0.195 ≈ 0.314, or about 314 newborns, close to the observed 330. Why the others are wrong: 38 and 648 are the other genotype expectations; 157 forgets the factor of two. Trap: Dropping the 2 in 2pq.

qs.q: Compared with newborns, adults have more HbAS and far fewer HbSS individuals. Which explanation best fits?
o: Selection against HbSS and for HbAS
Correct: heterozygote advantage and HbSS mortality shift adult counts.
Nonrandom mating among the adults who were screened
Mating affects offspring genotypes, not survival of the adults themselves.
Genetic drift: random changes in a small adult sample
Samples of 1,000 make large chance shifts unlikely.
New mutations converting HbAA to HbAS during childhood
Somatic changes do not alter inherited HBB genotype.
qs.x: Correct: Genotype frequencies change between birth and adulthood only if survival differs. HbSS children often die young without care, while HbAS children survive malaria better. This is balancing selection maintaining the allele. Why the others are wrong: Drift is unlikely with large samples; mutation does not convert genotypes in a lifetime; and mating patterns affect the next generation, not survival. Trap: Invoking nonrandom mating whenever genotype frequencies depart from expectation.

qs.q: Which feature of the study design limits conclusions about selection?
o: The adults were too young to have reached reproductive age
Adults aged 20–40 are of reproductive age.
Electrophoresis cannot separate hemoglobin A from S
Electrophoresis does separate HbA and HbS.
Different people were screened at birth and in adulthood
Correct: cross-sectional groups may differ for reasons besides survival.
Screening newborns at random introduces selection bias
qs.x: Correct: Comparing two different cross-sectional samples assumes that adults born 20–40 years ago started with the same genotype frequencies as today's newborns, and that migration has not changed the population. A cohort followed from birth would be stronger. Why the others are wrong: Electrophoresis distinguishes HbA and HbS; random selection is a strength; and the adults are of reproductive age. Trap: Treating two snapshots as if they followed the same people.

qs.q: Why are HbAS individuals partly protected from severe falciparum malaria?
o: Heterozygotes produce antibodies against all Plasmodium species
Protection is not due to a special antibody response.
HbS binds the parasite directly and prevents it from entering cells
HbS does not block invasion directly.
HbAS red cells lack the receptors that all parasites need
Plasmodium falciparum can still invade HbAS cells.
Infected HbAS cells sickle and are cleared
Correct: early sickling and clearance limit parasite growth.
qs.x: Correct: Parasite metabolism lowers O₂ inside infected HbAS cells, promoting HbS polymerization and sickling. Sickled infected cells are removed by the spleen, limiting parasite growth. Why the others are wrong: HbS does not block invasion, the cells still have the required receptors, and no special antibody is made. Trap: Confusing sickle trait protection with Duffy-negative protection against P. vivax.

passages.title: Translational motion, forces, work, energy, and equilibrium in living systems · passage
text: Static equilibrium requires both zero net force and zero net torque. In analyzing the spine, the erector spinae muscles act at a small angle to the spine and a short distance from the lumbosacral joint, while the weight of the upper body and any held load act at much longer horizontal distances when a person bends forward.
Researchers modeled a 70-kg person lifting a 20-kg box with the trunk bent 60° forward. Distances are horizontal from the lumbosacral joint (Table 1).

qs.q: What muscle force balances the upper body weight alone?
o: This multiplies instead of dividing by the lever arm.
qs.x: Correct: F × 5.0 = 446 N × 25 cm, so F ≈ 2,230 N. Why the others are wrong: 446 N is the weight; 89 N inverts the ratio; the last multiplies wrongly. Trap: Inverting the lever arm ratio.

qs.q: Including the 20-kg box, what total muscle force is needed?
o: This is the box term alone.
This omits the box's lever arm.
qs.x: Correct: The box contributes (196 N × 45 cm) ÷ 5.0 cm ≈ 1,764 N, giving about 3,990 N in total. Why the others are wrong: Each omits a term or a lever arm. Trap: Adding weights instead of torques.

qs.q: Why does bending forward greatly increase the load on back muscles?
o: Horizontal lever arms grow as the trunk tilts
Gravity becomes stronger closer to the ground
Muscles lose half their strength when bent
Strength is not halved by posture.
qs.x: Correct: Torque equals force times horizontal distance from the joint; tilting moves the body's and the load's centers of mass farther from the spine, so muscle force must rise. Why the others are wrong: Weight and gravity do not change; muscle strength is not posture-halved. Trap: Looking for a change in weight rather than geometry.

qs.q: Why is lifting with the knees bent and the load close to the body safer?
o: It increases the muscle lever arm greatly
It removes the need for muscle force
It lowers the weight of the load
It shortens the load's lever arm
Correct: less torque at the spine.
qs.x: Correct: Holding the load near the body reduces its horizontal distance from the lumbosacral joint, which directly reduces the required muscle force and joint compression. Why the others are wrong: The muscle lever arm is fixed by anatomy; force is still needed; weight is constant. Trap: Thinking posture changes the muscle's own lever arm.

qs.q: What does the large muscle force imply about the compressive force on the lumbar disc?
o: It is zero because torques balance
Torque balance does not remove force.
Correct: muscle force and body weight both compress.
It acts upward, pulling the spine apart
It equals the weight of the box
qs.x: Correct: The vertical forces include the muscle force pulling down along the spine plus the upper body and load weights, so disc compression exceeds the muscle force. Why the others are wrong: Compression is much larger than the load; balanced torques do not imply zero force; the disc is compressed. Trap: Confusing zero net torque with zero force.

r: Horizontal distance to upper body center of mass

passages.title: How light and sound interact with matter · passage
text: In the Petrov laboratory, researchers measured dehydrogenase activity in a liver homogenate by following production of NADH, which absorbs light at 340 nm with a molar extinction coefficient of 6,220 M⁻¹cm⁻¹, whereas NAD⁺ does not absorb appreciably at this wavelength. The homogenate was diluted 50-fold in assay buffer before use, and 1 mL reactions in a 1 cm cuvette contained saturating substrate and NAD⁺ at 25 °C. Absorbance at 340 nm was recorded every minute. A blank containing all components except substrate was run in parallel to correct for non-enzymatic changes. The initial linear region of the progress curve was used to calculate velocity. The researchers wished to report the activity of the undiluted homogenate and to compare it with a published value from a different laboratory. The spectrophotometer was zeroed against buffer, and all readings fell within the instrument's linear range. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

qs.q: What is the change in A340 of the sample between 0 and 2 minutes, according to Table 1?
o: 0.187 is the change per minute, not over 2 minutes.
0.423 is the 2-minute reading itself; you still need to subtract 0.05.
qs.x: A(2 min) − A(0 min) = 0.423 − 0.05 = 0.373. Trap: Reporting 0.187, the change per minute, or the 2-minute absorbance of 0.423 without subtracting the 0.05 starting value.

qs.q: Why is a blank lacking substrate included?
o: A blank doesn't convert anything; it measures background change.
To increase the extinction coefficient of NADH
The extinction coefficient is fixed; a blank can't change it.
To detect absorbance changes that occur without the enzyme-catalyzed reaction
To ensure the enzyme is saturated
A blank without substrate can't show whether the enzyme is saturated.
qs.x: The blank accounts for background drift (e.g., contaminating reductants, instrument drift) independent of the reaction under study. Trap: Thinking the blank supplies the NADH or sets saturation, rather than showing the signal drift occurring without the enzyme reaction.

qs.q: Using Beer–Lambert, what is the initial rate of NADH formation in the cuvette (µM/min), and what activity does the undiluted homogenate have (µM/min)?
o: 30 µM/min in the cuvette; 30 µM/min in the undiluted homogenate
This forgets to multiply by the 50-fold dilution for the homogenate.
0.03 µM/min in the cuvette; 1.5 µM/min in the undiluted homogenate
0.03 µM/min misplaces the decimal; 0.1866 ÷ 6220 M⁻¹cm⁻¹ is about 30 µM/min.
1500 µM/min in the cuvette; 75000 µM/min in the undiluted homogenate
1500 µM/min in the cuvette multiplies by 50 one time too many.
30 µM/min in the cuvette; 1500 µM/min in the undiluted homogenate
qs.x: Rate = (ΔA/min)/(ε·l) = 0.1866/6220 = 30 µM/min in the cuvette. Multiply by the 50-fold dilution to get 1500 µM/min for the undiluted homogenate. Trap: Forgetting to multiply by the 50-fold dilution, giving 30 µM/min for the undiluted homogenate, or misplacing the decimal in the unit conversion.

qs.q: Which statement about this assay is INCORRECT?
o: NADH absorbs at 340 nm while NAD⁺ does not
This is true: only NADH absorbs at 340 nm.
Both NAD⁺ and NADH absorb strongly at 340 nm, so the signal reflects total coenzyme
The initial linear portion of the curve gives the most reliable velocity
This is true: the early linear part reflects the initial velocity.
Substrate must be saturating for the rate to approximate Vₘₐₓ
This is true: saturating substrate makes the rate approach Vₘₐₓ.
qs.x: Only the reduced coenzyme absorbs at 340 nm; that selective absorbance makes the assay possible. Trap: Choosing the statement that NADH absorbs but NAD⁺ does not, which is true, rather than the false claim that both coenzymes absorb at 340 nm.
